News.title: How Labour conference will be an opportunity for Burnham to put the party on an election footing
News.content:
POLITICS UNWRAPPED How Labour conference will be an opportunity for Burnham to put the party on an election footing







Next

AHEAD of his first trip to the United Nations this week, Andy Burnham was warned by aides the experience would be the political equivalent of “white water rafting”.

You hurtle through a manic gladhanding of fellow leaders while trying to avoid crashing into diplomatic rocks.



The most precarious section is inevitably tangling with Donald Trump, whose sheer force of personality reduces other premiers to passengers in their own meeting.

Paddling in the opposite direction is not advised – and can be downright dangerous.



That the PM avoided being chewed up and spat out by the erratic President was banked as a win by No10.

While Trump’s mauling of the “ridiculous” Chagos deal grabbed the headlines, Burnham’s team played up the firm defence of the Falkland Islands he gave behind closed doors.



The White House was left in no doubt about Britain’s unwavering position on the islands, sources say.

But senior insiders also say the President subjected Burnham to his usual shellacking over illegal immigration.

They say that Trump’s blistering criticism of countries failing to tackle migration during his main speech was primarily directed at Britain.

So while Burnham survived this time – he is after all only weeks into the job – failing to deliver could see the relationship sour. Just ask Sir Keir Starmer.



Just days after dancing around the world’s most powerful right-winger, Burnham will be on home turf at the Labour party conference in Liverpool this weekend.

Speculation had mounted that the PM could use the annual rally to galvanise the party’s membership and recharge its financial war chest ahead of an early election.

But that was before a mega-poll showed Labour would sacrifice its majority and force him into an unholy alliance with the Lib Dems, Greens and other nationalist parties.



He might want a mandate of his own, yet leading a shaky coalition with other parties calling the shots could be a gamble too far.

A No10 source said about the prospect of going to the polls early: “Not gonna happen.”

Liverpool, though, will still be an opportunity for Burnham to put Labour on an election footing – firing up activists, wooing donors and stamping his authority on the party.

And there should be no shortage of foot soldiers.

Labour expects this weekend’s gathering to be its most-attended conference ever by accreditation, in a boost for a new PM determined to show the party has its mojo back.



“Optimism” has become the buzzword among Labour chiefs in recent days, with the slogan “Hope Again” plastered across the conference.

One senior source said the gathering would be the first big opportunity to bring the party together behind the PM’s vision and put “more flesh on the bones” of the agenda he has sketched out since entering No10.

That will mean a heavy focus on giving families “breathing space” from the cost-of-living squeeze, “getting Britain believing again” and delivering “good growth in every postcode”.



There will be a string of policy announcements, although Burnham will keep his full 10-year plan under wraps until later this year.

“There’s only good things that can come out of this conference,” one long-time ally of the PM said.

Yet the Liverpool love-in will not be entirely free of awkwardness.

Labour MPs believe one of the biggest fault lines will be over North Sea oil and gas, with unions worried about protecting jobs on a collision course with environmental campaigners over projects such as Jackdaw and Rosebank

Burnham will also have to contend with some familiar faces from Labour’s recent past prowling the conference bars and fringe events.



A clutch of Starmer-era Cabinet ministers who lost their jobs in Burnham’s post-election purge are heading to Liverpool, with several booked for speeches, panels and media appearances.

And after their abrupt eviction from the Government, few would blame them for wanting to make their voices heard.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But this weekend is ultimately designed to make clear whose Labour Party it is now.

And while an early election may suddenly look a less attractive proposition, it does not mean Burnham will waste the opportunity to get his troops ready for one.

News.title: Exact date balmy 26C weather will hit parts of UK as Met Office confirms ‘final taste of summer’
News.content:
Next

WARMER weather is set to return this week with 26C temperatures forecast for parts of the country.

Met Office has confirmed these warmer conditions will offer Brits a “final taste of summer” before autumn progresses.

Temperatures in the capital are forecast to rise to 26C on Tuesday (September 29) after a wetter and cloudier start to September.



This comes as weather forecasts show “above average” temperatures for the end of September and moving into the beginning of October.



According to the Met Office: “These temperatures would be notably warm for late September and could offer a final taste of summer before autumn becomes more firmly established.”

Moving into tomorrow (September 27), Brits can expect to see balmier conditions, with warm sunshine in the south and the east forecast throughout the day.

Temperatures between the high teens and mid twenties are set to be enjoyed tomorrow at 4pm, with highs of 22C in London, 20C in Birmingham and between 18C and 19C in the north.

Monday is set for similar weather conditions, also ranging between 18C and 22C across the country.

Forecasts suggest it will be “mostly fine” on Monday before typical “wet and windy weather” arrives on Tuesday.

However, for large parts of the country, the very best of the weather this week will be on Tuesday.

London will see highs of 26C in the afternoon, alongside 25C highs in Cambridge, 24C in Birmingham, and even 25C temperatures as far north as Lincoln.



Mild conditions continue into next week as “longer drier interludes” are forecast to mark the beginning of autumn.

News.title: Betting shops ‘at heart of community life’ in Burnham’s own constituency, say voters
News.content:
Next

BETTING shops are at the heart of community life in PM Andy Burnham’s own seat — according to voters in his constituency.

They spoke out as bookies across the country blame shop closures on Labour tax hikes.



Pollsters Opinium found more than half the locals in Makerfield, Greater Manchester, believe the outlets made a positive contribution.

And one in four said they had placed a bet in the last year.



The findings come amid fears that another tax raid on gambling firms could hammer high streets and cost thousands of jobs.

Industry modelling claims higher Machine Games Duty could lead to as many as 1,470 betting shop closures, 34 casinos shutting their doors and almost 16,000 job losses.

Betting and Gaming Council Chief Executive Grainne Hurst said: “Makerfield tells a very human story about what betting shops mean to communities across Britain.

“The Prime Minister has said policies should face a ‘Makerfield test’ that if they don’t work for people here and don’t lift them up, they shouldn’t happen at all.”

Mr Burnham used the “Makerfield test” after winning the seat, saying policies that do not work for people in the constituency or “lift people up” should not happen.

Betfred founder Fred Done has also warned that further gambling tax rises in the upcoming Budget could devastate the high street betting industry.



The Sun’s Save Our Bets campaign is urging ministers not to hike betting duties at the Budget.

Chancellor John Healey will reveal his Autumn Budget on Wednesday, 28 October.

News.title: British Airways keeps Boeing 777 flying despite almost HALF the toilets being broken
News.content:
FAST AND LOOS British Airways keeps Boeing 777 flying despite almost HALF the toilets being broken







Next

BRITISH Airways is keeping a Boeing 777 flying — even though almost half its toilets are broken.

Passengers are having to queue for the loo at 30,000ft because four washrooms are locked.



Only two are working for the 84 First and Club passengers while the 170 in World Traveller class have to share three.

The plane, which does regular 11-hour flights from Heathrow to ­worldwide destinations including the US and India, also has no wifi.



In the next few days it has been scheduled to fly to and from the UK, New York, Los Angeles and San Francisco.

Passengers are not told of the problems before booking flights but get a scripted apology on landing.



One crew member said: “It’s unacceptable.

“Why are we hoodwinking passengers this way?”

Another said: “Staff are in the frontline of passengers’ upset at having splashed out on premium fares only to be offered a service that you’d be disgusted to experience on a cheap, no-frills’ carrier.”

BA said it had apologised to affected customers and “offered a gesture to help put things right”.



Sources said it hopes to repair the problem plane “in the next few days”.

News.title: Labour’s hated ‘holiday tax’ risks turning London into a tourism ‘ghost town’, top Tory warns
News.content:
Next

A PUNISHING holiday tax risks turning London into a tourism “ghost town”, a senior Tory says.

It could jeopardise the capital’s economic success if implemented by the Labour mayor Sadiq Khan.



The warning comes from Tory mayoral hopeful Sir James Cleverly after he put himself forward for the job.

He said: “I want to make sure that London is buzzing, London is vibrant, London’s attracting people, London’s contributing to the UK economy.



“The last thing we need is anything that would put that at risk, anything that would turn London into a ghost town.”

More than 20million foreign tourists visited London last year, contributing £40billion, he claimed.

He also said the PM’s “anti-London policies” were hurting the South.

The Sun has launched a Hands Off Our Hols campaign, warning it will price hard-working families out of staycations.



England’s local leaders are to get the power to introduce a fee per overnight stay.

Labour’s 10 regional mayors in England have committed to bringing in the visitor levy, but two Tory and two Reform mayors ruled out implementing the measure which could damage a city’s nightlife.

Mr Khan is enthusiastically pushing for the tourist tax to be charged at up to five per cent of the cost of a hotel room.

Trade body UKHospitality has warned it could add £100 to a family holiday.

Mr Cleverly quit Kemi Badenoch‘s top team to throw his weight behind running for London mayor.



If successful, he would be the first Tory to win the capital since Boris Johnson in 2012.

News.title: Jill Dando cops launch new probe into unsolved murder as hope CCTV could prove answers on mystery man
News.content:
Next

COPS have launched a fresh probe into the shocking unsolved murder of the adored TV star Jill Dando.

Detectives are re-examining CCTV of a mystery man who they believe could hold the key to cracking the 27-year-old case.



The Met is now using modern technology to enhance original footage from Putney Bridge Tube station, reports The Mirror.

It shows an unidentified man spotted around a mile from Jill’s Fulham home shortly after she was callously shot on her doorstep.



The force said: “In the 27 years since Jill Dando‘s murder, the investigation has been subject to numerous reviews, aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics.

“Recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology have provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station.



“This remains ongoing.”

The man, known as Man X, was filmed around 20 minutes after Jill was shot outside her home in Gowan Avenue, South West London, on April 26, 1999.



Cold-case officers are understood to have spent the past ten months finding and digitising the original footage.

It was believed to be buried among 223 boxes of material in police storage.

Now detectives hope clearer images could help establish who Man X was — and whether he was linked to the killing.

The footage is also being examined for possible links to Milorad Ulemek, a notorious Serbian paramilitary commander known as Legija.

Ulemek, a former French Foreign Legionnaire, led a unit involved in assassinations during the rule of former Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic.



A facial comparison expert previously identified similarities between Ulemek and Man X.

He said they had similar mouths, chins, hairlines and right sideburns.

Their noses and right ears were also said to be similar in shape and size.



A dent on Ulemek’s nose was also highlighted as matching one shown on a police e-fit released after Jill’s murder.

Two key witnesses have also said Ulemek resembled men they saw near the murder scene.

One woman was driving along Fulham Palace Road when she saw a man in a suit “running for his life”.

A month later, she picked out Man X in CCTV as the man she had seen.

But detectives dismissed her evidence, saying her original description did not match Man X.



Both men, however, were said to have been wearing suits and ties and had similar heights, builds and hair colour.

Jill’s neighbour Richard Hughes saw the gunman and believed he may have been carrying a mobile phone.

He said the killer “looked like” an e-fit produced by the female witness.

Another neighbour, Geoffrey Upfillbrown, also saw the killer and said the image looked “similar”, according to police notes.

A second key witness later said he was “80%” sure the man he saw near the scene was Ulemek.



Jill, 37, was ambushed from behind as she approached her front door.

She was killed instantly by a single bullet to her left temple.

At the time, Britain was bombing Serbia and Jill was one of the country’s best-known TV presenters.

She had fronted BBC shows including Crimewatch and Holiday.

Within hours of her murder, the BBC received a call claiming it was linked to a NATO attack on a Belgrade TV station.



There were also fears Jill had been targeted because she fronted a BBC appeal for Kosovan refugees 20 days before her death.

Nearly a year later, detectives focused on local man Barry George.

George, now 65, spent eight years behind bars after being convicted of Jill’s murder.

He was cleared at a retrial in 2008.

The case was moved to “inactive” in 2015 following a forensic review.



Ulemek is serving a 40-year sentence in Serbia after being convicted of helping to plan the assassinations of former Serbian president Ivan Stambolic in 2000 and prime minister Zoran Djindjic in 2003.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

George is currently facing trial over historical sex charges.

The Met investigation into Jill’s murder remains ongoing.

News.title: Afghan asylum seeker masterminded  crime ring which shipped £181million of stolen iPhones out of the UK
News.content:
PRISON CALLING Afghan asylum seeker masterminded crime ring which shipped £181million of stolen iPhones out of the UK







Next

AN AFGHAN asylum seeker masterminded a crime ring which shipped £181million of stolen iPhones out of the UK, a court heard yesterday.

Amir Khadikhel, his fellow Afghan Ismat Miakhel and Indian Mansoor Mohammed sent more than 62,000 to the Far East and Middle East using unwitting courier firms DHL and UPS.



The operation was uncovered ­following a tip-off from a victim who used the Find My Phone app to trace hers to a warehouse at Heathrow Airport.

A police raid recovered 3,000 stolen mobiles.



Suspects were later seen handing over phones and wads of cash outside a shop in North London.

A search of a London property led to phones being found under a hidden trapdoor and a further swoop recovered 299 more when some were heard ringing in sealed boxes.



Southwark crown court heard the phones had been stolen across the country.

They can be worth up to £3,700 in China because, unlike new phones, they are not subject to government restrictions.



Khadikhel’s lawyer said he came to the UK after fleeing Afghanistan in 2019, leaving behind his wife and child.

He said he was homeless and had mental health issues, and was lured into criminality by a person who housed him.

Khadikhel and Mohammed both admitted conspiring to receive ­stolen mobile phones, as well as participating in the criminal activities of an organised crime group.

Khadikhel also admitted conspiring to transfer the phones out of the UK.

Miakhel earlier admitted conspiring to receive and transfers stolen goods. Khadikhel, 35, of Wanstead, was jailed for 9½ years.



Miakhel, 33, of Walthamstow, got nine years and Mohammed, 30, of Wood Green, six years and five months.

News.title: Man denies attempted murder of two Jewish men stabbed in Golders Green
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

STAB DENIAL Man denies attempted murder of two Jewish men stabbed in Golders Green







Next

A MAN yesterday denied the attempted murder of two Jewish men who were stabbed in Golders Green.

Essa Suleiman, 45, also pleaded not guilty to attacking another man earlier the same day.

The case is no longer being treated as terrorism and Suleiman is currently being detained in Broadmoor secure psychiatric hospital, the Old Bailey heard.



Suleiman, of Camberwell, South London, is also accused of one count of possession of a bladed article in a public place following a series of attacks on April 29.



At 8.50am that day, a suspect armed with a knife arrived at an address in Great Dover Street, South London.

Ishmail Hussein received minor injuries and police carried out inquiries at an address connected to Suleiman.

Later that morning, he allegedly attacked two Jewish men in Golders Green, North London.



Shloime Rand, 34, and Norman Shine, 76, both received stab wounds.

Suleiman, a British national born in Somalia, appeared via videolink from Broadmoor hospital and spoke only to confirm his identity.

The case was adjourned for psychiatric reports and a three-week trial is due to go ahead from March 1.

The next hearing is due to be held on January 15.

News.title: 13 groups of people who automatically get free £30 NHS eye test - not all are means-tested
News.content:
13 groups of people who automatically get free £30 NHS eye test - not all are means-tested

Most people are advised to have their eyes tested every two years and those who don't qualify for free checks have to pay around £24-30 for them

View 2 Images Million of people wear glasses (Image: Getty)

Millions of people in the UK have sight problems which mean they must use glasses or some other form of eyewear. Figures show that around three in four adults wear spectacles, contact lenses or have undergone laser eye surgery.

‌



But eye tests can show a lot more than just if you are short-sighted or long-sighted and need help to correct your vision. According to Optomeyes, there are a number of major health conditions that can be identified through a test, including high blood pressure, diabetes, brain tumours, multiple sclerosis and high cholesterol.

‌



View 2 Images Millions of people can get an eye test free of charge (Image: Hiraman via Getty Images)

‌



It warns: "Your eyes are more than just windows to the world; they are windows into your health. Regular eye exams can be instrumental in identifying life-threatening conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, brain tumours, autoimmune diseases, and high cholesterol.

"By scheduling eye exams at the appropriate intervals, you can take proactive steps to protect your vision and overall well-being. Do not wait until problems arise – prioritise your eye health today."

The NHS recommends people have their eyes tested every two years but, unlike in Scotland where everyone can get a free eye test, in the rest of the UK you must pay to have it done privately unless you meet certain criteria to qualify for a free test. This typically costs between £24 and £30 depending on where you go. Asda is currently £24, Specsavers is usually £25 but currently offering it for £10, and Vision Express £30 but can include an advanced OCT 3D scan.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

However it is estimated around 30 million people qualify for free eye tests - and for many of them that does not matter how much they earn. Those with certain health conditions or who are thought to be at increased risk can also get them free of charge, alongside those with limited income.

The NHS has issued an alert on X advising people to have their eyes tested and that many might be entitled to this free of charge. These include those based on age, income and health risk - here's who qualifies:

‌



Free NHS eye tests

You're entitled to a free NHS sight test if you:

are under 16

are 16, 17 or 18 and in full-time education (this includes being taught full-time at a school, college, university or at home)

are 60 or over

are registered as partially sighted or blind

have been diagnosed with diabetes or glaucoma

are 40 or over and your mother, father, sibling or child has been diagnosed with glaucoma

have been advised by an eye doctor (ophthalmologist) that you're at risk of glaucoma

are a prisoner on leave from prison

are eligible for an NHS complex lens voucher – your optician can advise you about your entitlement

are entitled to or named on a valid NHS certificate for full help with health costs (HC2)

You're also entitled if you or your partner – including civil partner – receive, or you're under the age of 20 and the dependant of someone receiving:

Article continues below

Income-based Jobseeker's Allowance

Pension Credit Guarantee Credit

Universal Credit and meet the criteria

People named on an NHS certificate for partial help with health costs (HC3) may also get help with the cost of a private sight test.

News.title: Team GB hero Amy Hunt's relationship mantra as she reveals whether she has boyfriend or not
News.content:
Team GB hero Amy Hunt's relationship mantra as she reveals whether she has boyfriend or not

Team GB star Amy Hunt has spoken about her personal life away from her success on the track

View 2 Images Team GB star Amy Hunt has given an insight into her personal life (Image: Mattia Ozbot/World Athletics via Getty Images)

Team GB's Amy Hunt quipped that her stance on romantic relationships is “medals before men”. The 24-year-old has enjoyed a successful year which peaked in August.

‌



Hunt became the first athlete to win four gold medals at the same European Championships. In the space of six days, she clinched the 100m, 200m, women’s 4x100m relay and mixed 4x100m relay titles.

‌



After winning the 200m final, the second of her four-gold haul, Hunt asked into a TV camera: “Are you not entertained?” Her homage to Russell Crowe’s Gladiator offered a glimpse into Hunt’s personality.

‌



The Team GB star began training full-time after graduating from Cambridge University with an English degree and has lived in Padua, Italy for the last few years. With next year’s World Championships and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics on the horizon, Hunt is not prioritising finding a boyfriend as she chases glory on the track.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

Amy Hunt doubles down on Sydney Sweeney criticism after advert controversy READ MORE :

Keely Hodgkinson banned from wearing 'sexy' outfit after causing a stir READ MORE :

In an interview with The Times, Hunt admitted to telling her coach she is “medals before men”, showing her half-joking relationship mantra. She enjoys living alone in Padua, where she is surrounded by Renaissance and medieval culture, which formed a major part of her English degree.

‌



Explaining the difficulty of balancing romance with an elite sporting career, Hunt said: “What we do requires so much of ourselves in terms of time, sacrifice, emotions and energy that if you’re pouring that into the wrong person, it can have quite catastrophic effects.”

She's comfortably independent, as demonstrated by a solo holiday to St Lucia. She said: “I think it’s really cool to be able to go to a restaurant, take a book and have your own thoughts for company.” Hunt added: “There’s a whole big life out there, and I’m in no rush to settle down, to slow down.”

View 2 Images Hunt won four golds at the European Championships (Image: Daniela Porcelli/Getty Images)

‌



It has been an eventful year for Hunt, who won the 100m title and finished runner-up in the 200m at the UK Championships in June. The following month, she also claimed a 100m silver medal at the Commonwealth Games.

Hunt ended her season by finishing fourth in the 200m event at the World Ultimate Championships in Budapest this month. However, after the final, the Olympic silver medalist used her platform to criticise Sydney Sweeney’s controversial sports gambling ad campaign, which featured the actor covering her body with various items of sporting equipment.

In an appearance on Good Morning Britain, Hunt doubled down on her stance: "When we're trying to provide role models for young people and young women in sport, we really want to show that it's about what your body can do, not so much what it looks like.”

Article continues below

While Hunt took issue with Sweeney’s portrayal of women in sport, the European champion is accustomed to taking centre stage. Speaking to The Times, she said: “Every competition is performance. You’re trying to put together the most perfect, flawless movie ever.

“When we get into the arena, everyone is looking down at us. The spotlights are on us when we’re introduced. We’re receiving the adulation from the crowd and waving back.”

News.title: Heartbreaking tribute paid to two British women killed in horror crash in Romania
News.content:
Heartbreaking tribute paid to two British women killed in horror crash in Romania

A heartbreaking tribute has been paid to two 'fun' and 'full of life' women who died in a crash in Romania when on a rescue mission to transport dogs to a new home in France

View 4 Images Rachael Harvey-Purkiss (Image: Facebook)

A heartbreaking tribute has been paid to two 'beautiful hearted' British women who died alongside eight dogs after four vehicles were involved in a horror crash in Romania.

‌



The fatal collision involved two lorries, a van and the minibus the two victims were travelling in. The women, aged 41 and 61, were pronounced dead at the scene in Caraș-Severin county, western Romania, by paramedics.

‌



Allison Condon and Rachael Harvey-Purkiss' close friend has expressed her 'heartbreak' at the loss of her 'soul sisters'. Claire Dalton posted on Facebook: "I'm heartbroken... but there are others feeling much worse than me. This breaks my heart more than anything."

‌



View 4 Images The women both died in the horror crash in Romania (Image: Facebook)

The minibus, which was registered in the UK, was also carrying 10 dogs, eight of which have been killed. The horrific crash occurred on Thursday around 11am on the DN6 national road just outside Vălișoara village.

Enquiries carried out by police revealed the UK-registered vehicle went on the wrong side of the road and crashed head-on into a lorry registered in Romania, whose driver was injured in the collision.

‌



The lorry then hit another HGV, also registered in Romania, trapping the minibus between them. A van travelling behind the second lorry was also involved in the crash.

View 4 Images Rachael Harvey-Purkiss and her friend were transporting the dogs to France (Image: Facebook)

The friends post continued: "I lost two amazing and beautiful people yesterday in a collision on a Romanian motorway and life will never be the same and I was lucky enough to call them good friends.

‌



"They were on a rescue mission that was to move 10 of our rescues to safety in France. The most fun, bouncy, full of life, beautiful hearted people I have ever met and I loved them very much"

The women were transporting the rescue dogs to their new lives in France when the crash took place.

Claire added: "They truly were my soul sisters. They were the friends who were simply there — through the good days, the difficult days and all the moments when I wondered how I could possibly carry on.

‌



"Alison and Rachel were making this incredible journey for one reason: because they cared. They wanted to save dogs and they wanted to make sure they were safe, loved and given the very best chance at a new life in France.

View 4 Images The two women's bodies had to be extricated from the minibus by firefighters (Image: Facebook )

"And now I am grieving for my beautiful friends and for the precious dogs we have lost. I simply cannot comprehend what has happened."

‌



Allison's daughter Sammie originally posted on Facebook after she was concerned her mum wasn't answering any calls and found out there had been a crash on the road.

Claire said: "My heart breaks for Alison and Rachel’s families. I cannot begin to imagine the pain they are going through right now. Sammy has lost her mum, and there are families and people who loved Alison and Rachel whose lives have changed forever in the most unimaginable way.

"I am struggling beyond belief to even find the words to speak to anybody at the moment. There are so many thoughts and emotions going through my head that I don’t know where one ends and another begins. I feel completely overwhelmed by grief, disbelief and sadness.

Article continues below

"This was supposed to be a journey of hope. None of us could ever have imagined that it would end like this."

News.title: Best-value winter sun destinations for UK travellers this year - report
News.content:
Best-value winter sun destinations for UK travellers this year - report

A Post Office Travel report, which analysised 24 popular destinations, has crowned the top value-for-money destinations for British holidaymakers looking for a winter getaway

View 3 Images Start planning your winter sun holiday now (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

Travelling can be expensive but if you do your research before you book you can save a fair amount of money on your trip.

‌



A report by Post Office Travel Money has revealed the top value-for-money destinations for British holidaymakers looking for a winter getaway.

‌



With weather forecasting models suggesting daytime temperatures could plunge below 10C across much of the UK next month now is the perfect time to plan that winter sun holiday.

‌



View 3 Images Cape Town and the 12 Apostels from above in South Africa (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Cape Town in South Africa, Mombasa in Kenya and Tokyo in Japan have been crowned the most affordable, according to the report. Cape Town offers the lowest prices on goods commonly purchased by tourists, with the Japanese capital and the Kenyan coastal city following closely behind.

The report is based off a study of 24 popular holiday spots for Post Office Travel Money. The Winter Sun Holiday Costs Barometer is calculated using prices for everyday items such as an evening meal, drinks, insect repellent and sun cream. It does not factor in the cost of flights or accommodation.

‌



For the first time, the research included both short and long-haul destinations, covering only locations reachable without transiting through a Middle Eastern airport.

Cape Town has topped the chart as the best-value winter sun destination on numerous occasions, with prices dropping by 9.7% since March this year, Post Office Travel Money confirmed.

A three-course dinner for two, including a bottle of house wine, came to just £39.26 in Cape Town, compared with a hefty £119.26 in Scarborough, Tobago, which ranked as the priciest destination surveyed.

‌



In Mombasa, the same meal cost £42.78, while Tokyo came in at £48.50.

View 3 Images A crowded beach at Benalmadena on the Costa Del Sol in Spain (Image: PA)

Portugal's Algarve, Spain's Costa del Sol and Tenerife in the Canary Islands proved the most affordable among the eight European resorts assessed.

Article continues below

Of the overall ten cheapest destinations, four were located in Asia – namely Penang in Malaysia, Phuket in Thailand, Colombo in Sri Lanka and Tokyo.

Laura Plunkett, head of Post Office Travel Money, said: "Our research again picked up wide variations in the cost of tourist staples, particularly in areas like the Caribbean and in Europe.

"This means holidaymakers could save themselves money and cut the cost of their winter sun holiday by doing some basic holiday pricing research before booking."

News.title: More than half of parents give rent back to help children buy first home
News.content:
More than half of parents give rent back to help children buy first home

Just over a third (34%) say their children are living at home specifically to save up enough funds to buy their first property - but 45% of parents feel like a landlord to their own child

View 2 Images More parents are helping their kids get on the property ladder (Image: Getty Images)

More than half of parents are giving rent back to their adult children who are living at home to help them get on the property ladder.

‌



Nationwide research from Nationwide shows 54% of parents return some or all of the rent paid by their adult children to help them save for a deposit.

‌



Just over a third (34%) say their children are living at home specifically to save up enough funds to buy their first property - but 45% of parents feel like a landlord to their own child.

‌



More than two in five (45%) parents have waived rent payments for their child once in the past year, while more than half (52%) say they’ve let children off rent payments between two and six times in the last year.

View 2 Images It comes as mortgage rates continue to rise (Image: Tim Graham/Getty Images)

Millions of UK drivers warned pump prices could rocket to £2.50 a litre if Trump imposes diesel export ban READ MORE :

Parents are charging an average of £303 per month in rent to their kids for living at home – equivalent to more than £3,600 a year. However, this amount does vary considerably across the country.

‌



Parents in Greater London charge the most at an average of £415 a month, or £4,980 a year - compared with £187 a month, £2,244 a year, for people in Yorkshire and The Humber.

More than six in 10 parents (61%) have increased the rent they charge their adult child, while only one in five (21%) parents have a formal arrangement in place - and a further 14% say they would consider one.

The figures were released as households are dealing with rising fixed mortgage rates. According to financial information website Moneyfacts, the average two-year fixed deal is 5.92%. The average five-year fixed is 5.94%.

‌



Carlo Pileggi, Nationwide’s Head of Mortgage Products, said: "Behind many first-time buyer success stories are parents quietly helping along the way and it appears they are using new tactics to support their children.

"As saving for a home remains as challenging as ever, our research shows many of Britain’s parents are using rent payments as a way to help their children build a deposit, turning the family home and time spent living at home into a stepping stone towards homeownership.

"However, the findings also serve as a reminder that many aspiring first-time buyers do not have access to family support and continue to face significant challenges in saving for a deposit."

News.title: Supporters of WASPI compensation outnumber opponents by almost four to one, study shows
News.content:
Supporters of WASPI compensation outnumber opponents by almost four to one, study shows

EXCLUSIVE: More than 3.5 million women born in the 1950s lost out after the Department for Work and Pensions increased the State Pension age from 60 to 66 but did not properly inform those affected

View 3 Images Around half (47%) of voters believe women affected by State Pension age changes should receive full or partial redress (Image: Leon Neal, Getty Images)

Supporters of compensation for WASPI (Women Against State Pension Inequality) women outnumber opponents by almost four to one, according to a new analysis of more than 10,000 voters.

‌



Around half (47%) of voters believe women affected by State Pension age changes should receive full or partial redress, the Stack Data Strategy research showed. Just 13% believe the women were not wronged or should not be compensated.

‌



More than 3.5 million women born in the 1950s lost out after the Department for Work and Pensions increased the State Pension age from 60 to 66 but did not properly inform those affected.

‌



Keir Starmer’s government refused to roll out a compensation package, as recommended by an independent ombudsman back in 2024. But campaigners have been given new hope after Andy Burnham agreed to meet with them to discuss putting the scandal right, the Mirror reported in July.

WASPI new hope as Andy Burnham set to meet campaign over redress options READ MORE :

WASPI campaign sets out next steps after judicial review challenge launched READ MORE :

View 3 Images Andy Burnham has agreed to meet with campaigners to discuss putting the scandal right (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

When presented with the Parliamentary Ombudsman's ruling and asked to choose between a range of options for how the Government could respond, more than eight in ten (83%) chose an option involving some form of financial compensation.

‌



The most popular options were paying the maximum compensation recommended and paying proportionate amounts of between £1,000 and £2,950 per woman.

In the Prime Minister’s own constituency of Makerfield in Greater Manchester, 48% of voters back compensation, while just 12%are against payouts.

‌



More than a third (37%) of respondents say the new Labour leader refusing to compensate WASPI women would make them less likely to vote for the party at the next election. Of 2024 Labour voters, a similar number (38%) believe they would be less likely to stick with the party if compensation was refused.

View 3 Images Angela Madden , chair of the WASPI campaign, said the poll sent a clear message to the government (Image: PA)

Angela Madden, chair of the WASPI (Women Against State Pension Inequality) campaign, said: “This research sends a clear message to ministers: supporters of compensation outnumber opponents by almost four to one.

‌



“We are pleased that Andy Burnham has recognised the harms experienced by WASPI women and has committed to meeting us to discuss what providing fair redress looks like. WASPI stands ready to work with the Government to identify a solution that is fair to both affected women and the taxpayer.”

A DWP spokesman said: “The Secretary of State set out the Government’s position in his oral statement to Parliament, including acceptance of maladministration and apology to the women affected.

“Our focus now is on delivering an action plan to implement lessons learned in how DWP communicates State Pension matters going forward."

Article continues below

The MRP poll was carried out by Stack Data Strategy between July 8 and August 4 among 10,052 GB adults.

News.title: Men 'seen emerging from New York sewer' in latest bizarre incident – arrests made
News.content:
Men 'seen emerging from New York sewer' in latest bizarre incident – arrests made

Samuel Reveron, 25, and Kevin Rodriguez, 26, have both now been arrested after men were seen coming out of a sewer manhole in New York

View 2 Images Men were allegedly seen emerging from a manhole in New York this week (Image: AKI Autocare)

Two men have been arrested after people were seen emerging from a manhole in New York near to where Benjamin Netanyahu has previously stayed.

‌



Samuel Reveron, 25, and Kevin Rodriguez, 26, have been accused of conspiracy and trespassing following reports of men coming out of a sewer near East 61st Street and Park Avenue at around 1.38am on Wednesday.

‌



Three men were allegedly spotted in what the New York Police Department says is the latest incident, following others in which people have entered sewers looking for scrap metal or items of value that may have been washed away.

‌



This case led to fears that there might have been a connection with the UN General Assembly this week, with world leaders having arrived in the city.

View 2 Images Samuel Reveron is pictured leaving Manhattan Criminal Court (Image: Barry Williams)

Russian plans to weaponise winter freeze against Ukraine's civilians leaked READ MORE :

The manhole in question was close to the hotel where Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu has stayed previously, although he didn't on this occasion.

‌



"This incident fits that same criteria, but out of an abundance of caution given the UN General Assembly and the sensitivity of the location, the NYPD is conducting additional security sweeps with our federal partners," the police department said in a statement, the BBC reports.

The pair both “identified themselves as the individuals that entered the manhole” according to the court document, reports NBC.

Rodriguez and Reveron, both from Queens, were arrested on Thursday and during a hearing on Friday morning, the two men pleaded not guilty and were released from custody.

‌



Meanwhile Brian Kennedy, a lawyer for Reveron, challenged the claim that his client was in the sewer when speaking to reporters.

“It seems like not much of a case,” Kennedy said. “I understand that it is strange that it’s alleged he went (into the sewer). But there’s no connection to the UN or the appearance of Netanyahu or any other kind of nefarious scheme.

“It’s not advised to go into a sewer. Besides the grime and rats, there are other dangers down there. It’s not something I would be doing.”

Article continues below

There have been several other incidents this year where people have been caught on video coming out from New York sewers.

Some were spotted emerging from manholes in Brooklyn in May. Then in August, surveillance footage showed a person coming out of a manhole in Queens early in the morning.

News.title: Mum accused of murder as daugther, 14, 'goes to hospital with her baby's body'
News.content:
Mum accused of murder as daugther, 14, 'goes to hospital with her baby's body'

Dayjanay Thomas, 31, from Tacoma, has been charged with murder after she and her 14-year-old daughter allegedly turned up to a hospital with a baby's body

View Image The baby was taken to Mary Bridge Children's Hospital (file) (Image: GoogleMaps)

A woman has been charged with murdering her teenage daughter's newborn baby after the pair allegedly arrived at a hospital with the body in a box.

‌



Dayjanay Thomas, 31, is said to have travelled to Mary Bridge Children's Hospital in Tacoma, Washington State, with her 14-year-old daughter after the teenager gave birth to a boy in their home earlier in the day on February 10.

‌



An autopsy showed the baby was alive when he was born, and died as a result of eight sharp-force injuries, according to court documents. He is also said to have suffered several blunt-force injuries to his head. The manner of death was listed as murder.

‌



Thomas has been charged with murder and criminal mistreatment, and is being held at Pierce County Jail.

Russian plans to weaponise winter freeze against Ukraine's civilians leaked READ MORE :

It is alleged the teenage daughter gave birth at 5am on February 10 and immediately told her mum - while also saying she did not realise she had been pregnant.

The mother is also claimed to have not known her daughter was pregnant.

‌



Court documents say that rather than call emergency services, Thomas told her daughter they would have to wait for a friend to drive them to the hospital, reports Tacoma News Tribune.

The landlady arrived later and took them to the hospital at 6.45pm. The landlady claimed she did not know the teenager had given birth, but noticed Thomas was carrying a cardboard box.

The body was allegedly inside the cardboard box. Medical staff at the hospital contacted police and a search was made of Thomas' home, where blood was reportedly found in several locations including the bathroom, on clothes as well as on a serrated knife and a pair of scissors.

Article continues below

Detectives are said to have found text messages exchanged between Thomas and her daughter from the day the baby was born, including one from Thomas which read: "Okay you have to let them know that [the landlord] and I didn't know and just let them know you didn't know what was going on with your body."

Thomas was arrested on February 23 and charged with criminal mistreatment in connection with her alleged failure to seek medical care for her daughter after she gave birth. The murder charge was issued later.

Neither the teen nor the landlord has been charged in connection with the baby's death.

News.title: Clubs seek legal advice after Man City found guilty over financial rule breaches
News.content:
Premier League clubs have sought legal advice as to whether they would have a compensation claim over the Manchester City 115 charges case.

After a long wait for the outcome, City have been found guilty of a majority of the financial rule breaches they were accused of.

BBC Sport has also been told that the club will appeal.

It has emerged that a number of Premier League sides, prior to Friday's news, had already started seeking advice over whether they would have a case for financial compensation as a result of City's breaches.

It also emerged that:

Other Premier League clubs have been formally told about the independent panel's decision. A select group of club directors were informed by email and had to sign a non-disclosure agreement before they could read the document, a source told the BBC. It is not yet known when the decision of the panel will be announced officially.

Manchester City deny wrongdoing but being found guilty on the most serious charges means they could be looking at a points deduction serious enough to relegate them, large fines or even expulsion from the Premier League

A sanctions hearing will need to take place to decide the punishment. That hasn't happened yet and could take months.

An appeal would then take place - and while it is possible the punishment isn't made public until after that, there remains the possibility that any sanctions will be communicated before any appeal takes place

An appeal process could mean the uncertainty surrounding the case continues to cloud the top flight

It is understood a number of City players do not have relegation release clauses in their contracts in the event of the club losing their Premier League status as a result of any sanctions

The news that City had been found guilty was broken by the Athletic, which reported that 114 of the 115 counts were upheld.

It came 1,327 days after City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation, and 22 months since a hearing by an independent commission concluded.

No official announcement has been made by the Premier League, which has declined to comment.

BBC Sport has been told the independent panel has ruled, and the majority of the charges have been upheld.

Manchester City released a statement saying: "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."

One source, who held a senior executive position at one Premier League club before moving to another, said they expected clubs to submit individual compensation claims against Manchester City.

However, another leading lawyer told the BBC that process could be centralised by the league.

In June, Everton were told they must pay Burnley Â£35m after they broke profit and sustainability regulations (PSR) over a three-year period.

Burnley argued the breach impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League, and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated.

Everton have appealed, with sources saying they will "robustly and thoroughly" contest the ruling, but it provides an interesting backdrop to the Manchester City case.

BBC Sport has also been told that, in the event of being found guilty, City will appeal against the findings.

News.title: Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City
News.content:
It has taken more than two years, but a judgement finally appears to have been reached on the 115 charges levelled against Manchester City over breaches of Premier League financial rules.

Following a four-year investigation, City were charged and the hearing finally got under way on 16 September 2024.

BBC Sport has now learned a decision has been made, after the Athletic reported City had been found guilty on almost all of the charges.

We are not at the end of this process, however. Far from it.

But what does this mean for City's titles? What about their Premier League status? Will there be an appeal? And how long will it be before this saga does come to an end?

News.title: E-bikes seized by police sold on at auction, BBC finds
News.content:
Electric motorbikes seized by police forces in the UK are being sold on at auction, despite some fears they could end up back in the hands of criminals, the BBC can reveal.

Thousands are confiscated annually because they are suspected of being driven illegally, or used in a crime - most are later destroyed, but a BBC investigation has found some are sold on to members of the public in online auctions.

Across the UK, police sold 161 e-bikes last year and 54 in 2024, although the real number could be higher because not every force responded to the BBC's Freedom of Information request.

Some of the forces said they had now ended the practice, but others defended it as a way of putting "money back into policing".

Six forces responded to say e-bikes they had seized had been sold, including large forces such as West Midlands Police and Police Scotland.

The figure includes electrically-assisted pedal cycles, which look similar to bicycles and have a motor that kicks in as a rider pedals, as well as electric motorbikes, which are usually more powerful and are propelled only by their motor.

E-bikes have become controversial because some think they are linked to crime and anti-social behaviour.

Recent BBC reporting has highlighted cases across the country of balaclava-clad young men riding illegally on footpaths and intimidating residents.

There have also been a number of pedestrian deaths, including 86-year-old grandmother Gloria Stephenson, who was struck at a zebra crossing in Sunderland last year by an illegal e-motorbike.

News.title: I'm not tempted to call an early election, Burnham says
News.content:
Andy Burnham has insisted he is not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process".

During a round of BBC interviews ahead of Labour's annual conference, the prime minister said his focus was on helping people with the cost of living and supporting businesses.

Recent polling has suggested Labour's position has improved since Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer in Downing Street in July, although Reform UK and the Conservatives are not far behind.

An early general election could give Burnham a mandate of his own and free him from commitments made in Labour's 2024 manifesto. The next general election must be held by August 2029.

Asked by ITV Calendar if the next election would be in 2029, he replied: "Yes, that's when the next election will be.

"All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead."

News.title: Burnham not doing enough to boost growth, says Starmer ally
News.content:
A cabinet minister under Sir Keir Starmer has said Andy Burnham's government is not focused enough on boosting economic growth and needs to act with "more urgency".

Speaking to the BBC two months after being sacked in Burnham's cabinet reshuffle upon entering office, Peter Kyle said he wasn't making a "criticism" but "pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government".

"If the destination means prosperity, it means freedom for people to do new things, and it means security for people and families, then why wouldn't we put our foot down and get there quicker," the former business secretary said.

It comes as Labour prepares to gather in Liverpool for its annual conference.

Burnham will address the conference on Tuesday and has said his speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role."

He has previously said his time as Greater Manchester mayor had given him "a clear theory of growth" stressing his belief in the importance of devolving powers to local areas.

Giving regions and nations more control would, he has argued, create the conditions for "good growth in every postcode".

Kyle served as science secretary and later business secretary in the Starmer government, but has now returned to the backbenches as the MP for Hove and Portslade.

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, he said the government should be willing to take decisions that involve "short-term" pain in order to deliver economic growth, suggesting a delay to expanding workers' rights.

"We might need to look and have honest conversations with unions about how we sequence some of the rights going forward in order to make sure that we get growth into the economy in the shorter term," he said.

The government's Employment Rights Act was passed in December 2025 but some of the changes are not due to come into force until next year.

The former minister also suggested introducing a "tax growth test" which would measure the impact of each tax on the economy and asking government experts to review "obstacles" to growth.

Asked if there was enough focus on growth in the government, Kyle replied: "I don't think there is and that isn't a criticism - it is pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government.

"I think we need to up our ambition, I think that we need to act with more urgency when it comes to economic growth."

Chancellor John Healey is due to give his first Budget on 28 October, but faces rising debt costs and warnings of slower economic growth.

According to the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the UK economy is expected to grow by 1%, slightly less than the 1.1% previously forecast.

News.title: Smoke rises from burning Greek cargo ship near Mykonos
News.content:
A fire broke out on the deck of a truck ferry sailing north of Mykonos on September 25.

According to the Hellenic Coastguard, the blaze required an "extensive firefighting operation", but it is not clear how it started.

All 28 staff and the single passenger on board were safely evacuated using lifeboats, they added.

News.title: 'It's a brutal adjustment': How to cope when your child goes to uni
News.content:
"Sometimes parents send their child to university and they're not even worried, but then these group chats create a worry that something might be wrong," says Rayyah Uddin, 20, a third-year student at the University of Nottingham.

She knows of WhatsApp group chats being set up by parents of first-year students at her university and has also seen parents use TikTok to share their worries about their child not making friends, and asking other parents for their help.

"These are issues the students should really be figuring out for themselves, and it is better if parents try and talk to their child rather than immediately jump to other parents," she says.

Not hearing from your child all the time isn't necessarily a cause for concern - "they might just be having a really good time and are getting absorbed into university life," Rayyah adds.

Parent social media groups can be useful, according to psychologist Charlotte Armitage, but not when they are used to share private difficulties, track movements or ask questions that the student is capable of asking themselves.

"Constant checking, tracking or intervening may soothe the parent in the short term, but it can inadvertently communicate to the young adult: 'I am not sure you can cope without me.'"

"Of course, where there is a credible safeguarding concern, a significant change in behaviour, or a known risk to their wellbeing, parents should act."

News.title: How the bare nails trend became a class issue
News.content:
Manicures have been whispering messages about the wearer's position in society for as long as they have existed, according to fashion journalist Suzanne E. Shapiro.

"Women's bodies - and sense of self-presentation - have always held huge political and cultural significance," Shapiro, who wrote Nails: The Story of The Modern Manicure, tells the BBC.

Even back in 13th century Imperial China, the lengthy talons grown by nobility and the delicately carved brass nail shields which usually guarded them were a symbol of a life unmarred by manual labour.

A single layer of the rose-tinted waxy salves which were popular in the 1800s was a sign of vigour and health, but two layers - in an era when cosmetics and artificial beauty were tied to virtue - was the mark of a vain or "loose" woman.

And the red at-home nail lacquer, released by Revlon in the early 1930s, was a badge of honour for modern women rebelling against that kind of oppressive judgement.

But it was women of colour who really made manicures an accessible and fashionable form of self-expression, historians say.

Entertainer Josephine Baker, disco icons Dianna Ross and Donna Summer, and Olympic gold-medal-winning sprinter Florence Griffith-Joyner - whose dramatic acrylic sets often distracted headline writers from her record-setting performances - have all pioneered nail art.

"These were times that it was hard for black women to be able to express themselves," says celebrity nail artist Celeste Hampton.

"[Nail art] allowed black women to express our form of softness, our form of femininity, our form of beauty."

And when waves of Vietnamese refugees gave rise to the nail bar in the 1970s, professional manicures were no longer the preserve of the rich.

But, like many luxuries, as they became more popular and more accessible to the masses, the wealthy began pivoting â a textbook example of behaviour known as "counter signalling", Rudolfo says.

"The same way that logo bags are considered gauche or quiet luxury is more aspirational, bare nails are considered the trend now.

"The examples are almost always white women or celebrities... [and] they'll often conflate class and taste with that bareness."

Others point out bare nails often demand their own time-consuming and costly routine.

"The irony in all this is these natural nails are not natural either," Shapiro says. "They also require a lot of grooming and sometimes pretty premiere services."

Few would argue there aren't valid feminist questions for the beauty industry to answer, around unrealistic standards for example, but the largely female-run nail sector also feels empowering for many women.

"I feel like nail care has very much had a 'for women, by women' sort of ethos around it," Shapiro says. "The first salon opened in New York City was owned by a woman, and she was a remarkably independent one... a lot of the first entrepreneurs offering product lines, opening salons were women."

Hampton admits she's saddened by the way trends have been â and continue to be - weaponised.

"We're taking the fun out of nails... Anyone should be able to wear what they like - nail polish or bare nails," she says. "Why is there an argument? Why is there beef?"

Scanlon too is a little baffled.

"For me, it's like, just stop judging ourselves and everybody else," she says. "Some people like to have the nails done, some people don't.

"I suppose the question that I was posing was, is it doing anything for you?

"The truth of it is: it's not that deep."

News.title: Man City found guilty of majority of 115 financial rule breaches
News.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching.

The Athletic , externalis reporting that the sanctions have not been decided but that the independent panel has reached its decision, finding the club guilty of all but one count.

The Premier League declined to comment.

Asked if the report was correct, City did not comment either way.

Instead they released a statement saying the "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality".

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence," it added.

BBC Sport has also been told that, in the event of being found guilty, City will appeal against the findings.

Other Premier League clubs are believed to have been informed about the independent panel's decision and have sought legal advice as to whether they would have a compensation claim.

News.title: UK ticket holder wins £111m EuroMillions jackpot
News.content:
A UK ticket holder has won Friday's Â£111m EuroMillions jackpot, National Lottery operator Allwyn has confirmed.

One mystery player matched all five numbers â 11, 12, 15, 38, 49 â plus the two Lucky Star numbers â 10 and 12 â to scoop the major prize.

Allwyn's senior winners' adviser Andy Carter said it was "fantastic news for a UK EuroMillions player" who has secured the "life-changing" sum.

It marks the third time a UK winner has claimed the jackpot this year.

On 10 March, one UK winner took home a Â£181m jackpot - the third-largest in UK National Lottery history - while two UK-based winners shared a Â£125m jackpot with a French player in April.

"Be sure to check your tickets and get in touch if you think you might be tonight's lucky winner," Carter urged.

The record for the largest EuroMillions prize for a UK player currently stands at Â£195m - won by an anonymous player in 2022.

EuroMillions draws are held every Tuesday and Friday night across nine European countries.

Tuesday's jackpot now stands at an estimated Â£14m.

News.title: Noah Woods left playground through gap in fence, inquest hears
News.content:
Suffolk Coroner's Court heard from police that Noah had left the playground, walked into a memorial garden and left that through an open gate. He then ran down a path on a new housing estate towards nearby Decoy Pond.

Det Ch Insp Matt Connick from Suffolk Police told the court that CCTV showed Noah in the play area being looked after by a relative, which was "part of a normal routine".

The detective said Noah "left through a gap in the fence leading to the memorial garden where he left through an open gate".

After he had left the play area, he was closely followed by the relative trying to catch up with him, Connick added.

The inquest heard the relative had shouted out to Noah, who lived in neighbouring East Bergholt, but he went out of sight shortly afterwards.

Another man was said to have joined the search and then police were called.

At the time of the search, volunteers were told that Noah was non-verbal and partially deaf.

A statement from Brantham Parish Council, which maintains the play area at Merriam Close, said it was "deeply saddened by Noah's death and our thoughts remain with his family and all those affected at this extremely difficult time".

"The parish council understands that there was a break in the internal fencing, being constructed to separate the play area from the memorial garden, however the whole of the area at Merriam Close, including the play area and memorial garden are completely enclosed by appropriate perimeter fencing," it said.

"The council will co-operate fully with any investigation and, while inquiries are ongoing, does not consider it appropriate to comment further."

News.title: Daniel Thomas pleads not guilty after dinghy slashed
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has pleaded not guilty to criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the Channel with a knife.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, was arrested after the livestreamed video on Tuesday.

Thomas, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in Hampshire via videolink, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.

He pleaded not guilty to both charges and was remanded in custody until his next court appearance at Portsmouth Crown Court on 29 September.

News.title: Some BBC channels and radio stations may well have to close, director general says
News.content:
Brittin took over as BBC director general in May after a decade as president of Google in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

Asked by Kuenssberg if he would allow a programme to be made and presented by AI, Brittin replied: "I would do, within guardrails."

He added: "We want to experiment with this technology and understand what it can and can't do, but I'm here because I believe in human creativity.

"I don't think anything we do should be replaced by AI. I think there are lots of places where AI can help us make the licence fee go further, but also help us in our decision-making and creativity. But it's not a substitute for humans."

He also warned of the danger of a handful of tech companies having too much control over information in the future.

"We're also in this moment where AI is in takeoff. So I think there's a danger that six companies will control access to information in future and the creation of information and misinformation," he said.

"Six companies, none of them European, let alone British. In that world, here's the BBC. It's the most trusted organisation by over half a billion people."

Asked if he trusted big tech companies he replied: "There's a lot of platforms out there, so I wouldn't trust any platform innately.

"And I think what you do is you keep under review how those things work and whether your content can show up in the right place and fulfil its mission.

"I think the BBC and our apps and services should be the antidote to the algorithm. Everywhere else you go is driven by some commercial interest."

The interview will be available on BBC Sounds and YouTube on Saturday 26 September, then on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg on BBC One and iPlayer at 09:00 BST on 27 September.

News.title: NHS to suspend staff suspected of snooping on patient records
News.content:
NHS staff in England suspected of looking at patient records without a valid reason will be immediately suspended as part of a "zero-tolerance crackdown" on snooping.

Those under suspicion will also be locked out of NHS computer systems, preventing any further viewing of confidential records, including from home.

NHS England chief executive Sir Jim Mackey has written to every trust, ordering the measures to be introduced immediately to strengthen protection against data breaches.

The move follows a series of high-profile incidents involving the records of Nottingham and Southport attack victims and a child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire.

This week, Bristol Foundation NHS Trust said it had launched an internal investigation after it emerged the medical records of an 18-year-old had been accessed years after his death.

The boy's mother, Paula McGowan, told the BBC she was "deeply concerned and hurt" and called for the NHS to do more to deal with the problem.

News.title: PM rules out giving Wales independence referendum powers
News.content:
The prime minister has ruled out handing powers to hold a referendum on independence to the Welsh government.

Andy Burnham said other UK nations do not have such powers and he did not "think we can create a different arrangement for Wales".

He added that the decision should be made jointly with Westminster, arguing that the UK Parliament has to have a "say on an issue of that magnitude".

Wales First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said last week he would seek powers to hold an independence referendum, although he ruled out staging one before the next Senedd election in May 2030.

Burnham also said he was open to looking at the Welsh government's "Cynnal" plans to trial offering Â£10 a week for 15,000 children aged under six, in households already receiving universal credit.

This would require the agreement of the Department for Work and Pensions and HMRC to avoid the payment being taxed or other benefits - paid for by the UK government - being reduced.

"I'll certainly ensure that there's a proper discussion about the issue," he said.

"I mean, I did things as mayor of Greater Manchester without there having to be any tax implications.

"So I'm not quite sure why that arises in this in this instance, but we will have a look at it for certain."

News.title: Jeffrey Donaldson victim describes 'profound impact' of child sex abuse
News.content:
The victims of child sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson have described the impact the abuse had on them.

Donaldson was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

The former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader appeared at Newry Crown Court for a hearing prior to his sentencing in October. He is seeking to appeal his convictions.

The prosecution barrister told the court that one of the women said her childhood had been stolen, while the second said the abuse affected her every day.

In her submission to the pre-sentencing hearing, Rosemary Walsh KC outlined what she described as the "salient facts" that were heard during the course of the trial.

She also described the impact the offending had on both victims, whom were described during the trial as Complainants A and B.

She said both complainants often wondered what life would have been like if they hadn't experienced the abuse.

In her victim impact statement, Complainant A described the "profound impact" the abuse had on her.

Walsh said the complainant believed her childhood had been "stolen" and that she felt an "enormous amount of anger that is always simmering away under the surface".

Walsh said the abuse Complainant B had suffered affected her "every day and every relationship", and that she had to fight on a daily basis the wish that she would die.

The prosecution barrister also outlined further aggravating and mitigating factors.

She said, in sentencing, the youth of the victims had to be taken account, as well as the "multitude of offences", which "spanned a considerable period of time", and the fact there were two victims.

Donaldson's defence barrister Keiron Vaughan KC told the court that the 63-year-old was "of previous good character" and that there had been no offending of this type over the last 18 years.

"In that period of time, Mr Donaldson has or did achieve significant things in his life," he said.

"I readily accept that these convictions obliterate all those achievements that he has made in his life, and that's certainly something he will have to live with."

Vaughan said he acknowledged the court would impose a "lengthy custodial sentence", but that he had complete confidence that the court would treat Donaldson in the same way it would any other defendant of a similar age and in similar circumstances.

Addressing Donaldson directly, Judge Paul Ramsey said: "Mr Donaldson, I will be sentencing you as soon as I can next month."

A British man has died after falling about 200ft while descending from the summit of a mountain in northern Spain, according to local law enforcement.

The 28-year-old mountaineer fell down a vertical gully on the east side of the Torrecerredo – the highest peak of the Cantabrian Mountains – on Thursday afternoon, the Spanish Civil Guard for the Asturias region said.

Spanish emergency services received a report that a person had fallen at the location at around 2.20pm.

A mountain rescue team was deployed aboard a helicopter and the mountaineer’s remains were located after flying over the area, the Civil Guard said.

Two specialists were lowered to retrieve the man’s body, alongside his belongings which had been scattered during the fall.

The incident occurred during the descent from the Torrecerredo peak, at approximately 65ft below the summit, the Civil Guard said.

The mountaineer’s body was transported to La Morgal, a regional sports and aviation facility in Llanera near the Asturian city of Gijon.

A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said: “We are in contact with the local authorities following reports of the death of a British national in Spain.”

Torrecerredo, which has an elevation of approximately 8,690ft (2,649m), is the highest peak of the Picos de Europa mountain range.

Sepa Asturias, the public body in charge of emergency services for the Asturias region, said it also responded to an incident in the Jou Sin Tierre area of the mountain range on Thursday afternoon.

A 54-year-old French woman was subsequently transported to hospital after she suffered a leg injury, according to Sepa Asturias.

A choir blasts a local hymn complete with musical instruments as congregants, mostly women clad in white dresses, dance and clap along. The Quaker meeting house in western Kenya is a sharp contrast to the deafening silence that is the norm among practitioners of the faith in the United States.

The atmosphere feels similar to Pentecostal churches, with the hymns and spiritual declarations very familiar to those sung in other churches. But the Friends Church in Cheptulu bears no sign of the cross, paintings or sculptures of Jesus Christ, which is the norm in most Christian churches.

Quakerism originated in 17th-century England when George Fox, who objected to the Anglican emphasis on ceremony, founded the group. In the 1640s, he said he heard a voice that led him to develop a personal relationship with Christ, described as the Inner Light.

There are an estimated 400,000 members worldwide of the Religious Society of Friends, or Quakers. About half live in Africa with most in Kenya, where Americans introduced the religion. Quakers in the U.S. believe in the Inner Light and eschew loud worship and preaching in favor of silently awaiting individual messages from God.

In Kenya, 90-year-old Thomas Amalemba, who was born to a Quaker father and a Salvation Army mother, remembers the days when music was slower and different from the current music that has been modernized by the introduction of contemporary instruments.

“The old people when we go to the church service, we feel uncomfortable,” Amalemba said.

In Amalemba’s Cheptulu Church, senior pastor Kennedy Shiverenje said the music needed to be relevant and appropriate to the local context.

“We needed to capture the youth and re-energize the elderly so that our service is vibrant,” Shiverenje said.

Adding more tempo to attract young followers

In most Quaker houses of worship, there is no clergy, pulpit or altar. No one sings or chants, burns incense or lights candles. They do not speak until a message from God moves through them.

In Kenya, the Quakers worship loudly.

When American missionaries from the Friends United Meeting in Indiana arrived in the hilly western Kenya town of Kaimosi in 1902, they introduced a version of Quakerism that featured slow hymns and evangelism. They invested in schools and hospitals that helped convert many locals.

Pastor Shiverenje’s grandfather was the first pastor of the Cheptulu church, which stands on a hill near their family’s home. He believes silent worship, or the unprogrammed version of Quakerism, may not have won his grandfather, who was among the first converts.

“If you just brought an unprogrammed service where people sit silently, I’m not sure people would concentrate,” he said.

Over the years, Kenyan Quakers have grown in numbers after adding more tempo to the music and incorporating modern musical instruments to attract young people, who previously found them boring.

“We used to joke about how our grandmothers would sing the songs so slowly, taking forever to finish a single song until they eventually dozed off. They wouldn’t even clap their hands, let alone play African drums. The songs were the slowest I had ever heard in my life,” Rose Oside remembered.

At a recent Sunday service in Cheptulu Church, which has been around for 100 years, it was mostly young people who led praise and worship sessions. Even when the older women led a hymn before a baby dedication program, they were still guided in their tempo by the keyboard played by a young Quaker man.

Catherine Ikalakala has been a Quaker for almost 50 years. She remembers when young people avoided going to church.

“The young people used to see us singing slow motion while other churches had faster music,” she said. “So they used to go to other churches and so we bought a keyboard that has brought all these young people to church.”

The role of pastoral ministers has modern importance

Evangelism isn’t practiced by Quakers who follow silent worship. They believe in growth through self-convinced followers. The Friends Theological College in Kaimosi now boasts of more than 400 students on campus and online.

College Principal Robert Wafula said the training ensures the correct message is taught to congregations and has helped in other countries such as Rwanda, where the government closed 70 Quaker churches in a recent crackdown led by untrained pastors.

Wafula said the role of pastoral ministers is especially important in the modern world, where political frictions often threaten peace in the community. He noted that Quaker doctrine, which is founded on peace, has been useful during ethnic tensions and postelection violence in Kenya, as well as in regional conflicts.

“Quakerism has spread peace across East Africa, for example in Rwanda and even in the Congo, where Quakers are participating in peace-building through the major groups,” Wafula said. “We have a pastor from this college working in the peace center in Rwanda.”

The college now houses a Quaker Archive program. Among the archives is the old Bible, written in the local Maragoli language, used by early Quakers and the first converts.

With the missionaries gone, the church has made changes to ensure it keeps spreading, but some of the updates have rattled the older generation.

Pastor Shiverenje said the mission was initially funded by donors, but now the locals have to raise funds for programs to continue.

Amalemba agreed change is important. But he warned the emphasis on congregants giving money in church created a sense that they were “buying blessings.”

Linet Mmbone, an assistant librarian at the college, said a group of researchers realized young people needed a reference point and embarked on a project to speak to early Quakers and obtain material like notes from early yearly meetings.

“Because we don’t want to lose our dignity as Quakers, we want to go back to the roots and conduct our services the way the early Quakers used to do it,” Mmbone said.
