Eel is his favorite training food, he's only 11 years old, and he found his niche in his sport when he was in kindergarten.

His thing is esports.

Meet Yuki Kurihara, the Japanese elementary school student who defeated Kang Dongshin of South Korea 10-2 on Saturday in the final of the Puyo Puyo Champions puzzle game at the Asian Games.

He defeated Tanarak Wongkitikun of Thailand in the semifinals, 10-1. The Thai player is a relative old-timer at 28.

Kurihara is believed to be youngest-ever gold medalist in the Asian Games, which date from 1951 in New Delhi, India. And he’s certainly the youngest in these Asian Games.

Japanese media has reported he trains eight hours daily and still keeps up his grades in school.

Esports was held in the Asian Games for the first time three years ago in Hangzhou, China. It was so popular that tickets were sold by lottery. It's also an audience favorite in Japan.

Youth is being served at the Asian Games. Kamus Wong is a 12-year-old competing for Hong Kong in skateboarding, and 13-year-old Yu Zidi of China won three gold medals in swimming.

A relative senior citizen, 17-year-old Japanese swimmer Shin Ohashi set a world record on Thursday in the 200-meter breaststroke.

England return to action for the first time since heartbreak in the World Cup semi-finals and their subsequent victory in the third-place play-off, as they face Spain in the opening fixture of this season’s Nations League.

Thomas Tuchel’s men have been given a tough task in their Nations League A3 group opener, against the world and European champions, with this the two sides’ first meeting since the Euro 2024 final - another crushing loss for the Three Lions.

Luis de la Fuente has signed a contract to extend his spell as Spain head coach until at least 2032, while Tuchel remains at the helm of England despite an inquest into their World Cup disappointment, and all eyes will be on his side as they look to bounce back.

The Wembley clash will also see two of the contenders for this year’s Ballon d’Or go head-to-head, as England captain Harry Kane goes up against Spain’s star forward Lamine Yamal. Kane scored an incredible 73 goals for club and country last season.

The top two sides in the group will progress to the Nations League quarter-finals, with matches against Croatia and Czech Republic also scheduled for this international break. Here’s everything you need to know.

When is England v Spain?

England face Spain at Wembley Stadium on Saturday 26 September, with kick-off at 7.45pm BST.

How can I watch it?

Viewers in the UK can watch the match on ITV1 and streaming service ITVX.

Team news

Thomas Tuchel has seen a raft of withdrawals from his squad, with Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Tino Livramento, Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo all pulling out injured, while the likes of Reece James and John Stones were unavailable for selection anyway due to injury. Morgan Gibbs-White and James Garner have been called up as replacements.

Spain are missing Pedro Porro and Joan Garcia, while Marcos Llorente has retired from the international game.

Predicted line-ups

England XI: Pickford; Quansah, Konsa, Guehi, O’Reilly; Anderson, Scott; Saka, Bellingham, Gordon; Kane

Spain XI: Simon; E Garcia, Cubarsi, Laporte, Cucurella; Rodri, Pedri; Yamal, Olmo, N Williams; Oyarzabal

It was a tiger safari that got me interested in birds. Alongside our search for big cats, we spent our time watching bee-eaters and rufous-bellied eagles. The birds of India are so colourful: lilac-breasted rollers, kingfishers – even the pigeons can be green.

But then came a surprise: I asked the naturalist on safari which bird they’d most like to see. The answer: “A ruff in its breeding plumage.” I looked it up. It’s rare, but you can spot this wading bird in all its finery right here in the UK, in Norfolk.

A curiosity was born. Back home in south west England I could see myself getting into birdwatching. But without a holiday itinerary or a helpful guide, I didn’t understand how.

Birdwatchers can seem like a tough crowd to join. In my limited experience of encountering them on trips, they took things very seriously: out before the crack of dawn, back after dark, wielding very expensive cameras and scopes. I had imposter syndrome.

open image in gallery Ruffs in their breeding plumage ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

What happened next was a series of false starts. I snuck around, constantly in fear that “serious” birders would find out and tell me to stop. I’d surprise people precariously balanced on cliffs with timidly whispered questions. Eventually, I realised that random people in the forest aren’t always going to be your friend. What I really needed was a community.

Nothing gets people together like a spectacle. The turning point came last winter, with a word-of-mouth tip about the half a million starlings that perform murmurations on the Somerset Levels near me. I went for my birthday.

Finding my flock

Seeing the starlings, I managed to find my flock. People of all ages and experience levels are drawn to this event. I found female friends, also in their thirties, who wanted to join. Soon, every few weeks I was visiting the Somerset marshes and Severn Estuary: for migration staging, breeding season, nesting season.

India might have had colour, but the UK had its charms – we’re right on the East Atlantic Flyway, and our coastlines see many avian visitors. I love seeing something new in a landscape I thought I was familiar with, and having an outdoor hobby for winter, when shorter days make getting out for dawn and dusk easier prospects. I saw my first dipper in the Lake District and my first Manx shearwater on Lundy Island.

Despite my furtive early attempts, it’s not the solitary hobby I thought it would be. Birding bleeds into other interests – I take binoculars on hikes with friends; I’ve dragged people to osprey nest viewpoints. And it’s not isolating; you can’t help but spout enthusiasm for it to others.

open image in gallery A starling murmuration first inspired Eloise ( Getty Images / iStockPhotos )

A national pastime

I’m not alone – the RSPB, which manages more than 200 nature reserves in the UK, has reported a 47 per cent increase in regular birdwatchers across Britain in eight years, including a tenfold increase in 16 to 29-year-olds taking part.

For Jamie Wyver, editor of the RSPB Magazine, taking up the hobby is simple.

“One of the many wonderful things about birding as a hobby is just how easy it is to get started. A pair of binoculars really helps to open up the world of birds and nature but they’re not a must-have for beginners. Simply going out for a walk, taking time to really see and listen to the wildlife around is enough,” he says.

Birding apps are a huge help: “Being able to see or hear a bird, then use a phone to identify its calls, makes it so much more accessible and you’re building your own knowledge at the same time.” The UK is the second-largest user in the world of Merlin, an app trained to identify more than 1,000 bird species by song.

Starlings aside, there are plenty of other UK birding spectacles that bring people together. “Species like puffins, ospreys or golden eagles never fail to get the heart racing,” says Jamie. Meanwhile, the RSPB celebrates Dawn Chorus Day in early May, and organises a garden birdwatch in spring.

open image in gallery Puffins 'never fail to get the heart racing' ( Getty Images / iStockPhoto )



Birders on tour

My next step is to take birding on holiday. Rachael and Dan Brown are professional ecologists who run Wild Discovery, a wildlife watching tour company based in Scotland with trips in the UK and further afield. While serious birding trips can involve box-ticking lists of hundreds of species, beginners might spend more time learning about identification, and about seeing the bigger picture.

“There’s always a story behind the bird,” says Rachael, “whether it’s the huge migrations, or really weird nesting habits, or what they feed on, or how they interact with the animals. We take the pressure off that listing element.”

Have they seen a rise in interest in birding? “I think it’s becoming more socially acceptable to like birds and wildlife,” says Rachael. “Now you’ll see people walking around with binoculars. I never used to see that.”

open image in gallery Beginner wildlife trips focus on identification rather than box-ticking ( Getty Images / iStockPhoto )

Rachael’s partner, Dan, loves helping newer birders, reassuring me that my local hide is more welcoming than I initially thought. “If someone asks a question, we’re always there to help,” he says.

Rachael suggests that beginner birders look at volunteering opportunities – that’s how she met people when first moving to Scotland. There are ornithology clubs across the country, including local groups where birders readily share sightings and alerts for rare birds.

Organisations like the RSPB and the British Trust for Ornithology also have youth clubs.

“It doesn’t matter who you are, what your background is or level of interest,” says Rachael. “There are people out there who will be on exactly the same wavelength as you. You’re definitely not alone going into birding.”

open image in gallery The Scottish islands are home to some spectacular wildlife, including white-tailed sea eagles ( Getty Images / iStockPhoto )

Top places to visit for a beginners’ birdwatching holiday

“Visiting places like Mull in Scotland always provide unforgettable experiences,” says Jamie. In fact, there are plenty of sites around the Scottish islands, from Islay to the Western Isles. “Shetland is always, always a great one because you can see birds so well and so closely,” adds Dan.

In England, Jamie recommends Bempton Cliffs in Yorkshire, home to half a million seabirds. For me, the Somerset Levels, restored to provide habitat for bitterns in the 1990s, has become my patch, whilst Dan points out that the Isles of Scilly are famous for turning up rare birds.

Further afield, the Danube Delta Biosphere Reserve is Europe’s biggest reed bed and one of the world’s best-preserved river deltas, hosting migrating birds from as far away as Siberia and China and explorable by boat. In Southern Europe, Spain’s Donana National Park is one of the most vital protected areas for migrating birds on the continent.

For years, John Green has kept a note in his wallet that reads: “In 1990, 12 million children died under the age of five. Last year, fewer than five million did.” It’s a pocket-sized symbol of hard-boiled optimism. A reminder, he tells me, jetlagged and nursing a beer in a hotel lobby, “that hope is the correct response to this mess, as opposed to despair”.

Granted, carrying around a note like this is exactly the sort of thing a character in a John Green novel would do. The bestselling author fills his books with such irresistible quirks: the boy with cancer who smokes unlit cigarettes; the boy who collects the last words of famous people; the boy obsessed with anagrams. That Green, 49 years old and born and bred in Indiana, should support, of all the football teams in the world, AFC Wimbledon is another eccentricity worthy of his novels. He’s here in London for a match.

Green has been a staple of YA fiction ever since his 2005 debut Looking for Alaska made every girl who read it resent her parents for their unimaginative choice in baby names. But it was his 2012 novel The Fault in Our Stars, about two teenagers with cancer who fall in love, that propelled him, somewhat uncomfortably, into a tier of celebrity rare for novelists, with his work tweeted about by Kim Kardashian and parodied on Saturday Night Live. In 2014, Green was named one of Time Magazine’s most influential people, the same year a blockbuster adaptation of his novel hit cinemas.

Over the years, he and his brother Hank also amassed a tremendous following with their vlogs about mental health, bowel movements, medical injustice and everything in between; today that number stands at 4 million. His book signings were attended by thousands of fans – some of whom would show up at his house uninvited. It got to be too much for an introvert with anxiety and OCD. “The solution in the end was to get less famous,” Green laughs, “to write about Dr Pepper and tuberculosis for 10 years.” His non-fiction endeavours were no less successful – Green’s last two books, a collection of essays published in 2021 and a meticulously researched history of tuberculosis in 2025, both debuted at No 1 on The New York Times nonfiction bestseller list – but they put a safe distance between the author and his readers.

Green’s new novel, Hollywood Ending, is his first in nine years. It follows two young actors who are shooting a buzzy arthouse film based on the life of Andy Warhol; Juniper is a former child star seeking legitimacy and Kai is a promising unknown on the cusp of superstardom. Thrown together by this film, they navigate the choppy waters of their early twenties, their inherent complexities magnified times a billion by their celebrity.

Like a lot of his readers, I have, over the years, wondered what Green – teen whisperer – makes of the social media landscape facing today’s youth. For someone nearing 50, he is better placed than you’d think to answer. “I’ve been on the social internet for 20 years so I’ve seen both sides of it, good and bad… mostly bad these days,” says Green, who had 5 million followers on Twitter before he logged off for good in 2022. “And for a young actor, or just a young person, you can’t divorce your public self from your private self with any clarity. Everybody is exchanging their private selves for public attention in a way that’s mediated by these five or six super-rich guys.”

Green is still on YouTube, though, where together with his brother he makes videos about Chernobyl, infectious diseases, and Big Tech lies. “Hank and I talk about this all the time,” he says. “You know, are we part of the solution because we’re trying to make a certain kind of content and make educational videos – or are we part of the problem just because we’re participating in this toxic soup?” They haven’t quite landed on an answer yet.

In the book, social media is painted as both exhilarating and deadening. As the premiere approaches, Kai and Juniper see their follower counts tick up almost like a doomsday clock ticking down to some spiritual catastrophe. Green knows firsthand that those numbers mean nothing. “It changes my life not at all, except that it gets me in rooms that I otherwise couldn’t get into,” he says, recalling how exciting it had felt when he and his brother reached 2 million subscribers on YouTube. Hitting the third million and then the fourth, he says, “I remember thinking, well, this is starting to feel a little empty.”

open image in gallery John Green greets fans at the premiere of ‘The Fault in Our Stars’ ( Getty )

Hollywood Ending is Green’s first adult novel – which is not to say it is wildly different in tone. His protagonists may not be in their teens, but Hollywood Ending marks a return to that same intoxicating sphere of young adulthood so richly realised in his earlier books. For Green personally, that period was the most important of his own life. “It’s when a lot of doors close off to you,” says Green. “You have to start making choices. You can’t leave infinite doors open anymore. It’s a fascinating time. Very hard. I wouldn’t want to do it again. I found being 23 harder than being any other age.” Fourteen comes close.

It was also in his early twenties that he worked as a chaplain at a children’s hospital, six months that led directly to his interest in public health. Today, Green is a vocal spokesperson for global health equity, lobbying US congress and pharmaceutical companies and raising millions for health charities. It’s the reason he carries around that note in his pocket.

“I remember leaving the hospital for the last time and thinking I’ll never have a job that important, and I haven’t,” he says. “I saw a lot of kids die when I was a chaplain and it was really, really hard. I still feel angry about the tragedy of maternal and child death; nobody should die as a child for reasons that we know how to treat and prevent.”

open image in gallery Shailene Woodley and Ansel Elgort star as Hazel and Gus in ‘The Fault in Our Stars’ ( Twentieth Century Fox )

Reading a John Green book as an adult is a different experience to when you are a teenager. The first chapter ends with a handsome boy gifting a beautiful girl a drawing of herself, and features dialogue such as: “I act because I get a break from being my goddamn self.” It’s writing that invites you to lower your defences; it calls for you to roll on your back and expose your soft pink belly. It asks that you not be a cynic. A big ask, Green knows. “Irony is a form of armour and I’m always trying to disarm the reader,” he says. “It’s hard work because I know people bring a lot of cynicism and irony to the process of reading, and I totally get that. I do it too.”

I’d wager that Green does it less than your average adult. Nearly in his fifties, he has managed to hold on to the sort of endearing sincerity you shed after adolescence. “I am a very earnest person, achingly annoyingly earnest,” he says. “If it’s between erring on the side of coolness or the side of earnestness, I always am going to choose being earnest because I don’t want to be cold to the world or what the world has to show me.”

Some might call it cringe, I say with a smile, a word that has been applied to Green’s writing at various points, but a descriptor he doesn’t shy away from. “I find that actually, if you listen to conversations, people say cringy stuff pretty often,” he laughs. “It’s a very fine line between earnest and cringe and I’ve spent my whole career, even in my non-fiction writing, trying to find that line.”

If teenagers are reading Hamlet, they can read a John Green novel

He is less concerned about the line between adult and young adult fiction. “I think teens are infinitely intellectually capable,” he says. “There are ways that they think about death or loss or suffering that are different from the ways adults do, but they’re still thinking about it. I mean, most of the people who are going to read Hamlet this year are teens. If they’re reading Hamlet, they can read a John Green novel.”

Not everyone feels the same. Green is, if you can believe it, the author of the most banned book in the United States. Thanks to a fleeting moment of awkward oral sex, Looking for Alaska – an award-winning novel that had been studied at schools for its honest exploration of grief and love – is now barred from many of those same classrooms across Florida and Iowa. It’s also banned at Green’s former high school in Indiana, where he still lives. “It’s uncomfortable to be in the grocery store and know that two out of every 10 people in Indianapolis who recognise me recognise me as somebody they think is harming kids,” says Green. “My books were banned in the town north of me. My doctor’s there; I go there all the time, and it’s so weird to think that kids aren’t allowed to access my books in this school’s library.”

open image in gallery Over six novels, John Green made a name for himself as the king of YA ( Puffin Books / Dutton Juvenile )

What’s ironic is that most people banning the book have never read it. “I would say this about the social internet in general in 2026: the decontextualisation of story is everywhere and it’s infuriating,” he says. “We should have fewer opinions about books we haven’t read. Most people who have a [snarky] opinion on Twilight have never read Twilight.” For what it is worth, you will never catch Green saying a bad word about Twilight.

Green wishes to make clear that he is not the main character in the censorship story. “I often feel like they put me on these lists so they can say, ‘Look, we also ban books by white guys.’ Almost all the other books are by queer authors or authors of colour,” he says. “It bums me out mostly because it makes it so hard for librarians and teachers in the United States to do their jobs. The cost of teaching a book that’s controversial is potentially your career now.”

open image in gallery The cast of ‘Looking for Alaska’ ( Hulu )

As for the near-decade break from fiction, Green chalks it up to his inability to answer a simple question: what would the point be of another John Green novel? “I knew what other people’s fiction was for, but I didn’t know why there should be another book by me. What did I have to offer or contribute?” he says.

Eventually, he landed on an answer. “I wanted to write a book about how we survive what we have to survive and how essential it is to be un-alone,” says Greene, citing a moment in Hollywood Ending when a journalist asks Juniper what she wants viewers to take away from her movie. “Juniper says, ‘I want them to feel the power of art and the power of love,’ and her publicist tells her, ‘You have to say that without sounding like you’re puking.’ That’s what I want people to feel: the power of art and the power of love – but I have to say it without puking.” John Green, still the most earnest man alive.

‘Hollywood Ending’ is published by Penguin Random House and is out now

News.title: Carreras’ try-of-season contender helps Bath eclipse Harlequins
News.content:
And they kept playing, it was not until Richards scored in the 72nd minute that the game was decided. Still for Bath, a five-try victory away from home, felt like a decent return.

If they were to stand any chance of finding a way back into the game, Quins had to score first after the restart. They were rewarded for their attacking intent after running from a scrum deep in their half, with Murley cutting a brilliant line before Pedro Delgado drove over for his side’s third try.

Quins had the opportunity to further cut the deficit when first Sam Riley carried down the left wing and Cameron Anderson drove into the Bath 22. But as Quins looked to pick and go, Beno Obano and Guy Pepper combined to hold the ball up over the line.

It felt like a significant moment and when Riley was shown a yellow card for a high tackle on Obano moments later, the odds against a Quins comeback lengthened again. Yet there was something sticky about their resilience.

“I am really happy with the grit and the fight that they showed, particularly in the second half,” said Gilmore. “We had some massive defensive sets on our goal-line which we withstood. I reckon they were the moments last year that Bath would probably run in three tries really quickly and kick the score out, which is good.”

Bath emptied their bench, including the introduction of England flanker Pepper, but they could not pull away as expected in the final quarter, despite some impressive contributions by Tom de Glanville.

It was left to their line-out maul to score their first points of the second half, with Richards touching down to seal Harlequins’ fate. Still, there were enough promising glimpses to give Harlequins supporters hope that more encouraging days lie ahead.

News.title: Manchester City found guilty of 114 charges
News.content:
Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules. It is a decision that, if upheld, would equate to one of the biggest scandals in football history.

City face a range of sanctions from a fine to points deductions and even expulsion from the Premier League. Or a combination of all, under rule W51 of its handbook. No punishment has yet been announced.

If the verdict is upheld, with City expected to appeal, it will also raise question marks over the 20 trophies the club have won under Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, whose Abu Dhabi group took over in 2008.

The charges can be broken down into five categories and relate to a period from 2009-23 in which City won six League Cups, three FA Cups, seven league titles and the Champions League. There is the provision for removing past titles, but that would appear remote.

Of the 115 charges:

Fifty-four were for failing to provide accurate financial information from 2009-10 to 2017-18

Fourteen were for failing to provide accurate details for player and manager payments from the same period

Five were for failing to comply with Uefa’s rules from 2013-14 to 2017-18

Seven were for breaching Premier League profitability and sustainability rules from 2015-16 to 2017-18

Thirty-five were for failing to co-operate with the investigation from 2018-23.

City have been the dominant force in English football for most of that time, but that status is under threat with a verdict that will send shockwaves around Europe and could have huge ramifications for the club.

That is unless they can win an appeal, with sources cautioning it still may take up to another two to three years for the case to be resolved, following on from an already five-year investigation.

Case is far from being resolved

The Premier League’s rules provide for an independent appeal board with broad powers, including the ability to uphold, vary or overturn the independent commission’s decision.

It would therefore appear that despite the verdict, the case is far from being resolved and punishment decided. The details of the commission’s findings, when published, will be crucial to determining what happens next.

But if it is upheld, the verdict also opens up the possibility of City facing legal action from other clubs who feel they missed out on trophies and even merit money from league placings.

It is understood Premier League clubs are already discussing legal action and possible compensation claims as a result of the guilty verdict.

News.title: Britain sends team to South Sudan as country braces for Ebola
News.content:
British Ebola specialists have been deployed to South Sudan because of fears the haemorrhagic fever will spread from neighbouring Congo.

A rare form of Ebola, known as the Bundibugyo species, is spreading rapidly in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where more than 7,800 people have caught the virus since May, 3,700 of whom have died.

To prepare for the threat of imported cases, Britain has positioned three experts in and around the South Sudanese capital, Juba. They will assist and train local authorities on infection control, set up awareness campaigns for local communities, and test people crossing the border for the virus.

The team is employed by the UK Health Security Agency’s (UKHSA) Public Health Rapid Support Team (PHRST), which is regularly sent to the epicentre of disease outbreaks overseas – for instant the cruise ship at the centre of a deadly hantavirus in the South Atlantic earlier this year.

The current Ebola outbreak is the fastest-growing ever recorded and is on course to become the largest in history, overtaking the 2014-16 West Africa Ebola outbreak, in which around 30,000 people contracted the haemorrhagic fever and roughly a third died.

Experts fear it is only a matter of time before the virus spreads to South Sudan, which shares a 500-mile border with the DRC. Thousands of people cross the frontier each day to work, attend school and trade goods, mostly fish, in lucrative markets between the two countries.

If the virus gained a foothold in South Sudan, which became the newest country on earth after severing ties with Khartoum in 2011, experts fear the consequences would be catastrophic and worsen an already dire humanitarian situation.

“It’s so variable as to where the outbreak is spreading at the moment, there are cases from some of the border towns [with South Sudan],” Ed Newman, director of the PHRST, told The Telegraph.

“There’s a feeling [Ebola could spread] any day. Maybe you could say we’ve been lucky so far,” Mr Newman said, on the sidelines of a UKHSA conference in Manchester.

News.title: Russell capitalises on Antonelli error to take Azerbaijan GP pole
News.content:
Russell – who begins the weekend 81 points behind the Italian – simply has to capitalise. And he really should do. Even if Antonelli hadn’t crashed out, he has looked on a different level this weekend, dominating practice and qualifying. Russell topped Q1, Q3 and Q3, securing the 12th pole of his career with a lap which was nine tenths quicker than his best lap in Q2 and eight tenths quicker than Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, the next fastest driver. He could hardly believe it himself.

“That was a pretty decent lap,” he told his team over the radio on his cooldown lap. “How much was [the gap]?”

“Just over eight tenths to Leclerc.” came the response. “Woah!”

This has not been the easiest season for Russell, who began the year the overwhelming favourite for the title, having dominated his younger team-mate over the course of last season. So he could be forgiven for feeling proud of having done such a good job.

“It’s been a while so it definitely feels good,” he admitted. “This was probably the biggest pole margin of my whole career, including my F2 and F3 days.

“The lap felt really sweet, car’s been feeling really great this weekend. On a track like this where you can hug it, it feels amazing.”

News.title: Buttler injury derails England chase and sends Sri Lanka series to decider
News.content:
Enter Buttler to play a wonderful counter-attack, whacking Wellalage for four and six and dumping leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage over the rope twice as he raced to 41 off 22 balls.

Buttler was at a crossroads after the T20 World Cup in February. Despite England making the semi-finals, he averaged just 10 in the tournament to complete a third poor World Cup in a row. A break with his family, and a very good Indian Premier League, where he made a crucial technical correction, changed his fortunes.

Matthew Hayden, the batting coach at the Gujarat Titans, asked him whether he was watching the ball closely enough. Buttler discovered that, now 36, he is a right-eye dominant batsman, so with Hayden’s help he opened up his stance to give himself a better view of the ball. A summer rich in runs has followed with an average of 51 for England and a strut back in his body language. The injury has surely ended Buttler’s summer and there are worries that he could be out of the Pakistan ODI triangular tournament next month as well, just to add to the night’s woes.

This was not a vintage England performance. Atkinson made a crucial error on the boundary, dropping a straightforward chance off Kusal Mendis on 17. It kickstarted Mendis, who went on the charge smashing 51 in 24 balls. He put on 137 in 120 balls with Kuminda Mendis. Josh Tongue had an off day going at seven an over and Jofra Archer was given similar treatment, although he bowled better than figures suggest, as anything wayward with pace on the ball was hit away.

Overton was more effective with his cutters and slower balls, while Ahmed did at least bag a couple of wickets, credit for keeping his head after some early rough treatment. Kusal Mendis was given out leg before on 99 but overturned the decision and stroked a four next ball for a deserved hundred.

News.title: Oil jumps after Saudi thwarts missile attack
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. A global rout in bond markets deepened overnight as traders expect the US to keep raising interest rates.

Japan’s 10-year bond yield surged to 3.08pc on Thursday, its highest level since 1996, as markets responded to stronger than expected US economic data and higher oil prices.

It followed sharp rises in the US on Wednesday, when the yield on 10-year Treasuries – a benchmark of global borrowing costs – surged as high as 5.12pc, up from 4.96pc. It was the biggest jump since the “liberation day” tariff turmoil in April last year.

Bonds were sent into turmoil as traders bet that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates three times by April next year in an effort to bring down inflation. Money markets suggest there is a 70pc chance of the Fed following this month’s first rate rise in three years with a second in October.

This followed closely watched industry data on Wednesday, known as PMIs, showed US private sector activity jumped unexpectedly to a five-year high in September.

Meanwhile, oil prices spiked 3.9pc on Wednesday to move back above $100 a barrel, risking an inflationary spiral in the world economy.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “The main driver was a strong batch of PMIs, along with a rebound in oil prices, which both led to mounting speculation about faster rate hikes.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) US borrowing costs hit highest since 2007 on fears economy overheating | Yield on 10-year Treasuries soars amid inflation concerns as oil prices rise

2) Diesel prices surge as Trump mulls 90-day US export ban | Pump prices could exceed £3 per litre in Britain if Washington imposes ‘catastrophic’ block on exports

3) England’s first new reservoir in 30 years delayed despite drought warnings | Havant Thicket, in Hampshire, will now be completed in 2034, five years after initially planned

4) Timpson customers ask for extra belt holes after weight-loss jabs | Boss of key cutting chain credits Ozempic and Mounjaro after surge in requests

5) Chinese carmaker’s new EV battery will charge in under five minutes | Geely says its latest system is fastest in industry as brands approach ‘physical limit’

What happened overnight

Debt markets were in turmoil after Japanese bond yields hit 30-year highs.

As Tokyo markets reopened after a three-day holiday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond yield jumped to its highest level since 1996.

This came after a steep sell-off in the US market overnight. Oil prices remained around $103 a barrel and the dollar held gains after Tehran’s leader vowed to never surrender following a warning by Donald Trump that he could “annihilate” Iran.

Japan’s benchmark stock market, the Nikkei 225 rose 1pc to 65,645.10, as some chipmakers got a boost from the recent interest in AI. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.7pc to 8,702.00.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng lost 0.3pc to 24,762.39, while the Shanghai Composite dipped 0.9pc to 4,545.09. Trading was closed in South Korea for the Chuseok autumn harvest holiday.

News.title: Zelensky lashes out at EU
News.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky lashed out at the European Union over its moves to weaken sanctions on Russian oligarchs.

In his address to the UN General Assembly, the Ukrainian leader warned that beyond making life “more comfortable” for Russians, “it also gives the war more time for Putin to send poor people into the kill zone. So Russia’s revenues must remain a target.”

His criticism came after France and Luxembourg successfully pushed for sanctions exemptions for Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, Russian oligarchs, on Tuesday.

Kyiv branded the decision “shameful and unjustifiable”. The men are known to share close ties to Vladimir Putin and have net worths of $14bn and $16bn, respectively.

In his fourth address to the UN as a wartime leader, Mr Zelensky said it was paramount that the international community increased pressure on the Kremlin to stop “the madness” of the war spreading.

Under pressure from Donald Trump to halt attacks on Russian energy targets, Mr Zelensky defended his country’s aerial offensive for successfully depriving Putin of revenue for his war.

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said.

‘End the war before winter’

Washington has recently attempted to revive the long-stalled negotiations between Ukraine and Russia. On Tuesday, Mr Zelensky implored Mr Trump to help Kyiv end the war “before winter”.

Mr Trump appeared optimistic, suggesting an agreement would happen “more quickly than people understand”.

Sergei Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that Russia was prepared to negotiate for a lasting peace but would not “pause the war”.

Mr Zelensky sought to remind world leaders that the conflict was not constrained within Ukraine’s borders at a time when the global community was distracted by a myriad of conflicts and crises.

Citing the support of Iran and North Korea for Russia, he warned that Putin’s war kept “spreading further”.

“Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and take another country instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” Mr Zelensky said at the UN.

He noted that fighters from at least 47 countries were helping to prosecute Moscow’s war against Ukraine and urged leaders to prevent their citizens from being dragged into the conflict.

After Mr Zelensky’s address, reports emerged that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s envoy, was on his way to the US where he would meet Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Trump administration representatives.

Sources told Reuters that the meeting would take place in New ‌York on the sidelines of the UN summit.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, also confirmed Mr Trump had invited his Russian counterpart to attend the G20 summit of world leaders in Miami in December.

Sports.title: Football isn’t rugby and it isn’t cricket, it can bring out the worst in people – booze ban end must be trialled first
Sports.content:
Next

ANDY BURNHAM wants to give football fans their beer back.

His argument is that if you can sit in a rugby stadium, at the cricket or at a concert with a pint in your hand, why shouldn’t you be able to do the same at a football match?



Because football isn’t rugby. It isn’t cricket. And it certainly isn’t an Oasis concert.

Football brings out the very best in people. It can bring strangers together, create friendships that last a lifetime and turn 50,000 people into one enormous choir.



However, it also can bring out the worst in people.

The chanting can be disgusting. The racism can be vile. The sexism can be ugly.

The tribalism that makes football so intoxicating when it is positive can become something altogether less attractive when it turns nasty.

Now add alcohol. What could possibly go wrong?

I know, I know. Most football supporters can drink a pint without suddenly becoming a hooligan.

Most people can consume alcohol responsibly.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Most supporters are also perfectly capable of celebrating a goal without climbing on the roof of the stadium and setting fire to a corner flag.

But laws are not usually written around what most people do.

They are written around what happens when things go wrong.

The ban on drinking alcohol in sight of the pitch was introduced back in 1985, when football violence was a very real and very serious problem that needed tackling.



The legislation was part of a wider attempt to deal with the culture of hooliganism that had blighted the game.

Football has changed enormously since then.

Stadiums are safer. Crowds are different. And families are more prominent.

The game is now a global entertainment business, rather than the preserve of a particular sort of supporter.



And there have already been trials allowing alcohol in the stands in the women’s game.

While the Football Supporters’ Association and many clubs support looking again at the rules.

So perhaps the Prime Minister has a point.

There is also something rather appealing about his instinct to challenge old rules simply because they are old.



But football is still football.

The UK Football Policing Unit have warned that it would be “incredibly rash” to change the rules without proper examination and consultation.

They also point out that alcohol can play a significant role in violent and disorderly behaviour among a minority of football supporters.

The question should be whether the ban still works.



And if the answer is that it doesn’t, then prove it. Trial it.

Do it in selected stadiums. Do it at selected matches. Have proper monitoring.

Look at arrests, disorder, assaults, stewarding incidents and complaints.

See whether supporters actually drink more or whether they simply stop disappearing to the pub before kick-off and consume their beer more slowly.



Then we will have evidence, rather than ideology.

Because there is another problem with the idea — when someone scores a goal, what happens?

We already have fans jumping up, hugging strangers and losing whatever remains of their common sense.

Give every one of them a pint in their hand and, suddenly, the goal celebration risks becoming a beer shower.



Which, in England, would at least have the advantage of being warm.

Nobody should pretend football has exactly the same relationship with alcohol as a day at the cricket. It doesn’t.

Perhaps the blanket ban is no longer necessary.

Football has changed enormously since 1985 and the behaviour of the vast majority of supporters has changed with it.



But if we are going to change the rules, let’s not do it because a politician wants to be seen as the man who gave football its pint back.

Do it because the evidence says it is safe.

Trial it. Monitor it. Measure what happens when the beer is in the stands, rather than in the concourse.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Because if it works, everyone gets what they want.

And if it doesn’t, we may discover that the one thing football supporters really didn’t need was something else to throw when their team concedes.

Sports.title: Rodri breaks silence on Man City’s guilty verdict as he becomes first player to speak out about 115 charges

RODRI declared no one can strip Manchester City of their titles and said he still believes they are innocent.

That is despite his former club being found guilty on a bombshell 114 of the 115 charges leveled against them by the Premier League.



City have always denied any wrongdoing and will appeal the verdict.

Rodri won four Premier League titles, five domestic cups and the Champions League under Pep Guardiola, but insists their silverware was not won with money.



The Spain international cited the club’s 2020 Court of Arbitration for Sport case, in which a two-year Uefa ban for breaching Financial Fair Play rules was overturned, as a reason to believe the club are innocent.

Rodri said: “We faced something similar in 2020, a similar judicial process.A different accusation but similar process.



“There as well in the first instance we were found guilty but we believed in the club and the innocence that the club maintained and in the end we were acquitted.

“I believe in the justice system and I believe in the innocence of the club.

“What we did, they cannot take it out of us. It is something that is not paid by money, it is paid with effort, partnership and being shoulder to shoulder every day.

“We had a lot of success over the years and here at Wembley so I can tell you everything was deserved and we had one of the best eras of English football.”

Sports.title: Man City charges - what happens now?
Sports.content:
Reports claim that an independent tribunal has reached decisions in Manchester City's 115 charges case. Sky Sports analyses what could happen next in the inquiry...

What is the appeals process?

If any of the breaches are proven, it is highly likely Manchester City will appeal. In this case, both sides can appeal within 14 days of the judgment.

Any appeal would be heard by a new three-person commission.

A judgement can be appealed on grounds such as fraud, misconduct, or gross unfairness by the arbitrator. City cannot appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).

In 2014, City chairman Khaldoon al-Mubarak said he would rather spend £30m on the best 50 lawyers in the world and sue UEFA for the next 10 years than agree a financial penalty for alleged Financial Fair Play breaches.

Premier League rules on appeals and role of the Appeal Board

A party to the proceedings that wishes to challenge a decision of the Commission may do so under Section W of the Premier League Rules.

An Appeal Board is appointed by the chair of the independent judicial panel, Sir Gary Hickinbottom, and must have three members, one of whom should have held judicial office, and would sit as the chair of the Appeal Board.

The proceedings of the Appeal Board are confidential and heard in private.

The Appeal Board has wide discretion in respect of the appeal, and may allow it, dismiss it, or make any order that it deems fit (including varying the order of Commission).

What are the potential punishments?

There are a range of sanctions available to the independent commission which include fines, points deductions and other sporting sanctions.

The Premier League do not have set sanctions for financial rule breaches. Clubs decided not to have them because there were fears clubs would break the rules and just take the punishment if they knew what the punishment was going to be.

In February 2025, Richard Masters said the Premier League were looking at having a Sanctions Grid - setting out agreed sanctions for different rules breaches.

Everton were deducted six points on appeal during the 2023/24 season and then two points for profit and sustainability rules (PSR) breaches. Nottingham Forest were deducted four points in the same season.

In the 2008/09 season, Luton Town were deducted 30 points (10 points for illegal payments to agents and 20 points for exiting administration without a Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA).

In 2021/22 seson, Derby County were deducted 21 points (12 points for entering administration and nine points for financial irregularities).

Can sanctions be imposed while an appeal is under way?

There would be a separate hearing to determine sanctions.

Would the appeal be the end of the matter?

The appeal would be the end of this part of the process. No appeal to CAS would be possible.

There would likely to be more legal cases though, with clubs potentially taking action against City over missing out on trophies and Champions League qualification.

Sports.title: Lankshear scores on debut as England U21s beat Kazakhstan
Sports.content:
England came from behind to beat Kazakhstan 4-2 in an entertaining affair at Molineux to all but book their place at the European U21 Championship next year.

Slovakia's defeat to the Republic of Ireland earlier meant England's win put them six points clear with two games left, with a hugely superior goal difference and on the brink of qualification for the tournament in Albania and Serbia.

Kazakhstan sit at the bottom of Group D and their last win in the competition came in June 2025, so it was a big shock when they took the lead over the group leaders in the third minute courtesy of Artyom Litosh's close-range strike.

England soon showed their quality, though they required some luck when Ali Turganov's own goal got them level before Chelsea defender Josh Acheampong produced a striker's finish to put them in front.

Kazakhstan again stunned Molineux to get level through Saif Popov before the break but England managed to secure the win through Max Alleyne's second-half strike before Will Lankshear's debut goal wrapped up the points.

Many expected England to make a quick start but it was the minnows who put themselves in front when Miras Omatay's corner landed at the feet of Litosh who was left unmarked six yards out to poke home in the third minute.

The Young Lions were level after Kazakhstan tried to get rid of a ball into the box, but a clearance from Sultan Askarov ricocheted off the back of Turganov to get them level.

Lee Carsley's side were in front six minutes later when Chelsea youngster Acheampong lined one up from range and fired into the bottom left corner with a pinpoint strike.

The game developed into shooting practice for England, however, against the run of play, Kazakhstan came biting back again and after Popov saw his first effort saved by James Beadle, it bounced back in his favour to turn home the rebound.

A neatly worked free-kick routine got England's noses back in front as Ethan Nwaneri's floated free-kick was nodded back across by Acheampong who turned provider for fellow centre-back Alleyne to sweep home.

Beadle was called into action again to stop Kazakhstan from equalising at the end before Lankshear went down the other end and poked home from Jobe Bellingham's cross to seal the win.

Sports.title: Warrington reach Grand Final after penalty drama and Leeds' last-kick miss
Sports.content:
Warrington Wolves are into the Grand Final for the first time since 2018; The two points came from a penalty for an escort on George Williams; The play-offs are under way, live on Sky Sports, and continue through until the Grand Final from Old Trafford on October 3

Warrington Wolves through to Super League Grand Final after controversial penalty with 14-12 win over Leeds Rhinos

Highlights from the Super League semi-final clash between Leeds Rhinos and Warrington Wolves.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Warrington Wolves made it through to the Super League Grand Final with a 14-12 victory over Leeds Rhinos, a controversial penalty proving the difference at Headingley Stadium.

It marks Warrington's first Grand Final since 2018 and they have never been victors in the big dance before. Leeds, meanwhile, are left waiting once again, with their last Grand Final victory coming all the way back in 2017.

The flashpoint of the match came in the 66th minute when James McDonnell was pinged for an escort on George Williams. It appeared as though Williams had potentially run into the Leeds man's line, but despite the Rhinos using their Captain's Challenge the decision was upheld and Ewan Irwin sent over the conversion to win the game.

Remarkably, with no time remaining on the clock, Jake Connor attempted to send over a penalty for Leeds from 62 metres out to level the game but could not get enough power on it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Warrington Wolves charged ahead of Leeds Rhinos after a controversial penalty call.

The game was level at 12-12 at the break in what was an enthralling contest. Leeds Rhinos had got onto the scoreboard through converted tries from Ryan Hall and Jake Connor, while Warrington had gone over through James Bentley and Luke Yates.

Warrington will find out their opponent for the Grand Final on Saturday when Wigan Warriors host Wakefield Trinity, live on Sky Sports, with kick-off at 5.30pm.

The Super League Grand Final then takes place on Saturday October 3, with kick-off at 6pm, live on Sky Sports.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jake Connor and Leeds choose to kick the penalty to tie the game from over 60 metres which lands well short after controversial penalty call in the last minute of the match.

Penalty the difference as Warrington into big dance for first time since 2018

The strategies of both teams became clear early on. Leeds, rocked by the losses of backs Lachie Miller, Maika Sivo, Ash Handley and Jack Bird, put their emphasis through the middle, relying on their pack to win the attritional battle.

Meanwhile, Warrington put their focus on an aerial bombardment of Hall at the end of their sets. That paid dividends as early as the fifth minute when Matty Ashton out-jumped the try-scoring legend and found Toby King, who passed in field to Bentley for the former Rhino to open the scoring.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Williams' pinpoint kick finds Matty Ashton, who brilliantly keeps the move alive before teeing up Toby King to send James Bentley over to give Warrington the lead.

But Leeds would hit back 12 minutes later. Hall would get the better of Ashton this time as the Warrington flier made a defensive misread and slipped, giving Hall the space to score from Brodie Croft's cut-out pass.

Warrington wasted a gilt-edged chance soon after, with Albert Hopoate unable to ground a Williams grubber despite having no Leeds defenders around him.

The Rhinos punished them within minutes. It was a try crafted and finished by Connor. The current Man of Steel kicked over the Warrington defence, Ned McCormack got there first, passed to Kallum Watkins, who drew the last defender and put Connor away for a score. His two conversions gave Leeds a 12-6 lead.

That, however, was nullified before the break. Williams' flat pass found Luke Yates, who wriggled out of Cooper Jenkins' grasp to score by the sticks. Irwin's second goal put the game level at half-time.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A brilliant piece of skill from Jake Connor sees him chip over for Ned McCormack and Kallum Watkins is then brought into play before returning the ball to Connor, who rolls over to score.

The second half was an attritional battle, with neither side giving an inch. They both made errors with the ball but were unrelenting in defence.

The breakthrough eventually came, in controversial circumstances. McDonnell was adjudged to have taken out Williams while chasing a kick, albeit it appeared harsh. Leeds' Captain's Challenge was unsuccessful and Irwin slotted over the penalty for a two-point lead.

The drama wasn't over though. While Warrington handled the closing period well, there were moments. Connor thought he'd come up with a clutch 40/20 out of nothing, only for Warrington to successfully overturn the call as Keenan Palasia had offloaded after the tackle was completed.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the moment the full-time whistle blew and Warrington secured their place in the 2026 Grand Final with scenes of heartbreak for Leeds Rhinos.

Then, with the final play of the game, Leeds received a penalty, and Connor opted to go for two to level the game from 62 metres out.

Headingley held its breath, but his kick fell short, allowing Warrington to kick the ball dead and secure their passage to Old Trafford.

Just 12 months earlier in the play-offs St Helens had a penalty from 60 metres out with no time remaining but opted to kick to touch and stunned Leeds with their 'Left to Wright' finish. The Rhinos will never know if they could have done the same.

Arthur: That penalty call should not deciding game of this magnitude | Burgess: There's nothing to celebrate about yet

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jon Wilkin has his say on the controversial penalty call that rewarded Warrington Wolves with the win over the Leeds Rhinos.

Leeds Rhinos head coach Brad Arthur to Sky Sports:

"It's a tough loss. I'm extremely proud of the boys.

"Everything that could go wrong probably did this week. But we didn't use it as an excuse.

"We fought really hard, and I'm really disappointed. I feel like the game has been decided by a really tough penalty.

"That penalty should not be deciding a game of that magnitude.

"There was plenty of fight, but in the end it wasn't enough. The only thing we could control was our attitude, and ours was excellent.

"We didn't want it to end this way. It would have been nice to let the two teams decide the result I reckon."

Warrington Wolves head coach Sam Burgess to Sky Sports:

"There's nothing to celebrate about yet.

"It's out of our hands in that moment [Connor's penalty], so what was going to be was going to be.

"I'd composed myself either way. You've got to save the emotion.

"I was nervous, and I wanted us to experience this as a group together, getting to the final week of the season.

"We want to enjoy this week and make the most of it. And get our best performance onto the field. We want to do eveyrthing that will help that."

Saturday September 19: Warrington Wolves 35-12 Hull KR

Semi-finals

Semi-Final 1 - Friday September 25: Leeds Rhinos 12-14 Warrington Wolves

Semi-Final 2 - Saturday September 26: Wigan Warriors v Wakefield Trinity, 5.30pm KO on Sky Sports

Sports.title: White promoting Fury-AJ: 'Who's going to stop me?'
Sports.content:
Dana White, one of the most powerful figures in combat sport, has reaffirmed his involvement in staging the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua mega-fight

The heavyweight superstars have nursed a rivalry for more than a decade, but only now has a fight between the pair been finalised, with the show set for December 11 at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff.

"I think it's a fight that people have been waiting for, for over 10 years. So to finally have it done, I'm sure boxing fans are excited," White told Sky Sports News.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tyson Fury says he's using the Anthony Joshua fight as a warm-up to take on Oleksandr Usyk. Credit: FurociTV.

The announcement for the richly anticipated mega-fight stated that Saudi financier Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and White were staging the bout, although Eddie Hearn, who promotes Joshua, has publicly claimed the American cannot be involved.

"Well, I think that the press release speaks for itself," White responded. "I've been saying since the beginning of the talks of this fight that I was going to be involved in the promotion of it.

"I mean Eddie Hearn must spend 24 hours a day doing interviews. I've never seen a guy do more interviews in my life, but it's all good.

"It's all good for the fight and I think a lot of people have become aware of the fight by the fight not being done yet.

"You think Netflix [care] what Eddie Hearn thinks? I guarantee they do not. I mean: 'not involved in the promotion of the fight', I'm sitting here promoting the fight right now

"Who's going to stop me?"

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Johnny Nelson shares his thoughts on Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua, with the fight being announced to take place in Cardiff on 11 December.

Hearn has also suggested holding the all-British clash in the UK is a victory for Joshua's side.

"What did I lose? What have I lost? I promise you I've lost nothing," White said. "I am not involved in either side of this thing. I'm involved on the Turki side."

The Fury vs Joshua main event is expected to take place in the early hours of the morning on December 12, catering to a global audience.

After plenty of speculation that the fight could be held in the US, Wales' Principality Stadium, which crucially has a roof, was ultimately selected as the venue.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Andy Scott and John Dennen react to the news that Tyson Fury will fight Anthony Joshua in Cardiff on 11 December.

"There was a lot of behind-the-scenes stuff going on," White said. "In these types of fights, especially when you have a guy who's putting the money up being Turki Alalshikh, you go where the money is and try to create as much revenue as you can.

"The fighters are getting paid. Everybody's got to make some money.

"So we ended up doing it in a stadium where we didn't have to worry about timing as much. You can close the roof and the fight with two British heavyweight champions stays in the UK."

Sports.title: Tuchel questions whether Palmer is desperate to play for England
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel is unsure how desperate Cole Palmer is to play for England.

Palmer was a controversial omission from England's World Cup squad in the summer, with an injury-hit season impacting his form.

After a summer off, it appeared Palmer was returning to a high level in the early weeks of this campaign, with six goal involvements in seven games for Chelsea. That output earned him a recall to the England group for the Nations League matches with Spain, Czech Republic and Croatia - but Palmer withdrew from the squad due to injury.

It is the second time Palmer has been called up for the national team and then withdrawn with a fitness problem since Tuchel took charge of England at the start of 2025. Palmer has also missed three England camps entirely with injury and wasn't selected for another.

Put to him that Palmer doesn't seem desperate to play for England, Tuchel responded: "It's hard to argue against what you're saying."

Image: Palmer has played in two of eight England camps under Tuchel

Asked where that leaves England, Tuchel replied: "It leaves us with Jude Bellingham, Morgan Rogers, Morgan Gibbs-White and Eberechi Eze.

"All in camp, all desperate to be here, all available and all ready to go. Ready to stop a holiday after one day in Dubai [as was the case with Gibbs-White] and fly back."

Tuchel added: "I can only judge him on what he [Palmer] is delivering for the national team and he's just missing too many opportunities.

"If Declan [Rice] calls me, and he explains to me, and I see against Brighton straight away that something is off that confirmed that impression, every case is different.

Image: Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice misses out through injury

"I know from Marcus [Rashford] and Kobbie [Mainoo] that they play with discomfort for their clubs. I know it looks strange if Kobbie and Marcus finish a game at the weekend for their clubs and then suddenly are not here, but okay - first of all, in doubt, we trust the players.

"I have no reason not to trust the players because they were with us in the US and they were fantastic. Tino Livramento also pulled out. This is normal.

"I just refuse to put too much into it. I refuse to believe it."

Palmer 'misses too many opportunities'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Tuchel was 'surprised' players wouldn't want to play for England and feels Palmer has missed too many opportunities

Palmer has played three times for Tuchel, across two camps, and the England boss had said earlier that his lack of availability is a problem.

"For sure it's a missed opportunity," Tuchel said.

"It's another missed opportunity. He misses too many opportunities.

"I don't blame him for it, it's just a fact. He misses way too many camps with injuries.

"I only want to rely on what I personally witness and see within my team. For that you have to be in camp. If you are not in camp there is a next level to impress that you cannot achieve because you can only do it with me on the pitch and with us on the pitch. It is a missed opportunity."

Palmer's availability for Tuchel's England camps March 2025: Palmer called up but then injured before camp

May 2025: Palmer called up and played away to Andorra

August 2025: Palmer not called up, suffering with groin issue

October 2025: Palmer not called up due to injury

November 2025: Palmer not called up amid continuing fitness issue

March 2026: Palmer called up and played against Uruguay and Japan

May 2026: Palmer available but not selected for World Cup

September 2026: Palmer called up, withdrew due to injury

Palmer played the full 90 minutes for Chelsea at Brentford on the Friday before the international break began. Asked what the specific injury issue is for Palmer, Tuchel rejected the suggestion this was a case of the forward's workload being managed.

"He plays with discomfort and pain and cannot play on the highest level with discomfort and pain," said Tuchel. "Chelsea informed us. That is my understanding. We're not managing load.

"This is not an 'international break'. It's a competitive environment, where the players love to train and be together. That's what we created. We will never compromise on that.

"We will never let this feeling creep in that the players don't want to come [to England camps]. We focus on the guys who absolutely want to play for England."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Palmer got off to a flying start in the 2026-27 Premier League season

Analysis: Is Tuchel losing patience with Palmer?

Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol:

"It sounds like Thomas Tuchel is almost losing patience with Cole Palmer because for the past two years since Tuchel has been the England manager, Palmer has hardly ever featured for England, he always seems to be injured.

"But Palmer has started every game apart from one for Chelsea this season - and I'd put money on the fact he'll be playing for Chelsea as soon as the international break is over.

"Tuchel basically said, 'if you're not here, you can't impress me' and it opens the door for someone else to impress the England manager.

"If you still want to impress Tuchel, you can still join up and take part in the England camp. There have been instances in the past, like Jude Bellingham - when he was going through a rocky spell in his relationship with Tuchel and he was injured - he still went joined up on international duty and that impressed Tuchel.

"So you have to ask why Palmer is not involved with England at all for the whole three weeks. Is his injury really that bad that it stops him playing or training, or showing his face at all?

"Palmer is also fighting to be the England No 10. England have also got Bellingham and Morgan Rogers so in Tuchel's mind, he doesn't feel that he needs Palmer that much because he has other options.

"Morgan Gibbs-White as well, who is going to have the opportunity to impress him over the next couple of weeks."

Kane: Everyone proud to play for England

Palmer is one of five players to have withdrawn from the original squad named by Tuchel, with Declan Rice, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford and Tino Livramento also making way.

England captain Harry Kane was asked about those withdrawals and whether he was concerned players weren't prioritising playing for their country enough at this stage of the season and international cycle after the World Cup.

"Everyone is extremely proud to be an England player," he said.

"Everyone has their own individual circumstances, physical situations, mental situations. That's down to the player and coach to talk and sort out.

"It's going to be a bit of a gruelling schedule [playing four games in 11 days] but I look forward to those things.

"Ultimately it's about what you do on the training pitch - and from the start of this week it's been at the highest level."
