World.title: OpenAI bots meddled with multiple US government agency sites
World.content:
OpenAI has acknowledged that it alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been meddled with by its AI bots acting improperly.

AI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions", including the SEC, Census Bureau and Education Department, the company said.

The disclosures come just days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that OpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme, Medicare.

Since August, public fears have grown around the potentially serious, even life-threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control.

OpenAI said that some of the data was accessed by AI agents, essentially bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, which were working to find "authoritative sources of public information".

But the company noted that some of the bots went beyond that and worked to bypass security measures on websites.

When attempting to get information from the Census Bureau, for instance, AI agents used tools reserved for software developers to access it, the company said.

OpenAI said all of the government data accessed by bots was public.

However, it noted that information that its bots accessed from the SEC, which regulates the US stock market and protects investors, was later published by AI agents on another website. OpenAI says this action was not intended.

In other instances that OpenAI disclosed on Friday, its AI agents transferred data when it should not have.

Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.

The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had opted in to allow OpenAI to train models using their data.

Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted: "This is not an appropriate use of this data".

It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.

Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog.

In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools "bypassed" security controls of some websites.

In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended.

OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details.

"Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said.

Not all of the instances involved in this incident were being considered a significant security breach, the company noted.

"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address."

World.title: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
World.content:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.

Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that this could be done "if the necessary conditions are met" and said these were contained within the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June.

"The choice now rests with the United States," he said, adding the plan was delivered to the US via Qatar.

Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC positive discussions were taking place through mediators, including about nuclear issues.

While the US has yet to deliver its official response to the proposal, the Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported that US President Donald Trump had rejected the deal., external

Trump was privately sceptical that Iran would meet his demands, it reported, and had told his staff that he saw a renewed bombing campaign as likely.

The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices.

It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.

"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi told reporters.

He did not specify what steps Iran wanted the US to take but added that "the actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU".

"I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," he added.

A US official told the BBC that the US was "in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush".

In an interview with CBS News, the BBC's US partner, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that the ceasefire process "will begin from the very day they accept it".

"We had previously reached an agreement based on the MOU that was signed in Pakistan... if the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before," he added.

Pezeshkian also said Iran would now allow UN nuclear inspectors into the country.

Rejecting claims that Iran is trying to develop a nuclear weapon, the Iranian president said: "If they wish to come in and have inspections, we can reach accords and agreements vis-Ã -vis that specific topic within the negotiations."

World.title: Russia targeting 'ordinary life' with attacks on Ukraine's data centres, Zelensky says
World.content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia has widened its attacks to target Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, seeking to cause maximum disruption for ordinary people.

"All this affects people's ability to stay connected, study, work," he said.

On Friday a Russian drone hit a business centre in the capital Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. A separate attack killed a 14-year-old boy. Israel's foreign ministry said he was an Israeli citizen.

Russia confirmed it had targeted a data centre site, saying it was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence.

About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages on Wednesday due to strikes.

Some firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.

In the north-western city of Lutsk, electronic information boards at public transport stops were not working on Friday, officials said. The city council said this was "due to damage caused by a Russian attack on data centres in Kyiv".

In Friday's social media post, Zelensky wrote: "The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centres, internet providers â for Russia, all ordinary life is simply a target.

"It is important that the world responds to all of this and that Russia feels the response to its terror."

Late on Friday, Zelensky said "additional decisions" had been made at his meeting with Ukraine's top defence and security officials to protect the country's data centres and other critical communications facilities to ensure their continuous operation.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said that Russia was seeking to disrupt the flow of "life-saving information" by targeting data centres.

"Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives. This is critical civilian infrastructure... It is not a military target. It is essential to keeping everyday life functioning," Sybiha said.

Zelensky's top adviser on defence technologies on Thursday admitted that "there may be local disruptions" following Russian attacks an the cost of internet services could increase to cover the costs of repairs.

But Serhii Beskrestnov stressed that Ukraine's internet network was highly decentralised, so the country "will not be left without internet access".

World.title: South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
World.content:
An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".

Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.

"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."

Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.

The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.

He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".

"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.

Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.

Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.

While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".

Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".

He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.

World.title: Inside the FBI hack: Agents fearful and angry after 'dangerous' data breach
World.content:
Groups similar to ShinyHunters - believed to be an English-speaking gang - have in the past been linked to swatting incidents, and even petrol bomb attacks against law enforcement officers and rivals.

The group claims it breached FBI systems on Monday and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.

The FBI has not responded to requests for comment.

However, on Wednesday the agency acknowledged the breach - saying it was "aggressively investigating" how it occurred.

For Michael McPherson, a former FBI agent who is now senior vice president of security operations at cyber firm ReliaQuest, the hack presents "a security threat which cuts to the core of agent safety, particularly their families".

He says agents understand the "inherent risks" that come with the job.

"But this incident reportedly includes personal data such as home addresses and contact information, which could expose family members who are normally insulated from the threats associated with such a career," McPherson says.

ShinyHunters shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.

The samples appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses.

The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.

The criminals also appear to possess highly sensitive medical information relating to thousands of special agents.

BBC News has seen samples of stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations containing information such as blood and urine test results, along with doctors' notes mentioning conditions including a "shellfish and banana allergy".

Agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical issues including "blood in the urine" and "high cholesterol" are now in the criminals' hands.

Cynthia Kaiser, who was the Deputy Director of Cyber at the FBI and now leads the Research Centre at Halcyon says ShinyHunters appear to already have lost control of some of the data which is circulating in various online groups of cyber researchers and could lead to harm even before the main tranche is published.

"A lot of the damage may already be done, and as we have seen in past FBI data breaches, that information continues to circulate the dark web years later," she said.

There are also concerns about the breach's national security implications, such as staff becoming targets for recruitment efforts by hostile foreign intelligence services.

World.title: White House bars CNN from travelling with Trump on Air Force One
World.content:
US broadcaster CNN has been barred from travelling with President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee on Saturday.

The move is the latest in a battle between the White House and the media after it was forced to lift its ban on some news outlets.

CNN was scheduled to fly with Trump for his trip to Tennessee for a college American football game until a note released on Friday night by the White House did not list the broadcaster on the media schedule.

The BBC has requested comment from the White House.

CNN has reported that no other outlet was listed as replacing them in the president's tentative schedule.

Last week Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists from the White House after accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.

All three media outlets said they were pursuing legal action, and accused Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.

Four television networks that have a daily rotation of White House coverage along with CNN - ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - had paused their broadcasts of the president in solidarity with the banned outlets.

The White House then launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, ahead of the United General Assembly in New York.

A federal judge has since ruled Trump barring news outlets from the White House was likely unconstitutional and the administration had to let them back in, at least for now.

However, the White House still denied entry to some CNN and MS NOW reporters assigned to cover arrivals for a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday.

A White House communications account earlier posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event, and every press call".

Regular US television coverage resumed on Friday after White House officials allowed reporters entry.

The president is set to attend a football game between University of Tennessee vs University of Texas College at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville from midday on Saturday.

World.title: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged', police say
World.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

Police in the US state of Mississippi have said that they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" and placed hanging in a tree.

The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs.

The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests.

In a news release, police said that the medical examiner had determined that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".

Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging was staged.

Fortune's mother told the BBC that she remembers the coroner telling her: "we're not treating this as [an] actual hanging." Her daughter, they told her, was dead before being placed in the tree.

Spivey also recalled police telling her the incident was "drug related".

Speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday, Spivey described how she knows her daughter fought for her life till the very end.

"I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey told reporters. Fortune leaves behind four young children, ages 7, 5, 4 and 1, she added.

Dressed in a shirt that reads "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she does not want to see any innocent people going to jail.

"I just hope they have the right people," she said.

Three people have so far been arrested in relation to the case, all of whom are black, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who has pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody in without bond.

A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in the case this week.

A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday.

The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country.

Representative Ayanna Pressley, Democrat of Massachusetts, cites at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress, external, which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers.

The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has been ruled a suicide.

World.title: Pope warns against 'losing humanity' to AI machines
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has issued a warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence (AI) at the start of his four-day visit to France.

The pontiff cautioned against "losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines" in wide-ranging remarks to Church and state officials at the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, following an hour of talks with President Emmanuel Macron.

Leo made a similar warning earlier this year when he spoke of the need for AI to be "disarmed" in the first major teaching document of his papacy.

In his May appeal, he mentioned the slave trade in relation to AI, suggesting that the world was in danger of normalising the exploitation of people once again.

The highpoint of Leo's visit to France is set to be a giant Mass attended by more than half a million people in Paris on Saturday, for which an altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde and a large area around the Champs-ÃlysÃ©es sealed off by police.

Large crowds are expected throughout the trip, reflecting an enthusiasm that the Church attributes to growing spirituality among the French and other Europeans.

He was greeted at Orly airport early on Friday by Macron, with the pair expected to deliver a speech later in the day in Metz.

Crowds were meanwhile gathering along a route to the Notre Dame, where the pontiff will later be driven in his popemobile.

The president will not be at any of the Pope's Masses, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion.

On Friday, Macron hailed Pope Leo's visit to France as a "great honour", stressing that French secularism "in no way negates religion".

Leo said that "authentic secularity" should not exclude religion "from the public sphere or from education".

In recent years, French politicians have often invoked France's brand of secularism to justify bans on religious symbols, including Muslim women's attire, in public spaces and schools.

World.title: AI, rote learning, and a new pedagogy, By Temitope Sodipo
World.content:
The value of education may therefore lie less in the job it qualifies us to do than in the lens through which it teaches us to see and solve problems. This is why I believe curiosity may become one of the most valuable skills in the new world of work. An individual’s willingness to learn, unlearn and learn again could prove more important than having mastered one particular body of knowledge.

The worries that we concern ourselves with daily appear to be on the increase. You would think that the offer of admission to study law in a Nigerian university would be a thing of joy. But my friend worries that law and several other professions, including medicine, accounting and pharmacy, face increasing disruption from the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI). Of particular concern to her was the length of time required to study these courses and the attendant costs. She was convinced that her nephew, who was offered the admission, had been pushed towards the profession by his parents, more for their own “bragging rights” than because it was what he genuinely wanted to do. Interestingly, her nephew has loved drawing from a young age.

Her concerns got me thinking about some broader questions. How relevant is our educational curriculum in an age of rapid technological change? Are we preparing young Nigerians for the world they will actually enter? More fundamentally, are we producing too many graduates without adequately preparing them for the changing nature of work?

For me, the real question is whether we are educating young Nigerians for specific jobs, or whether we are educating them to navigate a world in which the jobs themselves may change.

A university education should not merely be viewed as vocational training for one particular profession. Beyond the qualification it confers, education should develop transferable capabilities: reasoning, research, communication, analytical thinking, discipline and intellectual curiosity. These are capabilities that can remain relevant even when particular jobs or industries change. But this also raises an uncomfortable question: are our universities actually cultivating these capabilities, or are we still largely rewarding rote learning and examination performance?

AI is also changing the value of knowledge itself. Access to information is becoming easier and faster. What becomes increasingly valuable is knowing what questions to ask, being able to assess the quality of an answer, applying context, exercising judgement and recognising when something does not make sense. This is particularly important because AI can be confidently wrong.

The expectation should be that a graduate is capable of reskilling and upskilling throughout his or her working life. A degree should provide a foundation from which a person can continue to learn, rather than a narrow qualification that becomes obsolete when the nature of a particular job changes.

Consider a lawyer who moves into the entertainment industry. He does not suddenly become irrelevant because he no longer goes to court. His legal training should influence how he negotiates contracts, structures transactions, understands intellectual property and manages risk. Likewise, an engineer who moves into the fitness industry may approach the human body differently because of his understanding of systems and how different components interact.

The value of education may therefore lie less in the job it qualifies us to do than in the lens through which it teaches us to see and solve problems. This is why I believe curiosity may become one of the most valuable skills in the new world of work. An individual’s willingness to learn, unlearn and learn again could prove more important than having mastered one particular body of knowledge.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

AI is also changing the value of knowledge itself. Access to information is becoming easier and faster. What becomes increasingly valuable is knowing what questions to ask, being able to assess the quality of an answer, applying context, exercising judgement and recognising when something does not make sense. This is particularly important because AI can be confidently wrong. Imagine an AI-generated legal opinion that cites a non-existent case or relies on an incorrect provision of the law. The problem is not simply that AI can make mistakes. The more important question is whether the person using it has sufficient knowledge and judgement to recognise the mistake.

The future may not belong to those with the “right” degree, but to those who are curious enough to keep learning, adaptable enough to keep changing and discerning enough to know when human judgement matters most.

AI will undoubtedly erode many routine tasks, particularly those involving repetitive processes and predictable outputs. But this does not necessarily mean that entire professions will disappear. It may simply change the composition of work within those professions. A junior lawyer may spend less time reviewing documents and conducting routine research. An accountant may spend less time on repetitive reconciliation and may rely more heavily on automated systems.

This distinction matters when we advise young people about their future. We should be careful not to respond to technological disruption by directing them towards whichever profession we currently consider “safe”. There may be no such thing as a permanently safe profession. Perhaps the better question is: what capabilities will enable this young person to remain useful and adaptable as the world changes?

This brings me back to my friend’s nephew and his love of drawing. Conceivably, the answer is not necessarily to discourage him from studying law or insisting that he pursue art instead. The future may not belong to those with the “right” degree, but to those who are curious enough to keep learning, adaptable enough to keep changing and discerning enough to know when human judgement matters most.

Temitope Sodipo is a lawyer in the financial services sector. An avid gardener, birdwatcher and arts enthusiast. She writes from Lagos.

World.title: The global race for critical minerals, and Nigeria’s criminalisation of artisanal miners, By Adeola Akinremi
World.content:
Nigeria needs a policy shift from raid-and-detention enforcement of artisanal miners. The government should not focus on providing licences to the “big men” alone, just as it continues to do with oil blocs. It needs to formalise artisanal mining by providing appropriate types of licences for these small miners, safety training, geological information, equipment leasing, mineral-buying centres and environmental compliance.

This is the thought that I have not been able to shake off: the brutal deaths of thirty-seven Nigerians while in state custody in Minna, Niger State, after they were arrested for suspected illegal mining.

Their immediate families and all of us are suddenly thrown into mourning. It is horrific, gruesome and barbaric, and the circumstances around it remind us that the government is more reactive than proactive.

To be fair, the authorities moved relatively quickly to suspend some senior officials, condemn the deaths and set up an independent inquiry with credible people on the panel. But I would not leap to my feet to applaud the government. I’m stuck on the fact that a legal and regulatory framework that recognises and formalises artisanal mining could have helped prevent these avoidable deaths.

The government should be ashamed that 37 citizens died in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC). Three survivors have recounted what happened the night that their colleagues died. They claimed that NSCDC personnel sprayed some substance into the crowded cell and kept the doors locked, ignoring cries for help. Dauda Shehu, 29, told Reuters that “they sprayed something which smelled like a perfume. Hours later we started feeling throats itching, then we started struggling to breathe. People started dying.”

Now, we are made to ask that burning question: is criminalisation of artisanal mining a solution to illegal mineral extraction, or a policy response that deepens poverty, insecurity and state violence while leaving the powerful actors in the mining value chain untouched?

When 37 young men arrested for suspected illegal mining died in a crowded state cell, did Nigeria confront an unforeseeable health emergency, or the predictable consequence of treating poor artisanal miners as security threats rather than human beings entitled to safety, due process and dignity?

I’d argue that artisanal mining can be among the hardest labor that humans undertake. Yet Nigeria’s economic conditions have pushed many young men into finding livelihoods the hard way.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

For the basics, artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) is a largely informal economic sector that includes workers around the globe who use their hands and basic tools such as picks and shovels to extract vital metals from the earth, including cobalt, tin, tungsten and tantalum, as well as gold, diamonds, gemstones, iron, lithium and more. These workers, mostly poor, feed their families through artisanal mining. The same minerals extracted by poor people in dangerous informal economies are increasingly valuable to sophisticated global economies because they underpin technology, energy and the AI economy.

To be clear, metals are critical to the world’s economies. They are necessary for computers, mobile phones, airplanes, medical devices, electric vehicles, rechargeable batteries and much more.

Yes, countries like China and the United States, two of the world’s major economic powers, are going where they can find these critical minerals, using both informal and formal means to acquire them to serve their economic interests. Indeed, the current geopolitical competition over critical minerals is more complicated.

For example, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, China and the United States are in a duel. They are sending their billionaires, they are sending their envoys, and they are signing difficult-to-understand agreements with the DRC government. A US mining firm, KoBold Metals, backed by Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos, is among the companies pursuing critical-mineral opportunities in the DRC. It is like another scramble for Africa.

What happened in Nigeria is not simply a mining-safety story. It is policy a failure.

This event sits at the intersection of three policy failures: unregulated artisanal mining, weak rural livelihoods, and the treatment of people in state custody.

Artisanal mining is often grouped carelessly with “illegal mining.” That language is grave, to say the least. Some miners may operate without required licences, outside approved sites or in unsafe conditions. Nevertheless, they remain rights-bearing persons. Suspected regulatory or criminal violations do not remove the state’s duty to provide humane detention, adequate space, air, water, medical attention and timely judicial processing.

Nigeria’s broader artisanal-mining sector reflects economic reality. For many people in mineral-rich but economically marginalised communities, mining is a livelihood of last resort, sustained by unemployment, land pressure, limited agricultural returns and demand for gold, tin, columbite and other minerals. Enforcement that focuses narrowly on arrests, without viable formalisation pathways, can displace poverty rather than solve illegal extraction.

The Minna deaths also follow other fatal mining-related incidents in 2026. In February, dozens of miners died in a Wase, Plateau State, underground site, reportedly linked to toxic gas exposure. Reports placed the death toll at 37 or 38, with additional injuries. On 22 September, four artisanal tin miners, two men and two women, were reported killed when an unsupported pit collapsed in Baban Rafi, Bokkos LGA, Plateau State.

These incidents show that Nigerian artisanal miners face two different but connected hazards: occupational and governance danger.

The Minna deaths should be understood as a test of Nigeria’s rule of law. The government has a legitimate responsibility to regulate illegal and unsafe mining, but it has a duty to care as well.

The Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, has publicly stated that government institutions must never become “places of death,” and he is spot on. Many people working informally in artisanal mining are young, poor, underemployed and excluded from formal labour markets.

Nigeria needs a policy shift from raid-and-detention enforcement of artisanal miners. The government should not focus on providing licences to the “big men” alone, just as it continues to do with oil blocs. It needs to formalise artisanal mining by providing appropriate types of licences for these small miners, safety training, geological information, equipment leasing, mineral-buying centres and environmental compliance.

This formalisation should cost less and take less time. It can reduce illegal operations and address institutional failures, as experienced with the NSCDC. A formalised artisanal livelihood can help distinguish criminal profiteers from legitimate small-scale miners, prevent workplace disasters and reduce further loss of life.

This is my ask: Nigeria’s policy framework should treat artisanal mining as an economic sector requiring formalisation rather than criminalising livelihoods.

Adeola Akinremi is a public policy advisor, strategic communications expert, and the founder and CEO of Hintells, an AI-powered intelligence platform serving businesses and diplomatic missions in Washington, D.C. He has extensive multilateral experience advising on governance, economic and policy reforms across global markets and can be reached at: [email protected]

World.title: AfCFTA, African IP Summit to push intellectual property as driver of continental trade
World.content:
Government officials and policymakers from across Africa will be gathering in Kenya in November to discuss how intellectual property can support Africa’s trade and economic transformation.

The discussion will take place at the 7th edition of the All Africa Intellectual Property Summit organised in collaboration with the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) Secretariat.

The All Africa Intellectual Property (IP) Summit is a premier Pan-African multi-stakeholder platform “dedicated to advancing the role of intellectual property in driving Africa’s economic transformation, innovation ecosystem, and global competitiveness.”

The organisers, in a joint statement issued on Friday, said they are involved in a strategic partnership to strengthen the role of intellectual property in advancing intra-African trade.

The event, the 7th All Africa Intellectual Property Summit, is titled “Mainstreaming Intellectual Property for Africa’s Trade, Industrial & Creative Economy Transformation” and will run for three days, from 11-13 November.

Intellectual property (IP) broadly refers to legal protections for creations and innovations, including inventions, brands, artistic and creative works, designs, and other intangible assets.

The organisations stated that a stronger IP system could help African businesses protect their innovations and brands, commercialise their ideas, attract investment and expand into regional and international markets.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The adopted Annexes cover Utility Models; Traditional Knowledge, Traditional Cultural Expressions and Genetic Resources; Plant Variety Protection; Patents; Marks; Industrial Designs; Geographical Indications; and Copyright and Related Rights,” the statement read.

The summit will examine how the AfCFTA’s IP framework can translate into practical opportunities for African businesses, innovators, and creators.

It is also expected to examine implementation of the AfCFTA Intellectual Property Rights Protocol, including the role of intellectual property in promoting inclusive economic development.

The programme will also draw on perspectives from a Call for Papers, alongside an Innovation Pavilion designed to showcase African creativity, innovation, intellectual assets and business opportunities.

At the summit, policymakers are expected to adopt a Nairobi Declaration on Intellectual Property and Africa’s Economic Transformation.

The AfCFTA Secretary-General, H. E. Mene, described the summit as crucial to building a continental framework that supports African innovation, creativity and enterprise.

The Chairman of the All Africa Intellectual Property Summit, Sand Kalu, also said the partnership with the AfCFTA Secretariat is coming at an important moment for Africa’s intellectual property development.

“As the continent advances implementation of the AfCFTA intellectual property framework, the Summit provides an opportunity to bring policy, business, innovation and creativity together and examine how intellectual property can generate tangible economic value,” he said.

He also noted that the AfCFTA Secretariat and AAIPS will continue engaging stakeholders across Africa and beyond to discuss the future of intellectual property within the continent’s integrated market.

World.title: Police begin disciplinary action against inspector over anti-Peter Obi viral video
World.content:
The Lagos State Police Command has identified an inspector featured in a viral video and commenced disciplinary action over remarks he made while travelling in a public transport vehicle.

The officer, Osumah Frank, was identified in a statement posted by the command’s spokesperson, Abimbola Adebisi, on Friday.

Recently, in the video circulating on social media, the officer, who was seated in the front seat of a moving vehicle, spoke about Peter Obi’s 2027 presidential ambition and said an Igbo person could not become president of Nigeria.

He also said Mr Obi would not win the 2027 presidential election and made other comments about the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate and the Igbo ethnic group.

The Lagos State Command, however, did not give details of the remarks in its statement.

The command stated that Mr Frank’s remarks were made in his personal capacity and did not represent the position of the Lagos State Police Command or the Nigeria Police Force.

“The command has commenced appropriate disciplinary action against the officer in line with established regulations of the Nigeria Police Force; it also wishes to make it clear that the statements made by the officer were made in his personal capacity and do not represent the position, views or official disposition of the Lagos State Police Command or the Nigeria Police Force,” the statement noted.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It stressed that the inspector would face disciplinary proceedings in accordance with police regulations.

The Commissioner of Police in Lagos, Tijani Fatai, stated that officers were expected to maintain professionalism and treat members of the public with respect.

Mr Fatai said wearing the police uniform carried a responsibility to uphold the dignity and integrity of the force.

Previous cases

The police have taken similar action in other cases involving videos of alleged misconduct by officers.

In April, the Police Complaint Response Unit said a Lagos police officer was identified, queried and detained after a video allegedly showed him collecting N10,000 from a motorist.

In July, the Nigeria Police Force ordered an investigation after a video showed officers on the Lagos-Benin Expressway allegedly making derogatory remarks. The Force explained that the officers were identified and disciplinary proceedings initiated.

The Force has also said members of the public are not prohibited from recording police officers while they perform their duties in public.

Also, the Inspector-General of Police Olatunji Disu was not opposed to such recordings but cautioned against their misuse.

World.title: FCT senator insists Wike obtaining loans without NASS approval
World.content:
The senator representing the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Ireti Kingibe, has accused the FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, of obtaining loans without the National Assembly’s approval, as required by law.

Ms Kingibe, a member of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), made the allegation in a statement issued on Thursday.

This is not the first time the senator has accused Mr Wike of securing loan facilities for the Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCTA) without the approval of the National Assembly.

In August, Ms Kingibe made a similar allegation when she appeared as a guest on Channels Television’s Political Paradigm.

Mr Wike, however, denied the allegation.

Speaking on Tuesday, the minister said Ms Kingibe did not understand how government borrowing works, insisting that loans could not be obtained without the approval of the National Assembly.

“There is no way you can go and take a loan without the approval of the National Assembly. If you want to take a loan, you will include it in the budget and state that, in this aspect of the budget, the government will take out a loan,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Wike also said Ms Kingibe would not return to the Senate after the 2027 election, claiming that FCT residents had decided to support former senator Philip Aduda.

“I don’t want to comment about her. She is already packing her things out. The people of the FCT have made their choice. They are going to support President Tinubu and Philip Aduda for Senate,” he said.

Evidence

In her Thursday statement, Ms Kingibe challenged Mr Wike to provide evidence of the National Assembly’s approval for the alleged loans.

“As for not getting approval for the loans, I dare the FCT Minister to show the people of the FCT, and all, who have asked, the Votes and Proceedings of the day the approval was given. I cannot speak for the House of Representatives, but I know that it was NEVER brought before the Senate. The President, from whom the minister derives his powers, has always sought approval for ALL loans from the Senate.

“No Minister, no matter how powerful, is above the law. No public office holder is above scrutiny. And no individual has the authority to decide by personal declaration who the people of the FCT will elect in 2027. That decision belongs solely to the people,” she said.

Ms Kingibe also said she would not be intimidated or silenced over her scrutiny of the FCT administration.

“I also want to make this very clear: attempts to intimidate, silence, or demean women in government are totally unacceptable. Women who choose to serve in public office must not be expected to remain silent simply because they ask difficult questions or refuse to compromise their principles.

“I will not be distracted by personal attacks. I will continue to speak when the interest of the FCT demands it, scrutinise matters that require scrutiny, and stand firmly for the people I represent. I did not enter public service to be intimidated. I entered it to serve. The will of the people of the FCT will prevail on the day of the election,” she said.

What the law says about FCT borrowing

The FCT occupies a different constitutional position from Nigeria’s 36 states.

Under Section 299 of the 1999 Constitution, the provisions of the Constitution apply to the FCT as if it were a state. However, the Constitution vests the legislative powers ordinarily exercised by a state House of Assembly in the National Assembly, while executive powers ordinarily vested in a state governor are vested in the President.

Section 302 further provides that the President may appoint a minister for the FCT, who exercises powers and performs functions delegated by the President.

This means that, unlike state governments whose budgets are approved by their respective Houses of Assembly, the FCT’s annual appropriation is considered and approved by the National Assembly.

The National Assembly’s control over FCT public funds is reflected in the annual FCT Appropriation Acts. For example, the 2025 FCT Appropriation Act provided that all revenue accruing to the FCT, including statutory revenue, must be paid into the FCT Administration’s Statutory Revenue Account and that no money could be withdrawn from the account without appropriation by the National Assembly.

The Act also provided that, where appropriated expenditure could not be funded due to a revenue shortfall, the FCT Minister would have to seek a waiver from the National Assembly before incurring the expenditure.

Beyond the Constitution, the Fiscal Responsibility Act 2007 contains specific conditions for government borrowing. Section 44(1) requires any government or its agencies seeking to borrow to specify the purpose of the borrowing and provide a cost-benefit analysis detailing the economic and social benefits of the proposed borrowing.

Section 44(2)(a) further requires “prior authorisation in the Appropriation or other Act or Law” for the purpose for which the borrowing will be used. It also provides that proceeds of borrowing must be applied solely to long-term capital expenditure.

The Debt Management Office’s borrowing guidelines are more explicit about the FCT. For domestic borrowing from banks and other financial institutions, the guidelines require the FCT to submit evidence of approval by the FCT Executive Committee and a resolution of the National Assembly, as well as the relevant FCT Appropriation or other Act authorising the purpose for which the loan will be used.

World.title: El-Rufai’s ex-chief of staff dumps ADC, vows to deliver Zaria, Lere, others to APC
World.content:
Former Kaduna governor Nasir El-Rufai’s staunch ally and ex-Chief of Staff, Bashir Sa’idu, has defected from the African Democratic Congress (ADC) to the All Progressives Congress (APC), promising to mobilise thousands of his supporters for Governor Uba Sani ahead of the 2027 elections.

Mr Sa’idu, who also served as Commissioner for Finance under Mr El-Rufai, made the pledge when the governor’s Special Adviser on Domestic Affairs, Isa Lawal, visited him at his residence.

He said his return to the APC was not an individual move, adding that he had brought along a large network of supporters who would demonstrate their political strength during the elections.

Mr Sa’idu specifically promised to deliver the 11 local government areas that make up the Zazzau Emirate to the APC.

“I will not boast about my capacity in other areas, but in the 11 local governments of Zazzau Emirate, we will show our strength, and no one has the kind of followers that we have,” he said.

He also said the APC would secure more votes in Zaria Local Government Area than the votes recorded for former President Muhammadu Buhari in previous elections.

‘We did not leave ADC alone’

Mr Sa’idu said his defection was intended to prove wrong those who believed he left the ADC alone.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He cited Lere Local Government Area, where he claimed about 3,091 ADC card-carrying members joined the APC. He further claimed that there were groups of about 4,000 supporters in some other local government areas.

The former Chief of Staff said he moved to the APC with about 10,000 supporters, describing them as people who had demonstrated political loyalty to his camp.

“We will prove that Allah has endowed us with supporters, and these people believe in us politically. We have been meeting and fashioning out modalities of how we will win elections,” he said.

He added that his political network extended beyond Zaria to Igabi and Kaduna South local government areas.

Mr Sa’idu, however, acknowledged that his mobilisation would not prevent the state government from conducting its own political planning.

He said his group could either work alongside the government’s political structure or operate independently and meet at the polls.

From El-Rufai’s inner circle to Uba Sani’s camp

Mr Sa’idu’s latest move is significant because of his long relationship with Mr El-Rufai. The two knew each other since their days at Barewa College, Zaria.

During Mr El-Rufai’s eight-year administration in Kaduna, Mr Sa’idu held senior positions, including Commissioner for Finance and, later, Chief of Staff.

Mr Sa’idu was also among the prominent figures who followed Mr El-Rufai from the APC to the ADC.

Earlier in September, Mr Sa’idu and other El-Rufai associates announced their return to the APC and support for Governor Uba Sani.

Former commissioner Jafaru Sani confirmed that the group had returned to the APC, adding that they were bringing with them more than 150,000 registered ADC members.

The group also included former Kaduna North senator Abdu Kwari and other grassroots politicians previously associated with Mr El-Rufai.

The development came amid a broader realignment of Kaduna politicians ahead of the 2027 elections.

ADC primary deepened divisions

The political rupture followed the ADC governorship primary in May, won by former House of Representatives member Isah Ashiru with 86,113 votes.

Jafaru Sani, a former Commissioner for Education under Mr El-Rufai, came second with 29,580 votes. He rejected the outcome, alleging irregularities in the process.

The disputed primary deepened tensions within the former governor’s political network, with reports at the time pointing to dissatisfaction among some of Mr El-Rufai’s loyalists with the outcome and the direction of the ADC.

Mr Ashiru has since positioned himself as the ADC’s principal challenger to Mr Uba Sani in the 2027 Kaduna governorship contest.

El-Rufai speaks as former allies move away

Mr Sa’idu’s defection also came shortly before Mr El-Rufai publicly reflected on the changing relationships around him.

In a statement titled “My Relationships and the Aftermath,” dated 23 September, the former governor lamented that some former colleagues, friends and family members had remained silent or distanced themselves during his current difficulties.

He said his recent experiences had made him reconsider some relationships, but stressed that he bore no resentment and sought neither revenge nor retribution.

The timing has given fresh political significance to the return of former El-Rufai associates to the APC.

For Mr Sa’idu, however, the immediate challenge is now to translate his claimed grassroots network into votes.

World.title: Peter Obi reveals ‘connection’ with Soludo amid debt debate
World.content:
The 2027 presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has said many Nigerians might not know that he and his wife are godparents to Governor Charles Soludo’s children.

Mr Obi, a former governor of Anambra State, spoke on Friday at the 22nd Conference of the Guild of Editors in Enugu amid a debt debate between him and Mr Soludo’s administration.

The conference was themed: “The Ballot, the Media and the Task of Keeping Democracy Alive.”

Speaking as a guest at the event, Mr Obi dismissed insinuations that he and Mr Soludo were in dispute.

“People might not know. My wife and I are godparents to Soludo’s children.

“Yes. We are that close. We are not quarrelling. I will never quarrel with him. If I see him anyday, he and I will hug. If they say anything, I’ll answer them,” he said.

The former governor did not say how many of Mr Soludo’s children they serve as godparents to.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

PREMIUM TIMES reports that Mr Soludo has four daughters and two sons.

A godparent is someone who serves as a witness at a child’s baptism.

Children’s godparents are usually chosen by their biological parents, often because of existing close relationships between the two families.

Debt debate

Mr Obi then repeated what he said during his appearance on Arise News’ Prime Time on Thursday: that he left over $150 million in the state’s treasury when he left office as governor.

“Like I said yesterday, I did not leave debt in Anambra State. The day I left office, I left $150 million in savings.

“No other governor has left dollars before. If you see one, tell me,” he said.

‘Why I’ll never abuse Tinubu’

Mr Obi then said that although he might disagree politically with politicians such as President Bola Tinubu, he will never abuse him or any governor.

“I cannot abuse any governor. I cannot abuse anybody in government.

“I don’t need to abuse people even in the federal government. I’ve never abused anybody.

“Who has seen me calling President Tinubu’s name? Never! I will not do that. He’s the president of the country; he has all my respect,” he said.

The NDC candidate, however, said respect for public office holders should not prevent Nigerians and the media from questioning their decisions and performance.

The former governor stressed that the character and conduct of political leaders could influence the value of society as a whole.

He urged editors to scrutinise politicians based on their records, statements, and qualifications.

World.title: 2027: Soludo, others shouldn’t determine who Igbos will vote for as president – Onaiyekan
World.content:
The retired Catholic Archbishop of Abuja, John Onaiyekan, says the Igbo-speaking people of South-east should be allowed to freely choose their preferred presidential candidate without interference from state governors.

Mr Onaiyekan, a cardinal, spoke on Thursday during an interview with Afia TV in Enugu.

The cleric, who visited the state to attend the 22nd Conference of the Guild of Editors, was responding to questions about Governor Charles Soludo’s comment about the 2027 presidential election.

Mr Soludo had repeatedly argued that Igbo people should not “waste their votes” on the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, because, according to him, he would not win.

The governor has openly expressed support for the re-election of President Bola Tinubu, the All Progressives Congress candidate.

‘Igbo should be allowed to choose’

When asked about his comment, Mr Onaiyekan stressed that Mr Soludo or other governors are not in a position to make choices for Igbos.

“I don’t know what Soludo has told Ndigbo. All I can say is that Ndigbo should be allowed to choose who should be their president freely,” he responded.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The cardinal maintained that although governors are elected representatives, they should not determine how Nigerians cast their votes.

“It is not the duty of governors to teach, to tell people how they should vote,” he said.

“The governors will have their own votes now. Every governor will be able to vote. He will vote for himself. Let others do.”

The cleric emphasised that elections afford Nigerians an opportunity to express their political preferences.

He then urged Nigerians to exercise their right freely during elections.

“At least, that’s the only opportunity that we have to express our minds. Let us do it,” he added.

Background

Messrs Obi and Mr Soludo have been engaged in a war of words in recent years.

The face-off between the two politicians took a fresh twist in early September when the state Commissioner for Finance, Izuchukwu Okafor, claimed that Governor Soludo’s administration was still repaying loans and other debts incurred by Mr Obi and other past governors of the state.

Responding to the claim in a now-viral clip, Mr Obi said he owed no debt in Anambra when he left office as the state’s governor.

The NDC candidate subsequently reiterated that he did not incur any debt as governor but rather saved over ₦75 billion in the state’s account.

In response, the Anambra government released loan records, arguing that Mr Obi’s administration took out eight external loans totalling $123.7 million, with $92.35 million outstanding.

On Thursday, Mr Obi reiterated that he left over $150 million in savings for the Anambra State Government when he left office as governor in 2014.

World.title: RCCG receives 100 Nigerian returnees from South Africa
World.content:
From left: Pastor Belemina Obunge, Chairman of the RCCG Task Force on Repatriation and other officials of RCCG after briefing journalists at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos.

…says beneficiaries not selected on membership basis

By Olayinka Latona

The Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG) on Thursday received the first batch of 100 Nigerians returning from South Africa under a humanitarian intervention through which the church is funding air transportation for 500 Nigerian nationals stranded in the country.

The first batch arrived at about 8:30 p.m. from Johannesburg and was received at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos.

The intervention was approved by the General Overseer of the RCCG, Pastor Enoch Adeboye, following an appeal for assistance for Nigerians who needed to return home from South Africa.

Chairman of the RCCG Task Force for the Reception of Nigerian Returnees from South Africa, Pastor Belemina Obunge, said the church’s intervention covered the cost of air transportation from Johannesburg to Lagos, while relevant government agencies would handle the reception and onward movement of the returnees.

Obunge said additional batches would arrive as the necessary processes were completed.

He commended the Nigerian diplomatic missions in South Africa for initiating and coordinating the collaboration with relevant stakeholders.

Addressing concerns over the selection of beneficiaries, Obunge said the returnees were not selected solely on the basis of membership of the RCCG.

He explained that the Nigerian diplomatic mission in South Africa was working with the South African authorities on the profiling and documentation of Nigerians eligible to return.

“The Nigerian High Commission in South Africa is working with Home Affairs in South Africa, doing the profiling and documentation. Those who go through that process are being brought home,” he said.

Obunge added that the returnees were from different religious backgrounds.

“They are Muslims, Christians, all religions,” he said.

He said the church was working with government agencies to ensure that the returnees were properly received and transported to their respective destinations.

According to him, the church’s task force was at the airport to welcome the returnees, offer prayers and encouragement, and facilitate their orderly handover to the appropriate government agencies.

On continued support for the returnees after their arrival in Nigeria, Obunge said some state governments had already begun taking responsibility for their citizens.

He urged other state governments to welcome their returning citizens and support their reintegration into society.

“We use this opportunity to urge the states and governments to welcome their people home and see what they can do, as some have already started doing, to assist with the effective reintegration of their people into society,” he said.

The Chairman of the RCCG Central Mission Board, Pastor Amos Emoron, who led the church task force to receive the returnees alongside Obunge, also said the evacuees were selected without prejudice to religion, tribe or affiliation.

Officials of the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) and the National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons (NCFRMI), among other relevant agencies, received the returnees at the airport.

The profiling of the returnees subsequently commenced.

World.title: Alleged Fatal Assault: NLC declares strike in Delta
World.content:
File image

…Commissioner denies ordering attack as police arrest suspect, govt orders probe

By Egufe Yafugborhi & Ochuko Akuopha

ASABA — Organised labour has declared a strike in Delta State over the controversial death of a civil servant, Mr Unity Ekpevbughe Adeda, following an altercation at the office of the Commissioner for Secondary Education, Dr Kingsley Ashibogwu.

While the commissioner said the 54-year-old Deputy Director physically attacked him and denied ordering anyone to assault him, the deceased’s sister alleged that her brother was beaten, tied up and left seriously injured before he was taken to hospital, where he later died.

The Police Command has since moved into the controversy, announcing the arrest of one suspect, Lucky Adoh, and a manhunt for other persons allegedly connected with the incident.

The development also triggered an industrial dispute, with the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) declaring a dispute with the Delta State Government and directing workers to withdraw their services.

Ashibogwu, dismissing allegations that he assaulted Adeda, said: “Oh, I didn’t. Rather, the man even assaulted me, assaulted people in the office. There are video clips to it, where he was using his private vehicle to hit the staff vehicle.

“Before I knew what was happening, it was attack on me, physical. Direct attack. My clothes are there. I never ordered any person to touch him, I never touched him.”

He alleged that Adeda had threatened some workers before returning to confront him.

However, Ovwigho, the deceased’s sister, gave a sharply different account, saying she met her brother tied inside a vehicle at the hospital after receiving a distress call that he had been badly beaten at his workplace.

“I saw him tied up like a criminal. His entire body was filthy, blood was coming out of his mouth and nose, and his head was badly swollen,” she alleged.

She said Adeda told her that he had been summoned by the commissioner and assaulted by men allegedly acting on the commissioner’s orders.

“If you see pictures of him when they beat him up, you will be scared,” she said.

NLC Chairman, Goodluck Ofobruku, said workers could no longer accept what he described as an unsafe workplace.

“We’re declaring dispute with the Delta State Government. For that reason, we’re withdrawing our services with immediate effect.

“Whoever is responsible for the beating of this worker that led to his untimely death must be brought to book before we can come back,” he said.

The state Police Command, in a statement by its spokesman, SP Bright Edafe, said the Homicide Section of the State Criminal Investigation Department would conduct a “thorough and impartial investigation” into the incident.

According to the police, the investigation would include an examination of video footage, eyewitness accounts and medical records.

The state government has also constituted an administrative panel, chaired by the Permanent Secretary, Office of the Head of Service, Mrs Charity Ehimen, to investigate the circumstances surrounding Adeda’s death.

The panel was given two weeks to complete its assignment.

The government assured civil servants of the safety of their workplaces and reaffirmed its commitment to respecting the “dignity and sanctity of life.”

World.title: CNN blocked from Trump trip on Saturday
World.content:
CNN’s broadcast booth is seen in the press area of the White House in Washington, DC, September 18, 2026. Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP.

CNN reporters have been barred from traveling with US President Donald Trump as planned on Saturday, in a new move by the White House to limit the news network’s access.

The president last week sought to ban three US outlets – CNN, MS NOW and Politico – from the White House, accusing them of providing only negative coverage on him.

After journalists with the three outlets were blocked from entering the White House complex, a judge ordered their access to be temporarily restored, saying Trump’s move was likely unconstitutional.

For Trump’s trip on Saturday to Tennessee, CNN had been scheduled to be the TV network in the press “pool” traveling with him.

However, a schedule released by the White House on Friday evening did not list CNN or any of the TV networks in the TV pool rotation.

The pool is a rotating group of journalists that travel with the president and provide coverage to other outlets, due to limited space.

The White House schedule only listed a “Secondary TV” correspondent and crew: Lindell TV — a staunchly pro-Trump outlet run by his close ally, businessman Mike Lindell.

Earlier this week, when CNN’s White House access was still revoked, the top five US broadcasters made a rare joint move to halt pool coverage of the White House in solidarity.

“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting,” ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said.

CNN declined to comment when reached Friday by AFP. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Iran proposes Hormuz plan, Trump reportedly refuses
World.content:
Photo by Kevin Dietsch / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP.

Iran offered a plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz, Tehran said Friday, but within hours reports indicated that US President Donald Trump rejected the proposal.

The waterway key to the world’s oil supply is central to the conflict between the United States and Iran, which is at a stalemate after nearly seven months.

But new mediation efforts at the UN’s gathering of world leaders in New York this week offered some optimism of progress toward a deal.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital shipping channel.

“Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi said at the UN.

“The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure.

However, with hours of his comments The Wall Street Journal reported Trump had rejected the proposal, citing US officials familiar with the matter.

The report noted that the 80-year-old president was skeptical Tehran would meet his demands and added he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely.

Trump also posted an image to his Truth Social platform of a map showing the Strait of Hormuz circled and labelled “Trump Strait.”

Earlier media reports suggested the new plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon.

Frozen assets

It also reportedly calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade of Iran.

On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in an interview with broadcaster CBS that the ceasefire “process will begin from the very day they accept it.”

“We had previously reached an agreement based on the MOU that was signed in Pakistan…if the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before,” he added.

Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards, told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran’s demands.

The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran’s nuclear program.

But the deal broke down shortly afterward when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.

Iran requires ships to obtain authorization before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.

Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

World.title: When cancer fights back: New drug could reopen door to treatment
World.content:
Cancer cells, illustration.

By Sola Ogundipe

Cancer treatment can become a race against time. A drug works, the tumour shrinks, hope returns. Then the cancer changes. The treatment that once held it back starts losing its grip. Cancer cells find another way to survive, and a battle that seemed to be won begins all over again.

Read Also: We don’t need pity, we need jobs — Blind couple

Scientists at Baylor College of Medicine in the United States now say they may have found a way to disrupt one of cancer’s most frustrating survival strategies. The experimental drug, CS18, has shown early potential to weaken the biological defences that help cancer cells survive treatment and, crucially, make some resistant tumours sensitive to existing drugs again.

In laboratory experiments, CS18 restored the sensitivity of lung cancer cells that had become resistant to osimertinib, a drug used to treat certain lung cancers. When the two were combined, more cancer cells died. The researchers also reported reduced tumour growth in animal models, without major weight loss or other obvious signs of toxicity.

Published in Science Advances, the findings could point to a new approach to one of the most difficult problems in cancer treatment: drug resistance. However, CS18 is still an experimental compound and has not been established as a cancer treatment for patients and requires further research and testing.

For oncologists, treatment resistance remains one of the biggest challenges in cancer care. A drug may work remarkably well at first, but cancer cells can adapt. They can switch on alternative biological pathways, evade the treatment and continue to survive. Eventually, the cancer may return.

The study’s corresponding author, Dr. Weei-Chin Lin, professor of medicine, haematology and oncology, and molecular and cellular biology at Baylor College of Medicine, said “Therapeutic resistance is a major obstacle to achieving effective and durable cancer treatments. While some therapies are effective initially, many patients eventually relapse because cancer cells can activate compensatory and convergent biological pathways that allow them to overcome the toxic effects of treatment and survive.”

That was the problem the Baylor team set out to tackle. Instead of targeting one cancer pathway at a time, the researchers went after what they describe as a central control point inside cancer cells.

Their target was TopBP1 which is involved in several processes linked to cancer growth and survival. The researchers describe it as a biological “switchboard” because it helps regulate multiple pathways at once. They reasoned that disrupting the central control point could make it more difficult for cancer cells to activate alternative mechanisms for survival.

CS18 was tested against triple-negative breast cancer, ovarian cancer, lung adenocarcinoma, lung squamous cell carcinoma and acute myeloid leukaemia. The compound also appeared less toxic to non-cancerous cells in the laboratory experiments. The results became particularly interesting when CS18 was combined with cancer drugs already in use.

One of the most notable findings involved osimertinib. Some of the lung cancer cells used in the experiments had already developed resistance to the drug. Adding CS18 changed the response. The resistant cancer cells became sensitive to osimertinib again, increasing cancer cell death.

The researchers also found that combining CS18 with PARP inhibitors, another class of cancer drugs, produced greater cancer cell killing than either treatment alone.

Much more research is needed before the compound can progress through the stages required for human treatment, including clinical trials. The idea is bigger than simply killing cancer cells. It is about attacking the mechanisms that allow them to survive treatment in the first place.

If future studies confirm these findings, CS18 could eventually form part of combination therapies designed either to prevent resistance from emerging or to make resistant tumours vulnerable to treatment again.

For now, the Baylor findings offer a cautious glimmer of hope in a battle where resistance has often given cancer the upper hand. Cancer can fight back, scientists are now looking for ways to make treatment fight back harder.

Vanguard News

World.title: Too much light at night may quietly affect your heart
World.content:
By Sola Ogundipe

If your bedroom isn’t completely dark at night, a new study suggests it may be worth taking a closer look at how much light reaches you while you sleep.

Read Also: We don’t need pity, we need jobs — Blind couple

Research involving more than 11,000 people found that higher exposure to light at night was associated with subtle changes in the heart, including thicker and stiffer heart muscle.

The study doesn’t prove that nighttime light causes these changes. It does, however, add to growing evidence that exposure to light after dark may have implications for cardiovascular health.

Tonight, switch off unnecessary lights, draw the curtains, cover bright LEDs and put the phone away before bed. Keep the room as dark as comfortably possible.

The findings, published September 9 in the European Heart Journal, raise fresh questions about something most people rarely think about: how much artificial light surrounds us after sunset.

The research was led by Professor Lu Qi of Tulane University, New Orleans, USA. He noted that previous observational studies had linked nighttime light exposure with a higher risk of cardiovascular disease, but much less was known about what might actually be happening inside the heart.

“We carried out this research to find out what happens to the heart over time when people are exposed to too much light at nighttime,” Qi said.

The study involved 11,071 participants from the UK Biobank. Each wore a light sensor on the wrist for seven days, giving researchers a measure of how much light they encountered during the night.

About three years later, the participants underwent cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI. The scans gave researchers a detailed look at the structure of the heart and how well it was functioning.

The researchers compared people exposed to nighttime light levels above three lux with those exposed to almost no light at night. One of the clearest differences was found in the left ventricle, the heart’s main pumping chamber.

Those exposed to higher levels of nighttime light had thicker walls in the left ventricle. As the wall thickened, the space inside the chamber became smaller. The scans also showed that the heart muscle was less able to flex normally with each heartbeat.

Reduced flexibility can be an early sign of altered cardiac function. Changes were also found in the right ventricles and left atria, suggesting that the association was not confined to a single chamber of the heart.

The heart has to contract and relax with every beat. When the muscle becomes thicker and less flexible, it can become harder for the heart to relax properly and fill with blood.

Qi described the structural and functional changes as cardiac remodelling, a process in which the heart changes in response to prolonged stress or injury.

“This is the first study of its kind,” he said, adding that cardiac remodelling may initially be the body’s way of adapting to stress but could ultimately weaken the heart and contribute to heart failure. The researchers said the findings add to evidence suggesting that light pollution could be an emerging cardiovascular risk factor.

There is, however, an important caveat. The study found an association between nighttime light exposure and cardiac changes. It did not establish that exposure to light directly caused those changes. Other factors could have played a role, so the findings will need to be confirmed by further research.

Could a darker bedroom help? An accompanying editorial by Professor Thomas Münzel of University Medical Center Mainz, Germany, and colleagues argues that doctors may need to pay greater attention to how much light their patients encounter at night, particularly those already living with heart failure or atrial fibrillation.

They suggested that doctors ask about the sleep environment: how dark the bedroom is, whether the patient works night shifts and how much screen exposure occurs after sunset. The proposed changes are simple and inexpensive. They include blackout curtains, warmer and dimmer bedside lighting, and covering bright standby lights on household electronics.

But the issue goes beyond the bedroom. Modern cities remain illuminated long after sunset, with streetlights, buildings, shops, advertising signs and vehicles contributing to the glow. The editorial authors argue that cities can reduce unnecessary exposure through measures such as shielded light fixtures, warmer-spectrum bulbs and dimming or motion-activated streetlights.

For individuals, though, the first step may be much simpler. Switch off lights you don’t need. Draw the curtains. Cover bright LEDs. Dim your screens and put the phone away before bed. Then keep the bedroom as dark as comfortably possible.

So tonight, take a look around your bedroom. Turn off the lights you don’t need, draw the curtains, cover bright LEDs and put your phone away before bed. Keeping your sleeping space darker is a simple step you can take while researchers continue to study the possible heart effects of nighttime light.

Whether such measures can actually prevent heart disease remains to be established. Still, as nights become brighter, researchers are asking a question worth taking seriously: what happens to the human heart when the world around us never quite switches off?

Vanguard News

World.title: 37 miners’ death: CSOs demand mining sector overhaul; illegal operations deepen, fuel revenue flight
World.content:
File image.

By Luminous Jannamike & Gabriel Ewepu

ABUJA — The last thing many of the miners arrested around the Wushishi-Lukoto axis of Niger State could have expected when they were taken into custody was that some of them would not come out alive.

Read Also: Full List: 20 NSCDC officers suspended over 37 miners’ death; probe panel members

Between September 15 and 16, operatives of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC, raided suspected illegal mining sites west of Minna and detained about 65 artisanal miners.

By the early hours of September 17, dozens were dead inside an NSCDC detention facility along David Mark Road, Minna. Hospital footage showed 33 bodies in one ward. The Niger State governor subsequently confirmed that 37 detainees had died.

The official explanation initially pointed to a suspected disease outbreak, with the bodies sent for medical examination.

But survivors gave a different account, describing a severely overcrowded cell in which breathing became difficult. An intelligence assessment reportedly also pointed to overcrowding and inadequate ventilation as the likely causes of the deaths.

Whatever the final findings establish, one fact is already beyond dispute; 37 people arrested over alleged illegal mining ended up dead in state custody within one or two days.

Some of those arrested were minors or very young people. Amnesty International subsequently demanded an independent investigation into the deaths.
