Boyz coach Rudolph Speid named goalkeeper and team captain Andre Blake, Joel Latibeaudiere, Richard King, Isaac Hayden, Kasey Palmer, Ronaldo Webster and Tyreece Campbell in the starting team.

Starting team-

Andre Blake, Joel Latibeaudiere, Damion Lowe, Richard King, Isaac Hayden, Karoy Anderson, Kasey Palmer, Ronaldo Webster, Tyreece Campbell, Rumarn Burrell, Javon East.

World.title: 3-y-o with Erb’s palsy needs $3m for life-changing surgery in US
World.content:
The Wilson Family needs $3 million to fund Ayana's treatment overseas

KINGSTON, Jamaica — “Every child deserves the chance to run, play, laugh, and grow without being limited by an injury they never chose.”

Three-year-old Ayana Wilson from Riverton City in Kingston, is hoping for that chance, according to her family.

The toddler was injured during delivery following shoulder dystocia, resulting in a diagnosis of Erb’s palsy, a condition involving nerve damage affecting the shoulder and arm.

Ayana’s caregivers say despite the challenges she faces, she remains a happy, loving and vibrant child who wants what every three-year-old wants: to play with other children, explore the world, and enjoy her childhood.

However, the damage to her shoulder and arm has made many ordinary childhood activities difficult.

Ayana’s family reached out to Jamaican charity Crisis Support Charity Limited seeking assistance and her case was subsequently brought to Shriners Children’s in Philadelphia, where she has been accepted for further evaluation and treatment.

Ayana is scheduled to travel to the United States in October 2026 for medical evaluation and surgery, which the family describes as a chance for a new beginning— to use her arm more freely, play and participate more fully in childhood activities.

The three-year-old and her mother, Rosalee Eccles, have already obtained their United States visas, but the cost of traveling and remaining there for approximately six weeks following surgery and recovery is an obstacle to her treatment.

Anya’s father works for a local waste management company and the family says his modest income is used to meet their daily needs.

Eccles operates a small tuck shop in their community while caring for her family and helping to provide for their everyday expenses.

Noting that the cost associated with Anya’s medical journey is far beyond what the family can manage on their own, Crisis Support Charity Limited has shared a fundraising goal of $3 million to help.

The funds will assist with:

Airfare for Ayana and her mother

Accommodation for approximately six weeks

Specialised seating and support equipment required following surgery

Meals and basic living expenses

Transportation to and from medical appointments

Other essential expenses associated with Ayana’s medical care and recovery

“Every contribution, regardless of size, can help bring Ayana closer to the treatment she needs. Imagine being three years old and wanting to run, play, climb and participate with other children, while an injury makes many of those activities difficult,” the charity said.

“You may not know Ayana personally, but your kindness could become a meaningful part of her life story,” it said, noting that donations, no matter how small, matter.

Interested individuals, groups and companies can donate to Crisis Support Charity Limited at www.crisissupportycharity.org, specifying their beneficiary as Ayana Wilson.

The charity is urging people who cannot donate to share Ayana’s story.

“One child. One opportunity. One community coming together. Let us help Ayana get the chance she deserves,” the charity said.

World.title: KC principal responds to viral video of student being held over railing
World.content:
Kingston College Principal Dave Myrie speaking at morning devotion on Monday, March 31, 2025 as the school celebrated its 36th Boys’ Champs title. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Kingston College (KC) has launched an investigation after a video surfaced online showing a student being held by colleagues over a railing before falling.

In an official statement dated September 23, Principal Dave Myrie said the school’s administration and Board of Management are aware of the matter and are conducting a “thorough investigation” into the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Myrie said, however, that no student was injured.

“The School Administration and the Board of Management are aware of the matter and are currently conducting a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident,” Myrie said in the statement.

He assured parents, guardians, students and members of the wider KC community that the matter was being taken seriously and would be addressed in accordance with the school’s established policies and procedures.

The principal also reiterated the school’s commitment to maintaining what he described as a safe, disciplined and supportive environment for its students.

KC has also appealed to members of the school community to refrain from sharing or reposting the video.

According to Myrie, further circulation could unnecessarily compromise the privacy, dignity and welfare of the young students involved.

“Any further information considered appropriate will be communicated through the School’s official channels,” the statement said.

Myrie has served as principal of Kingston College since 2012.

– Howard Walker

World.title: Court walkout looms
World.content:
Defence attorneys staging a ‘silent protest’ outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston on Wednesday demanding that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Defence attorneys have been placed on alert to pull their services from the island’s courts for an entire week, starting next Monday, a move that will deal a significant blow to the Michaelmas term which began just over a week ago.

The lawyers arrived at the decision after a meeting on Thursday with Justice Minister Delroy Chuck which they say failed to produce any meaningful plans to reform the 2022 Firearms Act.

The emergency meeting was called following Wednesday’s ‘silent protest’ outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston, where members of the Jamaican Bar Association, the Advocates Association in collaboration with Bar associations across the island, armed with placards, demanded that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform.

Some hours later, Chuck indicated that he would be meeting with representatives of the bodies to hear their concerns.

However, following those discussions, defence attorney Tamika Harris, a member of the Bar Council of the Jamaican Bar Association and chair of its Criminal Practice and Procedure Subcommittee, who was a key figure behind the protest, told the Jamaica Observer that the meeting amounted to little less than an exercise in futility.

“The minister could not give a timeline as to when anything would be taken to the legislature, and he has asked for the discussion to be placed in writing but before [the Act was passed] the Bar Association… made a submission to Parliament. We are not asking for anything different, so it’s not like our argument is new,” Harris stated.

“The meeting, in my mind, was an opportunity for us to say the same things we have already said, but we have not gotten any response from the minister to, for example, say when he will go to Parliament [with proposed amendments]. I know everything takes time, but I did not get any idea of a plan to put in action. So the minister didn’t confirm that he was going to put a plan in action, so there is no resolution,” Harris declared.

As such, she said attorneys will be moving to action the next stage of their protest.

“He was very courteous and he listened. He expressed that he understood our concerns, but he did not go any further to say exactly if they were going to be dealt with and when, so there is nothing. I am aware he has already been presented with similar arguments by the director of public prosecutions and even the chief justice. I am going to ask my members to withdraw our services,” Harris told the Observer.

“We are going to use the opportunity, perhaps, to do quick education. The public needs to be aware that we are not saying legislation must be weak on persons who use firearms to terrorise our Jamaican citizens, we are not saying the legislation needs to be weak; we are saying that the legislation is to be fair and cognisant that not every case is the same,” Harris said.

The protests come just over a week after the justice minister’s comments at the Annual Assize Service of the judiciary. Chuck said, while the mandatory minimum sentences contained in the provision were being reviewed because of widespread concerns, “The security forces and a number of my colleagues feel that the Act is working and it is bringing down murders and shootings.

“It is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country, and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms. But it is under consideration,” Chuck said.

The comments triggered furious commentary from several quarters.

A week later members of Jamaica’s legal profession met on Saturday, September 19 to consider what they described as “the operation and impact of the Act, particularly its mandatory sentencing provisions and the restrictions placed on judicial discretion”.

In a statement issued following that meeting, the attorneys said, “The legal profession supports strong and effective laws to combat gun violence and punish those who use illegal firearms to murder, rob, terrorise and intimidate our citizens. Our concern is not with strong penalties. Our concern is with a sentencing regime that does not adequately allow judges to distinguish between offenders, offences, and individual circumstances.”

The Act, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for specified violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons. It establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities, and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

According to the advocates, their September 19 meeting “identified several areas of serious concern, including the restriction of judicial discretion; the proportionality of mandatory minimum sentences in individual cases; the diminished incentive for early guilty pleas; the resulting increase in matters proceeding to trial and pressure on an already burdened criminal justice system; the treatment of imitation firearms; and the consequences of certain provisions for licensed firearm holders”.

“The legal profession is calling for urgent amendments to the Act, including consideration of an ‘exceptional circumstances’ provision allowing judges appropriate discretion in deserving cases, meaningful sentencing incentives for early guilty pleas, reform of the certificate regime, and a review of the provisions governing imitation firearms and licensed firearm holders. The profession also calls for urgent, structured consultation with the Government, Opposition, Parliament, the judiciary and other relevant stakeholders on the proposed amendments”, the attorneys said in that statement.

World.title: Christiana clampdown
World.content:
Vendors on Wildman Street in Christiana on Thursday (Photos: Kasey Williams)

CHRISTIANA, Manchester — Mandeville Mayor Donovan Mitchell says, effective today, there will be a clampdown on unapproved buildings and illegal vending, as part of enforcement activities in the south-central town of Christiana.

“Yesterday (Wednesday) I came into Christiana and as the chairman of the local Board of Health I spent about five hours walking the streets of Christiana. I visited the abattoir. I visited the market. I visited the transportation centre. I looked at some businesses [and] buildings going up. I know at the council meeting early this month I made a statement and some people are up in arms and all of that… What is happening in the parish will not continue,” he said on Thursday while addressing the launch of Sam Fo Meats mobile application on Wildman Street in Christiana.

“I said it yesterday (Wednesday) to my team that Wildman Street, please be prepared, because I am going to be changing the entire look of Wildman Street. There will absolutely be no selling on the street. I am warning the businesses that are putting their sewage and grey water into our water channels to stop and stop before tomorrow [Friday] morning, because a team from the public health service will be coming out and we are going to make sure it cannot continue,” added Mitchell.

He pointed to the public safety concerns and hazards of waste water flowing on the busy commercial street.

“You cannot be walking on the street and all you are seeing is grey water. Businesses can’t build their buildings and put their grey water on the street. What about our children, the elderly? You are walking and miss your step in soap water and you break your leg and the first thing is they call the parish council,” said Mitchell, who chairs the Manchester Municipal Corporation.

“I am warning people who are building houses without plans from the Manchester Municipal Corporation. I am not holding bar; you have to do better. When a building collapses because you have not done the correct thing, who is the first person you blame? Government. Where was the Government when you were building? Not around, because you put zinc all around your place and you do what you have to do and when you are finished you open up the zinc and you see a building there that has not gone through the proper channel,” added Mitchell.

Pertaining to the Christiana abattoir, Mitchell said he is contemplating closing it for renovations.

“We are having some problems and I will tell you that maybe, based on the letters I am getting from the health services, I may have to close it even temporarily to make sure that things go right. I am warning, since I am in Christiana, that things are not going to be the same in Christiana. There has to be some changes,” declared Mitchell.

World.title: Skippa in int’l spotlight
World.content:
Dancehall artiste Skippa was named as one to watch by Jamaica Observer at the start of 2026 .

When the Jamaica Observer named Skippa one of its artistes to watch at the start of 2026, the prediction came with the expectation that the young dancehall artiste’s momentum was worth keeping an eye on. What has followed, however, stretches well beyond even his own expectations.

There was the touring, the growing audiences, the songs steadily finding new listeners, and, perhaps most significantly, recognition from one of the music industry’s most established brands — Billboard.

Still, as the artiste himself revealed, 2026 has so far surpassed his wildest imagination.

“We had goals around touring and growing the music, but everything kind of surpassed what we had in mind. The amount of shows, the places we’ve been received, the people connecting with the music in places we didn’t necessarily expect, and then Billboard on top of that — it’s been crazy,” he shared. “We’re grateful for all of it, because you can set goals, but sometimes the reality goes way beyond what you planned for.”

Speaking to the Splash, the entertainer said that, although he has been putting in the work, he was taken aback when he was named by Billboard as a Caribbean Rising Star. He admitted that the honour caught him completely off guard and that he had to resist getting swept up in the whirlwind that the moment ushered in.

“Honestly, I was taken aback. I’m not really the type to overreact, so I was just there trying to take in the moment,” he said. “Billboard recognising me as a Caribbean Rising Star, in a room with so many people who have been doing this at the highest level, that’s crazy. I’m grateful, for real, and it’s something I’ll always remember.”

For an artiste whose career has accelerated considerably in recent years, the recognition represents another marker in a journey that appears to be moving faster than he anticipated. Billboard may have just caught up to Skippa’s burgeoning career, but the proverbial writing was on the wall since the latter part of last year.

By December 2025, YouTube year-end statistics showed that the entertainer had already emerged as Jamaica’s third-most-viewed artiste on the platform, behind Chronic Law and Vybz Kartel, with approximately 79.9 million views. His numbers remained consistent in 2026, with the artiste repeatedly placing multiple songs among Jamaica’s most-streamed records.

Still, he remains humble, crediting his chart success to his loyal fan base rather than to a secret creative formula.

“I wouldn’t say I figured out some formula, because I think what really sets my work apart is that people just relate to me. I’m being myself and making music from my own experience and perspective, and people see themselves in that,” he said.

That connection, he believes, matters more than the numbers themselves — or any ‘trending list’ he may or may not find himself on.

“I don’t chase whatever trend is happening just because it’s working for somebody else. I just try to make good music and stay authentic, and the people decide what they want to run with,” he said.

It is a philosophy that has become increasingly important as the numbers have grown.

For Skippa, there is a difference between having a hit song and building something that can last.

“Consistency, for sure. I think that’s one of the biggest things,” he said. “You can have one song that catches fire, but building a career is different. You have to keep showing up, keep making music, keep performing, keep connecting with the people, and keep growing.”

With that mindset, the entertainer shared that he is looking at his recent success as motivation to go even further, rather than being tricked into believing he has somehow arrived.

“To come into this space and, in such a short time, see my name alongside artistes who have been doing this for years, that’s a big thing. It’s definitely something I’m grateful for and amazed by,” he said. “But I don’t look at it like I’ve arrived and that’s it. It just makes me appreciate the journey even more and motivates me to keep working.”

The entertainer sought to acknowledge the machinery working for his good behind the scenes. Naming his manager, Cristina; engineer, producer and DJ Travis; Chargie Records; Solitary Muzic; and Bankroller, among others, as people who have contributed to his progress, Skippa expressed that, “Everybody played their part, so when I’m on that stage accepting something like Billboard Rising Star, I know it’s not just about me.”

The prediction made by the Observer at the beginning of the year has taken on a life of its own. Having lived up to the ‘one to watch’ status, Skippa is now ready to take things to the next level as he cements his place among dancehall’s best.

World.title: Burnham’s AI agenda is already in disarray thanks to Trump
World.content:
Within the space of a week, however, Trump trashed any hopes that America will participate in global agreements on AI and POLITICO revealed that AISI’s usually privileged access to new AI models is now being delayed by the White House – which told leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic not to share their models with the U.K. until U.S. testers have finished ascertaining that they don’t pose a threat to American systems.

So if Burnham wants to stick to his plan of making U.K. the center for brokering international AI harmony he has to figure out how to bring the U.S. onside, or else press on without the U.K.’s closest ally.

When approached by POLITICO, a U.K. government spokesperson said: “The U.K. is a world leader in AI security, and the AI Security Institute continues to work closely with the U.S. government, international partners and leading AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic.”

Special relationship problems

The U.K. already has a track record for convening global meetings on AI safety, but it has also tended to stick by the U.S. when deciding whether to sit out specific international agreements.

In 2023 the U.K. hosted the Bletchley Park Summit on AI safety, which produced an agreement on the opportunities and risks of AI signed by 28 countries, crucially including the U.S. and China.

However, at the Paris iteration of the summit in 2025 the U.K. declined to sign a new declaration on the ethical development of AI alongside the U.S.

World.title: Dutch opposition party votes to join European Socialist family
World.content:
“There are only three European political families represented at all three levels [of the

EU],” the advisory committee wrote in a report, adding that the PES has “prime ministers, the President of the European Council, European Commissioners, and leaders of national parties.”

“The Greens … have fewer ministers, no members of the European Commission, and no

heads of government; consequently, their preliminary consultations carry less weight,” the

report went on.

PRO leader Jesse Klaver joined a PES meeting ahead of the European Council summit in June, alongside Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.

What about the MEPs?

European political parties and political groups in the European Parliament are closely

linked, but they are not the same thing.

A PRO spokesperson told POLITICO that the party’s eight MEPs are likely to remain in

their current parliamentary groups: four in the Socialists and Democrats and four

in the Greens/European Free Alliance.

The spokesperson said PRO would likely review the arrangement ahead of the next

European Parliament election in 2029.

World.title: Pope Leo calls for dialogue as France’s populist forces eye power
World.content:
The pope named no politician or party. But his defense of diversity and religious freedom lands as Le Pen’s National Rally campaigns against immigration ahead of a presidential election she hopes to win for the first time.

“This dialogue is all the more urgent in the context of present-day France, where the people of differing cultural and religious backgrounds are called to live together,” the pontiff continued.

Standing in front of French government members and church dignitaries, the pope also argued against pushing religion out of public life, weeks after the National Rally said it was in favor of banning the Muslim headscarf. “Righteous secularism doesn’t mean excluding religion from public spaces,” he said.

Macron said the pope brought “hope” to France and praised his work on artificial intelligence and human dignity.

The papal visit will take Leo from the Élysée to UNESCO, Notre-Dame Cathedral and a youth vigil at the Stade de France. He will celebrate Mass on Saturday, expected to gather 600,000 people on the Champs-Elysées in Paris.

French politics have become deeply polarized in recent years, with the far-right National Rally and the far-left France Unbowed gaining popularity, just as traditional parties struggle to attract voters after a decade of Macron’s presidency.

World.title: Zelenskyy warns $27B funding gap could leave Ukraine short of weapons
World.content:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (R) and High Representative of the European Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas (L) attend a joint press-conference following talks in Kyiv on October 13, 2025. | Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images

The president said he received a positive and constructive response from the EU during his diplomatic talks this week.

KYIV — Ukraine needs to secure $27 billion to plug a hole in its defense budget in the next two months or risk being unable to buy weapons early next year, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters in a WhatsApp chat Friday.

“Most of this money is for our drones, missiles, and supplies for our warriors. About a third of this money, perhaps even a little more, is for drones for January, February, and March. And if we do not order and pay for them in October and November, we will face serious challenges in January and February,” Zelenskyy said.

The president added that covering the deficit was a top topic of his negotiations with European partners: “I am urging the European Commission to provide the second tranche of the €90 billion [loan] sooner. Because, once again, we must have the necessary drones and missiles for January and February.”

World.title: Burnham plans first Berlin visit for talks with Merz
World.content:
Burnham took office on July 20 after replacing Keir Starmer, whose government had come under growing pressure following electoral losses, internal Labour Party disputes and weak public support. Starmer’s departure capped a turbulent final period in office in which domestic political problems increasingly dominated his government’s attention.

The change in leadership came less than a year after Starmer and Merz had made a major push to bring Britain and Germany closer.

The two governments signed the Kensington Treaty in July 2025. It laid out plans for closer work across defense and security, economic ties, transport and migration.

Defense has become one of the strongest parts of the relationship. Britain and Germany signed the Trinity House Agreement in October 2024, creating a framework for much closer military and defense-industrial cooperation. Since then, they have expanded work on joint weapons projects and military coordination while remaining major European supporters of Ukraine.

Burnham now has the chance to give those efforts new political momentum while setting his own approach to Europe. He entered Downing Street promising an intense domestic focus, but has since embarked on a diplomatic blitz, including meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy along with France's President Emmanuel Macron and U.S. President Donald Trump.

While Burnham is enjoying an early bout of optimism about his leadership, he will meet a German government facing significant domestic pressure.

Merz’s Christian Democrats suffered sharp losses in two state elections this month, while the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has gained support nationally. POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts the AfD at 28 percent, ahead of the Christian Democrats at 20 percent.

For both governments, the October meeting offers an early opportunity to show that the closer relationship built over the past two years can continue under new political leadership in London.

World.title: Von der Leyen ally slams EU Commission’s AI response
World.content:
The enforcement of the EU's 2024 AI Act, which mandates that companies take measures to avoid losing control of their models, "is not on the level [where] we would like to have it," he added.

The comments shine the spotlight on the European Commission's Artificial Intelligence Office, which was put in charge of enforcing the AI Act in August.

Voss also said the Commission's overall response to the fast pace of technological developments is lagging, singling out von der Leyen's State of the Union last week.

"The Commission ... also the State of the Union is not ambitious enough regarding digital developments," said Voss, who is a member of the German Christian Democratic CDU, to which von der Leyen belongs.

One area where Voss sees a need for further regulation is liability of AI companies when their technology does damage. "What has been wrong from the beginning of this mandate is not to think about liability of AI," he said. "This can have an effect on every company."

POLITICO reported Monday that other European Parliament members have floated a proposal to add product liability provisions to address gaps in the AI Act.

World.title: Pope’s artificial intelligence guru admits he doesn’t use AI
World.content:
Pressed on whether he had any principled objection to the technology, he declared, “I’m quite willing and happy to learn,” he added. “I feel it’s my moral duty also to use it so that I have personal experience, and I hope it helps me with my work.”

Speaking on the fringes of Axel Springer’s WELT AI Summit in Berlin, Czerny called on European politicians and bishops to respond more clearly to warnings about the risks of frontier AI models forfeiting human control and oversight.

“There should be a dialogue between the bishops and the European governments to express the concern of the population to handle this with openness and with creativity … Otherwise, we will say five months or five years from now, ‘Oh, I felt there was a disaster coming, but there was nothing I could do.’”

The Roman Catholic Church is stepping up involvement in recent discussions over the future of AI. Paolo Benanti, the Vatican’s adviser on AI, attended a meeting of tech executives convened by King Charles III in Scotland last week to discuss the opportunities and risks surrounding the technology.

Anne McElvoy is a Global Reporter for the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.

The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, The Telegraph, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

World.title: Deutschland und Spanien zetteln Papierkrieg zu „Made in Europe“-Auslegung an
World.content:
In der EU geht es um Aufträge, die einen erheblichen Teil der Wirtschaftsleistung ausmachen. Von Windparks bis hin zu Stahl und Zement für den Bau von Autobahnen und U-Bahnen.

Deutschland, das Exportkraftzentrum der Union, dringt auf eine breiter angelegte „Made with Europe“-Definition. Dies entspricht auch weitgehend dem ursprünglichen Vorschlag der Kommission. Er sieht die Aufnahme von Partnern vor, die Freihandels- oder Beschaffungsabkommen mit der EU geschlossen haben oder einer Zollunion mit der Union angehören. Der Kreis könnte bis zu 80 Länder umfassen.

„Deutschland lehnt Protektionismus und Diskriminierung ab“, heißt es in dem deutschen Papier. „Die EU muss ein verlässlicher Partner für ihre Freihandelspartner bleiben und ihren rechtlichen Verpflichtungen nachkommen.“ Außerdem wird darin eine „Opt-in“-Möglichkeit gefordert, um Staaten einzubeziehen, die EU-Firmen eine entsprechende Behandlung gewähren.

Dem deutschen Papier haben sich bisher keine anderen EU-Länder angeschlossen. Frankreich, die zweitgrößte Volkswirtschaft der Union, dringt wie Spanien in die entgegengesetzte Richtung und plädiert für einen restriktiveren Ansatz.

Der französische Industrieminister Sébastien Martin bestritt zwar nicht, dass Europa gegenüber Handelspartnern offen bleiben müsse, betonte jedoch, dass öffentliches Geld in die Produktion in Europa fließen müsse.

„Auch in Zukunft wird es möglich sein, Produkte zu haben, bei denen ein Teil der Wertschöpfung aus anderen Ländern stammt, aber die Produktion muss in Europa stattfinden, damit sie für öffentliche Fördermittel infrage kommen“, sagte Martin bei seiner Ankunft zur Sitzung am Donnerstag in Brüssel.

World.title: How Russia recruits Belarusians for war in Ukraine: Methods and consequences
World.content:
Russia has long regarded Belarus as a convenient reserve for topping up its manpower in the war against Ukraine, especially after suffering heavy losses at the front.

 

Minsk’s economic dependence, the political vulnerability of Aliaksandr Lukashenka's regime and the legal uncertainty around the Union State create conditions in which the Kremlin can act with considerable freedom.

In the Belarusian corner of the internet, in recent months a large number of adverts offering Belarusians the chance to sign a contract with the Russian army, have appeared. They are circulated everywhere – in Telegram channels, in Viber chats and in local community pages where people discuss everyday issues.

At times it looks almost surreal: nestled between posts about selling vegetables or finding a tutor, a sudden offer appears promising a "high salary, benefits and Russian citizenship" in return for going to war.

Investigations by DW, TVNET, CityDog and Current Time have documented a sharp increase in such posts. The human rights initiative Belpol regularly highlights examples of adverts in which recruiters use Belarusian phone numbers to inspire trust.

On Belpol’s Telegram channel you can see messages promising huge payouts, help with loans, "annulment of criminal convictions" and fast-track Russian citizenship.

On X, the OSB Belpol account posts screenshots of ads in which Belarusians are offered a contract with a one-off payment of 4.35 million roubles and rapid issuance of a Russian passport.

These examples are not isolated incidents but part of a systematic campaign targeting socially vulnerable people.

What recruiters promise

Belarusians are promised the equivalent of tens of thousands of euros, high salaries, housing, food, a military pension and life insurance.

Some adverts even talk about "sorting out problems with the law," which is particularly dangerous given that participation in an armed conflict abroad falls under the article on mercenary activities in Belarus' criminal code which carries a prison term of up to seven years.

Recruiters insist that the service is "legal," claiming it is not mercenary activity but "service in the army of the Union State."

A Russian Army soldier controls an area from a board of military helicopter in an undisclosed location in Ukraine, 9 July, 2026 AP Photo

Who signs up for a contract?

Research shows that among those recruited, the majority are men from small towns and villages, people on low incomes, with debts or with existing legal problems.

Many do not realise the legal consequences and some are simply looking for quick money, without understanding that they will be sent to the most dangerous sectors of the front.

Human rights activists point out that foreign contract soldiers are often placed in assault units, where casualty rates are particularly high.

The recruitment scheme is simple and effective. A person sees an advert on social media and writes to the recruiter, who is using a Belarusian phone number. They are then told about payments, benefits and the supposed "legality" of the service.

After that they are offered rapid paperwork and travel to Russia – most often via Smolensk or Pskov. There they sign a contract and become a member of the Russian armed forces. At that point there is almost no way back.

For those who agree to sign a contract, the consequences can be tragic. Beyond the risk of being killed, they face criminal liability in Belarus, possible loss of citizenship or restrictions on their rights.

Many end up as "cannon fodder" in someone else’s war, which they often barely understand.

Russia soldiers advance towards Ukrainian positions at the area of Huliaipole, 17 December, 2025 AP Photo

Public and state response

Belarusian society has generally reacted to this with alarm.

People complain about mass spam-recruitment; some turn to the Interior Ministry, but there is virtually no response.

The Lukashenka regime does not officially acknowledge that recruitment is taking place, but it does nothing to stop it.

Belarus is far too dependent on Russian subsidies to openly confront the Kremlin.

Furthermore, mobilisation measures inside the country are being stepped up, adding extra pressure on men of conscription age.

People walk past an army recruiting billboard in St. Petersburg, 24 March, 2023 AP Photo

Recruitment as part of Kremlin strategy

The recruitment of Belarusians is not about random adverts or the haphazard initiative of individual actors. It is a coordinated campaign built into the Kremlin’s strategy for expanding its pool of manpower for the war against Ukraine.

The legal framework of the Union State gives Moscow extra room for manoeuvre: formally, citizens of Belarus and Russia have "equal rights" and Russian institutions are trying to spin this as "equal obligations," including compulsory military service.

The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) warns that such an interpretation could become a basis for exerting pressure on Belarusians and attempts to mobilise them.

Russia is exploiting the vulnerability of Belarusian society, its information isolation and Minsk’s political dependence in order to turn Belarus into a source of manpower.

And the longer the war drags on, the more aggressive this campaign becomes.

World.title: ‘Godzilla’ El Niño to be the strongest in living memory. How can we prepare for the unavoidable?
World.content:
The ‘Godzilla’ El Niño is here, and it is already breaking records the world would rather have left unbroken.

 

Sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean have already surpassed the highest recorded during any previous El Niño, and the weather phenomenon is still strengthening. Between June 2026 and February 2027, experts estimate the extreme heat associated with it could contribute to 451,000 additional deaths.

The forecast has set off alarm bells among weather agencies, health authorities and governments around the world, including an unprecedented mobilisation by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) to prepare for the extreme weather ahead.

“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in early September. “The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”

But even as governments brace for what could be a devastating year of extreme weather, experts say there is still plenty that can be done to limit the damage – both now and in the future.

Why is this El Niño so concerning?

Records aside, many worry about what an El Niño of this strength could mean for weather around the world in the months ahead.

An El Niño event starts in the Pacific, but its effects can be felt around the world. When waters near the equator become unusually warm, they release heat into the atmosphere, pushing up global temperatures and changing where rain falls.

With ocean temperatures already at record highs, this El Niño could bring more intense heat, drought and heavy rainfall in vulnerable regions and push global temperatures to new highs – earning it the nicknames ‘Godzilla’ and ‘Super’ El Niño.

Some of those effects are already being felt. India has already experienced below-normal monsoon rainfall while southern Africa faces an increased risk of drought.

Even though Europe is unlikely to experience the most severe direct effects, El Niño can influence winter weather, and droughts or failed harvests elsewhere can disrupt supplies of foods imported into Europe.

The threat is already prompting governments to act around the world. This month, California Governor Gavin Newsom preemptively declared a state of emergency to prepare for potential flooding, landslides, coastal erosion and powerful winter storms.

How can we prepare for an unavoidable El Niño?

For all the preparations we make, one thing remains unavoidable: El Niño is a natural phenomenon. But even if we can’t prevent it, forecasts give us months to prepare.

“The key is to manage water and prepare for the changes in where and when rainfall occurs,” says Davide Faranda, research director at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and a lead author for the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

For example, he explains, governments can store and distribute water more carefully, better control how reservoirs and underground water are used, adjust farming schedules and irrigation practices, and prepare communities for droughts or floods.

The FAO has also offered concrete advice. Farmers, FAO officials say, can reduce losses by changing planting dates, irrigating at cooler times of day, storing water ahead of droughts and taking steps to protect their crops and livestock from extreme heat.

Some governments have stepped up with financial support.

The UK has pledged up to £15 million (€17 million) to help vulnerable countries prepare for this El Niño. The money will fund measures that range from vaccinating livestock before droughts to reinforcing homes before flooding and providing farmers with cash before harvests fail.

Climate action could limit future damage

Most El Niño events increase global average temperatures by around 0.2°C. While this is enough to trigger extreme weather conditions across the Global South, it is a fraction of the additional warming caused by climate change.

The burning of fossil fuels has pushed global average surface temperatures by approximately 1.3°C to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels, paving the way for Europe’s scorching summer that triggered mass droughts and wildfires.

El Niño’s impacts are therefore compounded by an already warming world. It’s why 2025 was the third warmest year on record – hotter than the El Niño year of 2016 – despite the naturally forming cool drag of a La Niña event.

Recent research suggests that climate change is turbocharging El Niño as well. A study published in August found that El Niños are 36 per cent stronger than before the industrial era, a trend researchers linked to human-caused warming.

If climate change is making El Niño stronger, then preparation will only go so far. But Faranda says cutting emissions can make a big difference over the long term.

A hotter planet means more extreme heat, more strain on water supplies and, in some places, more rainfall. Reducing emissions would not stop the natural climate cycle that leads to El Niños, he explains, but it would reduce the human-caused warming that is making those threats more severe.

That means the damage is not entirely beyond our control. “We cannot eliminate El Niño through climate mitigation,” Faranda says, “but we can reduce the extent to which climate change makes its consequences more severe.”

World.title: Ljubljana vs Zagreb: Which Central European capital should you visit next?
World.content:
Ljubljana and Zagreb are two seriously underrated capitals.

 

Both overshadowed by other destinations in their respective countries – Lake Bled for Slovenia, and basically anywhere along the coast for Croatia – these cities are more than overdue their time in the spotlight.

While people have slowly been waking up to the joys of Ljubljana, with its car-free city centre and fantastic creative scene, Zagreb next door hasn’t quite hit the mainstream just yet.

Hopefully we can change that.

(Plus, if after reading all this you still can’t decide between the two you can always “trip-maxx” and visit them both – you can travel between them by bus or train in just two-and-a-half hours).

Ljubljana Castle overlooks the city Dianne Apen-Sadler

Ljubljana

One of the things travellers comment on most when talking about Ljubljana is just how walkable it is.

Its centre has been closed to cars and other vehicles since 2007, and it makes the best parts of a European city break – walking around aimlessly and stopping in shops, cafés, and restaurants that catch your eye – infinitely better.

A good place to begin your wandering will be the Triple Bridge over the Ljubljanica River – not just because it’s incredibly central, but the bridges are UNESCO-listed as part of the works of Jože Plečnik in Ljubljana heritage site.

The Slovenian architect played a key role in the development of the city between the two World Wars, and you can see his works along the river embankments and at sites such as the National and University Library or the outdoor theatre Križanke.

For a closer look, you can visit Plečnik House, which offers a deep dive into his best-known buildings (both realised and not), and has his original furniture and tools amongst its collection.

If rambling has your stomach rumbling, head to Trubarjeva Street, which is dotted with independent shops, cafés and restaurants.

While I’ve obviously just spoken about the joys of meandering without a goal in sight, I do have to give a shoutout to Abi Falafel, which serves the best falafel I’ve ever eaten and think about constantly. High praise, given I live in Qatar which has plenty of great options to choose from.

Should you be in town on a Friday between March and October, you could also explore the Open Kitchen food market near the Central Market.

The city’s most iconic sight is, of course, Ljubljana Castle, which sits on a hill above the capital.

Originally built in the 11th century, much of the current structure is from the 15th and 16th century, and visitors can reach it via funicular railway.

Inside, you can learn about the fortress’ history, climb up the viewing tower, or buy a bottle of wine made with grapes on the slopes of the castle’s hill.

Ljubljana is also known for its alternative scene, the most famous of which is Metelkova Mesto, a cultural centre started from a squat in a former military barracks started in the 90s. Today, there are various art spaces here, and you can also attend club nights, the details of which are posted on the Metelkova website.

Zagreb’s most notable – and most colourful – site has to be St. Mark’s Church Dianne Apen-Sadler

Zagreb

Croatia’s capital is also plenty walkable, with many of the main tourist attractions concentrated in the Upper Town, although you can also make use of the extensive tram network.

To reach the Upper Town, you’ll pass through the Stone Gate, which dates back to the 13th century.

While you’ll no doubt have been through plenty of medieval gates while visiting other historic cities in Europe, Zagreb is notable for its shrine to Mary, which survived a fire unscathed in the 18th century and now serves as the city’s patron saint.

Zagreb’s most notable – and most colourful – site has to be St. Mark’s Church. First founded in the 13th century, the historic building’s roof tiles show the Zagreb city emblem as well as the coat of arms of Croatia, Slavonia and Dalmatia, the kingdom within the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

The Grič cannon in Lotrščak Tower is fired daily at noon Dianne Apen-Sadler

Time your visit to then pass by Lotrščak Tower for noon, when the Grič cannon has been fired daily since 1877.

An alternative to your bog standard history or archaeological museums, Zagreb’s Museum of Broken Relationships is a must-visit.

Featuring objects donated by the public from around the globe, you’ll find things inside like the “toaster of vindication”, taken cross country post break-up (“How are you going to toast anything now?”). Both depressing and hilarious, it’s proven so popular in recent years that a second location has since opened in Thailand.

Another popular attraction in the Upper Town is Zagreb Cathedral, but it should be noted that restoration works are still underway following the 2020 Zagreb earthquake.

While the Upper Town is all about medieval history, Zagreb’s Lower Town was built in styles popular in the Austro-Hungarian empire in the 19th and 20th centuries.

There’s plenty of greenery: The area is home to the Green Horseshoe, a U-shaped system of parks in the city’s squares, as well as the Zagreb Botanical Garden.

You’ll also find galleries and museums like the Archeological Museum, Ethnographic Museum and the Museum of Arts and Crafts, while those looking for restaurants, cafés and bars can head to the streets around Ban Jelačić Square.

World.title: Why are Norwegians buying more Chinese EVs despite growing scepticism?
World.content:
Chinese car brands are taking an increasingly large market share in Norway, even as their electric vehicles are being met with growing scepticism in the country, which leads the world in EV adoption.

 

According to a new survey by the Norwegian Electric Vehicle Association, conducted from 31 March to 3 May among nearly 15,000 EV owners in Norway, nearly one-third (31%) of Norwegian electric car drivers said they would avoid buying a Chinese brand for political reasons, compared with 23% a year earlier.

“New cars are, in practice, computers on wheels,” the association’s secretary general, Christina Bu, said in a statement.

“As data security and privacy receive more attention, it is only natural that more consumers become concerned about where the cars come from and how the data is handled,” she added.

A few years ago, Norwegian security researchers discovered that a car made by the Chinese maker NIO was transmitting data to China.

Other tests carried out on a bus from China’s Yutong revealed that the manufacturer had access to the vehicle’s control system and could, in theory, stop it or render it unusable remotely.

Sales of Chinese brands such as BYD, NIO and Dongfeng, and brands owned by Chinese companies like Volvo and Polestar, have nonetheless grown significantly in Norway, accounting for about 25% of new EV registrations in the first half of the year.

Back in 2019, they were virtually non-existent.

“This suggests that consumers weigh several factors against one another when they are buying a car,” Bu said.

“For some, factors such as price and technology are decisive, while others are influenced by moral dilemmas and uncertainty about data sharing and security issues,” she said.

Chinese-owned brands gain ground in Norway

In just a few years, Chinese-owned brands have gone from a negligible share of Norway’s new EV market to becoming its second-largest group by origin, according to an earlier report by the association.

The report suggested they could overtake European brands as soon as 2027 if current trends continue. It also said Norway could become one of the first European markets where Chinese EV makers gain a dominant position.

Gaining ground in Norway matters because the country leads the world in EV adoption. Electric cars accounted for 97.8% of new car registrations in the first eight months of 2026, according to the Norwegian Road Federation (OFV).

Norway remains far ahead of the EU, where electric cars accounted for 21.7% of new registrations between January and August, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA).

Chinese brands are gaining ground in the wider EU, too. Registrations across five groups with Chinese brands listed by ACEA rose by about 71% in August from a year earlier. Their combined share of the overall new car market climbed from 6.6% to 10.8%. This means that roughly one in nine new cars registered in the EU came from these groups. The figure includes brands with European roots, such as Volvo Cars, which is owned by the Geely Group.

In the EU, among the fastest-growing manufacturers were Leapmotor (up 211%), Chery (201%), BYD (129%) and Geely Group (24%). Registrations of cars made by US carmaker Tesla grew by 53%.

Tesla resistance falls

Political resistance to Tesla has fallen in Norway, too. According to the survey by the Norwegian Electric Vehicle Association, the share of respondents who said they would avoid Tesla for political reasons dropped to 24% from 43% last year. Musk’s political involvement and support for far-right leaders have drawn opposition to the brand.

“Last year, Elon Musk’s political involvement was highly visible and, unsurprisingly, provoked strong reactions,” Bu said.

“This year, there has been less attention on this, and that may have led to fewer people saying they would not have chosen Tesla,” she added.

Tesla remains Norway’s best-selling new car brand, with a 17.5% share of registrations so far this year, according to OFV data through 24 September.

World.title: Ceuta crisis reignites debate over suspending the EU’s right to asylum
World.content:
For now, suspending the right to asylum in the European Union is still only under consideration.

 

But the prospect is already setting off alarm bells among some left-wing politicians and those on the front lines of Europe’s asylum system, who fear that suspending a fundamental right of the EU would be both unprecedented and dangerous.

Earlier this month, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed in her State of the Union speech to introduce an emergency framework that could pave the way for the suspension of the right to asylum, a controversial measure that some capitals have already endorsed.

The proposed framework is a response to the Ceuta crisis, following the mass entry of 82,000 irregular migrants from Morocco in late July, with several thousand of them who are still in the Spanish exclave, waiting for their applications to be assessed.

A suspension of the right to seek asylum would be unprecedented at EU level, marking a radical departure from existing migration policy and prompting a major backlash.

Under current rules, any foreign national present in an EU country is entitled to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered the bloc, with each claim assessed on an individual basis.

Changing the asylum principle would result in allowing "collective pushbacks", with migrant people sent back outside the EU, irrespective of their personal situation.

According to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), this practice would breach the principle of non-refoulement and migrant's fundamental rights, as people could be returned to a place where they would face torture, inhuman treatment and threats to their life or freedom.

"Even at times of migratory pressure, States must ensure that people seeking asylum have access to asylum procedures and cannot deviate from this important principle of international law," UNHCR told Euronews in a statement.

Von der Leyen said the emergency framework would only be triggered "under a strictly defined set of criteria" and "allow for time-limited and strictly defined flexibility in standard procedures."

A Commission official told Euronews there is no clear timeline for presenting the proposal, and details remain unclear. The topic is likely to be discussed on Saturday at a Migration Conference in Munich, which features ministers and representatives from 18 European countries, the official said.

Meanwhile,civil society groups and MEPs are already pushing back against any mechanism that would allow governments to sidestep existing asylum safeguards.

“This would mean dismantling another piece of EU values,” Italian Socialist MEP Cecilia Strada, a prominent voice on migration issues, told Euronews. She argued that “exceptional circumstances” are simply an excuse to justify pushbacks, which are illegal under EU law.

In various judgments, the European Court of Human Rights has condemned Greece, Lithuania and Poland for this practice.

“This exposes people to being pushed back to places where they would face violence or death,” Michele LeVoy, director of the NGO PICUM (Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants), told Euronews.

However, the massive influx of irregular migrants into Ceuta sparked a broader debate over the right to asylum. As the crisis unfolded, several countries called for an emergency meeting, while Italy even reintroduced air and maritime border controls with Spain for a month, disrupting free movement within the Schengen area.

In addition, some countries have not shied away from suspending the right to asylum in the past.

Greece suspended the processing of asylum claims for one month in March 2020 and again for three months in July 2025, after a sudden increase in arrivals by sea from Eastern Libya.Poland imposed a similar measure on migrants crossing its border from Belarus in March 2025, during the peak of the weaponization of migrants by Russia and Belarus.

In both cases, national parliaments approved the temporary suspension, and the EU did not challenge the measures.

When the first one took place, von der Leyen did not criticize the measure. During a controversial visit to the border with Türkiye, she even described Greece as “Europe’s shield.”

“Given her record, we have to expect a mechanism that lets member states suspend asylum whenever they decide a border is under pressure,” Iftach Cohen, co-director of the NGO Front-Lex, told Euronews.

Von der Leyen said last week that the EU “will always comply with its values and fundamental rights” while protecting its external borders.

But other MEPs remained unconvinced.

“By making that point, von der Leyen echoes once again the xenophobic and populist rhetoric that far-right political groups have been using for years,”Greens/EFA French MEP Mélissa Camara told Euronews.

The Left’s French MEP Damien Carême said he is ready to launch legal action to enforce fundamental rights, arguing that “von der Leyen appears to have forgotten they exist”.

The Ceuta incident came against a broader backdrop of declining asylum applications and irregular arrivals across Europe, with both figures falling since 2023.

World.title: What is killing whale calves in Patagonia? bacteria under suspicion
World.content:
Hundreds of southern right whale calves have died in recent months in Argentine Patagonia, in an episode that has put scientists and authorities on alert. Initial investigations point to a bacterial infection as a possible cause of an exceptionally high mortality rate this season.

 

Just this week, dozens of dead whale calves have appeared on beaches in the province of Chubut, in southern Argentina. Cases have been recorded since June, affecting one of this species' main breeding grounds in the South Atlantic.

"The mortality rate among calves is quite high, especially this season," explained Mariano Coscarella, a researcher at the Marine Mammals Laboratory of the National Scientific and Technical Research Council (Conicet), speaking to AFP.

Bacteria among the main hypotheses

Veterinarians are now investigating whether erysipelas, an infectious disease caused by bacteria that are often present on the skin of these mammals, could be behind the deaths.

Authorities in Chubut have indicated that initial analyses point specifically to a common marine bacterium, although the investigation remains open to establish with certainty what is causing the fatalities.

Coscarella believes that for the moment the evidence points to a natural cause, but warns that a possible influence of human activity still cannot be completely ruled out.

The provincial government says it is working together with the scientific community to determine the origin of the episode.

One of the southern right whale's main calving grounds

Puerto Madryn and the nearby Valdés Peninsula form one of the major breeding refuges for the southern right whale. Every year, large numbers of whales arrive in these waters to mate and raise their young. These cetaceans can reach around 17 metres in length and weigh about 40 tonnes as adults.

In 2025, a record 2,110 whales were counted in the area, around 800 of them juveniles. This year, the tally stands at 1,375 animals, including nearly 400 calves, according to data provided by Coscarella.

Despite the high number of deaths recorded this season, the researcher notes that the episode does not, for now, pose a medium-term threat to the region's whale population.

The species' longevity is one of the factors behind that assessment. Local authorities estimate that a southern right whale can live for around 60 years.

World.title: The US lays groundwork for possible military action in Cuba, according to 'CBS News'
World.content:
The United States Army is reportedly taking preparatory steps for a possible operation involving Cuba, according to an exclusive published on Friday by CBS News, which obtained an internal Army message and spoke with several US officials familiar with the plans.

 

The US Army Reserve is examining whether it can provide US Southern Command with Military Police forces, medical staff and other support units within a period of 90 to 120 days, according to the document reviewed by CBS News.

The internal message does not explicitly mention Cuba. However, several US officials told the outlet, on condition of anonymity, that the request forms part of the military planning the United States is carrying out in relation to the island.

For the moment, there is no indication that any unit has been ordered to deploy, and the document does not specify where the forces would be sent or what kind of operation they would take part in.

Medical, logistics and military police units

According to the US network, the document requests information on the availability of six types of units that could be placed under the authority of US Southern Command, which is responsible for US military operations in Central America, South America and the Caribbean.

These include units specialising in logistics, transport, maintenance, fuel and supplies, as well as an engineer battalion.

The request also covers a medical brigade, teams capable of providing emergency surgery and treatment for wounded troops close to deployed forces, and a Military Police brigade, typically used for security, detention and other policing tasks.

A Southern Command spokesman contacted by CBS News declined to give details of possible movements or deployment timelines for operational security reasons, and said the command continually assesses military needs within its area of responsibility.

'A small neighbouring country' posing no threat

The report comes after months of rising tensions and threats from US President Donald Trump, who this week told the UN General Assembly that Cuba "is a failed state" and that it "will fall".

Meanwhile, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez stated in an interview with NBC News on Friday that the United States "will never be able to find justification" for launching a military attack against Cuba, and he dismissed the idea that the island would suffer the same fate as Venezuela:

"The U.S. government will never be able to find justification or any reason whatsoever to launch a military attack against a small neighbouring country that in no way poses a threat to its national security," he asserted.

World.title: Adieu, dear listeners!
World.content:
This week is the final Sound Kitchen program, and it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listeners Corner’s” with Paul Myers, plus a special musical choice from me to you. Just click the “Play” button above to join the feast!

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October, and today’s show is our last meal together. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 7 February: I asked you a question about the 68th annual Grammy Awards that took place on 1 February. You were to re-read our article “French DJ wins Grammy for Lady Gaga remix” and send in the answer to this question: Which six artists were given “Lifetime Achievement” awards?

The answer is, to quote our article: “On Saturday evening, Nigeria's Fela Kuti was posthumously awarded a lifetime achievement award, becoming the first African artist to receive the distinction.

The king of Afrobeat was one of several artists to receive the award, including Cher, Whitney Houston, Carlos Santana, Paul Simon and Chaka Khan.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question, suggested by RFI Listeners Club member Alan Holder from the English Isle of Wight. Alan’s question was: “What would be your ideal gift from your best friend or spouse? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Mohamed Elsayed Abd Elraheim from Elsharkya, Egypt. Mohamed Elsayed is also this week’s bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club members Hans Verner Lollike from Hedehusene, Denmark; Helmut Matt from Herbolzheim, Germany; Kashif Khalil from Faisalabad, Pakistan, and last but not least, gentle Debashis Gope from West Bengal, India.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 14 February: That week, I asked you a question about the Benin Bronzes, the trove of Nigerian sculptures and artifacts that were looted by colonial powers.

One of the most well-known organizations working for the return of these works is in Nigeria: it’s the National Commission for Museums and Monuments – the NCMM- which requested the return of bronzes from Britain that were looted from the Kingdom of Benin during the British Benin Expedition of 1897. Some of the sculptures date to the fourteenth century, but the bulk of the collection dates to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

And that week, the NCMM had a win, as my good colleague Melissa Chemam noted in her article: “Cambridge University museum set to return Benin bronzes to Nigeria”.

You were to re-read Melissa’s article and give the details of the artefacts to be returned. What did Melissa name in her article about the Benin Kingdom artworks that went home to Nigeria?

The answer is, to quote Melissa: “Among the returned bronzes that will travel in the coming months are wood and ivory sculptures, as well as commemorative heads of King Oba and Queen Mother Lyoba Idia.

The term ‘Benin bronzes’ refers to objects crafted from brass and ivory as well as bronze, which were seized during the colonial-era military expedition.”

The bonus question you answered that week was: “What do you know after all these years? What have you found are important life truths?

The winners are: Faithful RFI Listeners Club member Jayanta Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Jayanta is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club member Nasyr Muhammad from Katsina State in Nigeria, as well as RFI English listeners M. Ganesan from Goa, India, and three listeners from Bangladesh: Rafiq ul Islam from Naogaon, as well as Abdul Mannan and Mahfuza Akhter, both from Chapainawabganj.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Minor Swing” by Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grapelli, performed by the composers with Le Quintette Hot Club de France; "Water No Get Enemy" by Fela Kuti, performed by Fela Kuti and Africa ’70; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer; “L'hymne à l'amour” by Edith Piaf and Marguerite Monnot, sung by Edith Piaf, and “I Wish You Love” by Charles Trenet and Léo Chauliac, performed by Laufey with the Iceland Symphony Orchestra conducted by Hugh Brant.

With much affection from The Sound Kitchen team – Erwan Rome, Paul Myers, and yours truly, Susan Owensby - fare thee well!

World.title: Podcast: Pope in secular France, vultures and farmers, first divorce law
World.content:
With its strong commitment to secularism, France is not an obvious place for Pope Leo XIV to stage an appearance, but his visit is drawing interest from Catholics and non-Catholics alike. After nearly disappearing from France, vultures are making a comeback, but their return has created new tensions with farmers. And France's revolutionary first divorce law from 1792.

Advertising

Some 800,000 people have signed up to see Pope Leo XIV on his first official visit to France, a secular country where the Catholic faith no longer dominates. Francois Mabille, head of the Geopolitical Observatory of Religion at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs, looks at why France is of interest to the Vatican, and young people of different religions talk about what Pope Leo means to them. (Listen @0'00)

Vultures all but disappeared from France by the 1940s as people sought to eradicate the scavenger birds. A programme to reintroduce the four European vulture species to the Grands Causses plateaux in the southern Massif Central has been sucessful – so successful that some farmers say there are now too many. We visit a vulture feeding station to explore the close relationship between vultures and agriculture, and the tensions that arise with the return of wild species. (Listen @20'00)

In 1792, France introduced one of Europe’s first and most liberal divorce laws, as part of a broader revolutionary effort to enact liberté, egalité et fraternité in the family itself. (Listen @14'00)

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: White House bars CNN from covering upcoming Trump trip, broadcaster says
World.content:
CNN said its journalists have been barred from accompanying President Donald Trump on his upcoming trip to Tennessee. The episode marks the Trump administration's latest salvo against the major cable news network.

American news broadcaster CNN said its journalists were not allowed to board Air Force One for a planned trip with President Donald Trump on Saturday.

CNN was scheduled to travel on Air Force One to Knoxville, Tennessee, where Trump was expected to watch a college football game.

The news organization was to be the representative of the TV press pool for the weekend, meaning that it would cover the president and share video and information with the four other big networks that are part of the press pool.

CNN was replaced by Real America's Voice News, a conservative network, the Associated Press reported.

The episode represents the latest showdown between the Trump administration and media networks that the president believes to be unfavorable in their coverage.

Trump bans media outlets from White House To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump bans CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from White House

Trump earlier this week barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House after he said the networks report "fiction and lies."

Major TV networks, including DW, then cut off their pooled coverage of the president in solidarity.

A federal judge temporarily struck down the ban in a ruling on Thursday after the outlets filed a lawsuit.

But the order from the judge addressed "hard passes" to the White House grounds and didn't directly address pool duties.

World.title: TikTok agrees to settle with Alabama state over teen safety
World.content:
The settlement involves TikTok adding several child safety measures to its platform including time limits and increased parental control. It is similar to a recent settlement competitor Meta had reached.

Short-form content sharing platform TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance reached a settlement with Alabama, the southeastern US state said on Friday, days ahead of what would have been a revealing trial over teen safety and its impact on their mental health.

As part of the deal, TikTok agreed to pay $100 million (€87.7 million) to the state of Alabama and enact measures for teens including a two-hour daily use limit, restricted access for children and pauses after 15 minutes of use.

However, the payout could rise to $300 million if 40 other states sign similar agreements with the company within a stipulated time period, the document said.

What have TikTok and Alabama state said after the settlement?

"This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually ​enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens," a spokesperson for TikTok's US operations said in a statement.

Meta settles for $18B. What it means for you. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall sued the social media giant last year.

At least 27 other states and Washington DC have brought similar lawsuits. Apart from these, TikTok faces thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts and municipalities over its impact on teen mental health. Meta Platforms, Snap Inc and Alphabet's YouTube are also defendants in many of these ​cases.

"This is a great day for Alabama parents. Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction. TikTok has agreed to give parents real control over what their kids see and how much time they spend on the app," Marshall said in a press release.

With this, the company has settled all cases selected for trial against it, including claims by five young people and a Kentucky school district.

What were the allegations against TikTok?

The state of Alabama had argued that TikTok's endless stream of videos makes it the most addictive of social media platforms and that its algorithm specifically pushes young users toward content about violence and self harm.

The state held the app partially responsible for a teen mental health crisis and a significant increase in emergency room visits.

The lawsuit also accused TikTok of falsely claiming that it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users to have the app rated as 'safe for teens' on app stores.

It said that TikTok asks users to self-report their ages but also allows them to evade questions by viewing videos without creating an account.

That still earns the company data on viewing habits. Being able to scroll videos without signing in makes 'Kids Mode' an entirely useless feature, the lawsuit said.

France debates social media ban for teenagers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What measures will TikTok take?

As per the settlement, TikTok has to implement a series of safety measures, including:

Two-hour daily limit

Additional parental control limiting time on platform

'Productive pauses' interrupting continuous scrolling after 15 minutes, 60 minutes and 90 minutes

Restrict children access from 12 a.m. to 6 a.m.

Restrictions on push notifications during night and school hours

Robust measures to verify user age

Limits on discoverability of teen accounts by adults

Sending parents notifications of suspicious interactions between teen users and adults

Blanket ban on use of cosmetic filters by teens

Non-personalized feed for teens

Last month, Meta agreed to pay a massive $17 billion to 47 US states and territories in a similar case while agreeing to make changes to teens' access to its platforms, Facebook and Instagram.

It did not admit wrongdoing and conditioned $5 billion of the payout on TikTok, Snap and YouTube's adoption of the same terms. TikTok has not commented publicly about that deal.

World.title: Yemeni leader calls for general mobilization against Houthis
World.content:
Amid military escalation with the Iran-backed Houthis, the Saudi-backed head of Yemen's governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces.

Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, on Friday called for a general mobilization in the war-torn country.

"I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilization and national mobilization, to rally around their armed and security forces," al-Alimi, who is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a televised address.

The head of the governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces weeks after Yemen's government was dealt a major blow by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The Houthis have seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, allowing them to fully control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, igniting global fears about shipping through the chokepoint.

What else did Yemen's leader say?

In his address, al-Alimi also said that the objective of the mobilization is to "restore state institutions and extend sovereignty over the entire national territory," including the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control since 2014.

He added that anyone who defects from the Houthis to the government will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty.

Al-Alimi addressed residents of Houthi-controlled areas, urging them to protect their children and not send them to fight alongside the Houthis.

"The state does not view you as a party to the conflict but as its people and partners," he said.

Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Houthis escalate conflict

For more than a decade, the Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government. Although a 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, fighting has recently flared up again amid the wider conflict involving Iran.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have intensified their missile and drone attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia. They declared a maritime blockade and attacked Saudi targets in an attempt to stifle Saudi oil exports.

The Houthis accuse the kingdom of besieging Yemeni areas under their control. They attacked Riyadh for the first time in years over the weekend, marking a major escalation.
