World.title: From Baguio to Sepang, Iñigo Anton gears up for biggest race of his career in F1 weekend
World.content:
ALL SET. Iñigo Anton poses with his Formula 4 car during his 2025 Southeast Asia campaign. Anton will race car No. 33 under Axle Sports in the Formula Trophy Malaysia at Sepang this October.

With a rookie title under his belt, Baguio’s Formula 4 driver Iñigo Anton heads to Sepang as the only Filipino on the grid, taking on the Malaysian circuit with an F1 crowd watching

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – Iñigo Anton has raced in Sepang before. He has stood on its podium, battled other young drivers around its fast corners, and ended his 2025 Formula 4 campaign as the Southeast Asian series’ rookie champion.

When he returns in October, however, the same track will feel very different.

Formula 1 will be there.

The Baguio racer is set to compete in the Formula Trophy Malaysia at the Petronas Sepang International Circuit from October 2 to 4, a Formula 4 event running as a support race during the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

“This is the biggest opportunity of my career so far,” Anton said during a recent media briefing in Baguio. “The competition will be fierce, but we’ve put in the preparation. I’m ready to leave everything on the track and do the Philippines proud.”

Iñigo Anton prepares for a race during his 2025 Formula 4 Southeast Asia campaign. All photos courtesy of Karen Anton

The weekend itself is unusual. Formula 1 announced in July that Sepang would host the 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix after the original Bahrain race could not proceed earlier in the year amid the situation in the Middle East. The arrangement puts Formula 1 back at the Malaysian circuit for the first time since 2017.

For Anton, it creates a rare opening: a Formula 4 race on the same weekend, at the same circuit with the highest level of single-seater racing.

Familiar track, much bigger stage

Sepang is hardly unfamiliar territory. Anton competed there extensively during the 2025 Formula 4 Southeast Asia Championship, finishing third in the overall drivers’ standings and winning the Rookie Cup for BlackArts Racing. The official championship results list him as the top rookie of the season.

That experience matters because Sepang is not an easy circuit to learn on the fly.

The 5.543-kilometer track combines long straights, heavy braking zones, and fast corners, with heat, humidity, and sudden rain adding another layer of unpredictability. Formula 1 itself describes Sepang as one of the championship’s most demanding circuits.

Anton will race car No. 33 under Axle Sports, according to his camp, which also said he is expected to be the only Filipino driver on the grid.

Iñigo Anton celebrates on the podium with the Philippine flag during his 2025 Formula 4 Southeast Asia campaign. Anton finished the season third overall and the championship’s top rookie.

The Formula Trophy Malaysia opens in Sepang on the Formula 1 weekend before returning to the circuit for two more rounds in November and December. The difference this time is everything’s happening around the race.

An F1 weekend brings a far larger crowd, international teams, sponsors, media, and motorsport decision-makers into the same paddock. For young drivers trying to move up the single-seater ladder, visibility can matter almost as much as results.

That is why Anton’s family sees the October race as more than another start on his calendar.

“With Formula 1 making its much-anticipated return to Sepang, the global spotlight will be brighter than ever,” said his race manager and mother, Karen Anton. “Having our local racing pride fly the Philippine flag on this grand stage is a testament to years of grit.”

A racer raised in Baguio

Anton’s rise has been unusually long for someone still in his early 20s.

He began racing as a child under the guidance of his father, veteran racer Carlos Anton, progressing from karting and local circuit racing to international competition. By 13, he was already attracting attention for competing against much older drivers.

The University of Baguio later recognized him after he was named the Automobile Association Philippines’ 2022 Driver of the Year for circuit racing.

He eventually moved into single-seaters and made his Formula 4 Southeast Asia debut in 2023. By 2025, he was competing in his first full F4 season, taking podiums and eventually the rookie crown.

The road has not been perfectly smooth. Anton has had disqualifications, difficult weekends, and races where pace did not translate into the result he wanted. That is part of what makes the Sepang opportunity significant.

He is no longer arriving simply as the young Baguio racer trying Formula 4. He returns with a full season behind him, experience at Sepang, and a clearer idea of what international racing demands.

Iñigo Anton (center) with his mother and race manager Karen Anton, and father and coach Carlos Anton, during a media briefing in Baguio City on September 21, 2026.

His preparation for October includes physical conditioning, simulator work, and technical coaching. His camp said he has also been working under former Malaysian Formula 1 driver Alex Yoong, whose BlackArts Racing operation fielded Anton during his 2025 F4 campaign. The championship itself identified BlackArts as Yoong’s team.

Carlos Anton, who remains his son’s coach, said the job now is to translate preparation into race pace.

“He has the pace, he has the discipline, and he’s ready to race with the best,” he said.

More than a podium chase

Anton’s camp is openly targeting a strong result, even a podium, but the significance of the weekend is not limited to where he finishes.

Formula 4 is one of the entry points into the FIA’s single-seater development ladder. The cars are slower and less sophisticated than Formula 1 machines, but the discipline teaches the same fundamentals young drivers need as they move upward: qualifying pace, race craft, tire management, technical feedback, and consistency under pressure.

Very few Filipino drivers reach this stage, and fewer still get to race during a Formula 1 weekend.

Anton knows the opportunity may not come often. His sponsors include Motul, Alpinestars, Yokohama, Blu Coffee Distributors, Time Master Watches, Infiniteserv International Corporation, and Axle Sports, support that has helped sustain a career in one of sport’s most expensive disciplines.

The Philippine flag on his helmet and racing suit will therefore represent more than hometown pride when he reaches Sepang.

It will also mark how far a racer who learned his craft in Baguio has traveled.

Anton has already raced this circuit.

This time, the world of Formula 1 will be watching from just a few garages away. – Rappler.com

TWO DECADES AFTER. A costume used for Sofia Coppola's Marie Antoinette's movie is displayed during a press preview of an exhibition in the Versailles Palace to mark the 20th anniversary of the film, in Versailles, France, on September 21, 2026.

A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe

MANILA, Philippines — On September 19, the White House denied access to journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, following through with US President Donald Trump‘s announcement that he would ban them from the building’s grounds.

All three news outlets separately said their teams’ press passes were confiscated when their journalists went to the White House. They have signaled that they may contest the ban on the grounds that it conflicts with the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press.

On September 21, US District Judge Tim Kelly orders the Trump administration to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and blocked officials from enforcing the ban for 14 days. On September 24, the White House said it has reinstated access to the three news organizations.

At the Senate, the impeachment court voted on September 23 to lower the voting threshold for the conviction of Vice President Sara Duterte. The ruling, which passed with 13 votes in favor and one against, approved the September 8 appeal of Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo seeking to overturn the July 6 ruling of Presiding Officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero.

Meanwhile, former overseas Filipino worker and human trafficking victim Mary Jane Veloso was released from the Correctional Institution for Women on September 25. This comes a day after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. granted her absolute pardon, after more than a decade in detention.

World.title: Ilokano filmmaker spotlights real-life queer choir stories
World.content:
A former choir member himself, Ilokano filmmaker Ryand Angelo Ugalde shares the dilemma of a trans man singer: should he continue hormone replacement therapy or preserve the voice that helps fund his studies?

LAOAG CITY, Philippines – Eleven years ago, 24-year-old Ilokano filmmaker Ryand Angelo Ugalde was part of his high school choir. There, he saw the struggles of queers in musical groups and met another student who, like him, was struggling with his identity.

Fast forward to 2026: Ryand co-wrote and directed a musical short film about identity and the hurdles queer people face, highlighting the experiences of his trans man friend, whom he sang with in junior high school.

Ryand’s musical short film Piyesa(Piece) tells the story of a young Ilokano soprano, Kris — played by his real-life friend, fellow choir member, and 23-year-old trans man Nichole Ballesteros — who faces a dilemma about continuing hormone replacement therapy and preserving the voice that helps fund his studies.

A still from ‘Piyesa,’ an Ilokano musical short film. Photo courtesy of YVR

With the film picked as an official finalist in the 9th Sine Kabataan Film Lab and Film Festival this year, Ryand sees it as a love letter to his high school friend and to the trans community.

Although he was a bit skeptical about pitching his story — feeling it should be told by a member of the trans man community — he made sure his film stayed true to Nichole’s experiences.

Shared struggles

As classmates in the vocal music program of the Special Program in the Arts at Ilocos Norte National High School (INNHS) in seventh grade, Ryand and Nichole saw the gender roles in the choir.

As members of the INNHS’ Laoag City Children’s Choir and Samiweng Singers, both award-winning high school choir groups in the Philippines, they competed in the National Music Competitions for Young Artists and other national competitions together, eventually drawing closer as they support each other.

INNHS youth choir poses for a group photo, taken on May 14, 2016, during its second US concert tour in Los Angeles. Photo by Tess Fernandez Palacio

But Ryand noted that his time in the high school choir was difficult, as being openly gay made it hard for him to find a true sense of belonging.

“During those years, I was also struggling with my voice because I was going through puberty,” he said in a mix of Filipino and English.

Little did he know, his fellow choir member Nichole, who identified as a man, was experiencing the same struggle.

“Actually, parang nabigla ako sa environment sa school. Parang mabutengak pelang ag-out idi,” Nichole shared.

(Actually, I was overwhelmed by the high school environment. I was so scared coming out.)

In the choir, they had a rule that girls couldn’t cut their hair and boys couldn’t grow it long. “So, we really could not alter anything about us…self-expression was very limited for us,” Ryand told Rappler.

Nichole felt pressured to look like a woman, as a soprano in their choir, from seventh to 12th grade.

“In our group, Nyocks (Nichole) was really…it’s safe to say that she is the powerhouse since she is a soprano,” Ryand said.

Ninth grader Nichole shows off her attire for the 2018 NAMCYA held in Metro Manila. Photo courtesy of Nichole Ballesteros

The two friends, though, drifted apart as Ryand transferred to another school in eighth grade. Since then, they have not been in the same choir.

When Nichole entered college, he enrolled in the criminology program at Northwestern University and expressed his gender identity freely. There, he continued in the school choir, with a full scholarship from second to fourth year.

While he fully accepted who he is in college, he still faced the same challenges in the tertiary choir as he did in high school.

“Idi second-year-ak ket pangbabae talaga costumes ko. Tapos idi nag-fourth-year-ak ket in-try-ko sinaritaan ni conductor-mi if pwede ba akong magsuot ng panglalaki,” Nichole shared.

(Since second year, all my costumes in the choir were for women. However, when I reached fourth year, I dared to ask my conductor if I could wear men’s clothes.)

When he was granted permission to express his identity in his final year in college, he felt overjoyed, finally finding freedom to show his true self in their performances.

Nichole (leftmost) poses with Saguday Chorale wearing his male choir costume in 2025. Photo courtesy of Nichole Ballesteros

First acting gig

Nichole’s story then further inspired Ryand to make a short film about their community when he was contemplating a concept in 2025.

While struggling with his mental health during his first job after graduation, Ryand randomly saw a Facebook post by Nichole. This inspired him to conceptualize the story, drawing heavily on their past experiences in junior high school.

Ryand kept his friend’s experiences in mind while writing the concept with his co-writer, Jodie Dantes. As a chorister in high school, the director knew how restrictive traditional choirs can be for queer people — forcing singers into rigid soprano, alto, or tenor roles based entirely on birth sex, leaving little room for fluid gender identities.

‘Piyesa’ production crew prepares for a shoot at San Agustin Church of Paoay. Photo by Dannah Erika Eclarin

With the material in hand, Ryand reached out to Nichole about starring in Piyesa. Nichole accepted the lead role, bravely taking on his very first acting gig while simultaneously studying for the criminology licensure exam.

Ryand and Yuan Amandy, his producer, then pitched the story to Sine Kabataan. It was selected as one of the finalists, receiving a P200,000 production grant from the Film Development Council of the Philippines this year.

Starring alongside Nichole in the short film were members of the Nasudi Chorale of Mariano Marcos State University, a real-life collegiate choir group, as well as first-time actor Clarence Toledo, who portrays Ryand, the lead character’s friend.

Gender roles

Although he thought he could tell the story perfectly, Ryand experienced some hurdles as he worked on the independent, regional film.

While securing more financial backing proved difficult, Ryand found the creative challenge even greater: accurately capturing the unique struggles of trans individuals within the rigid structure of a choir in a short film format.

Ryand also related the metaphor of the film’s premise to society. “Aren’t we all part of a choir in the society? We have gender roles; we are told to be like this, to be like that, to perform a certain way, to act a certain way,” he said.

“Parang dapat alto ka lang, soprano ka lang, and kung anong dinidikta sa’yo ng society, yun ka lang dapat at yun yung susundin mo,” Ryand added.

(The society dictates some roles; for instance, you should only be an alto, you are only a soprano, and you must follow it.)

A still from ‘Piyesa,’ an Ilokano musical short film. Photo courtesy of YVR

In producing the film, the Ilokano filmmaker made sure his representation of trans people was treated with sensitivity. Aside from Nichole, he interviewed other trans people to understand their individuality and unique difficulties in society.

“Half of the direction was also coming from him (Nichole). I think, kasi nga…Hindi ko alam yung psyche ng mga trans men. Hindi ko alam kung paano sila mag-isip, gano’n,” Ryand told Rappler.

(Half of the direction of the film was also coming from Nichole. The reason for this is that I do not know the psyche of trans men. I do not know how they think as individuals.)

To ensure truthful representation, Ryand took on a consultative approach, collaborating closely with the trans community, the actors, and the production crew. He would also usually ask Nichole what he would do when he experienced a certain situation.

Nichole said he accepted the project since trans men are hardly featured in mainstream or independent films. Piyesa, he shtared, could be a way to tell more stories about them.

“[Maysa kadagiti napadasak ket] tawagandaka ti basang uray tay appearance-mo ket [panglalake],” Nichole shared.

(One of the experiences I have is being called a young lady even though I look like a man.)

Off-screen, the first-time trans male actor has not fully come out to everyone close to him, including his own family.

“Actually, diak inbagbaga kaniada [ti family’k] nga about trans man daytoy film-mi. Mabuyadan to lattan,” he shared.

(Actually, I did not tell my family that our film is about trans men. They would only know once they watch it.)

Ryand (center) with Nichole (left) and Clarence during their shoot at San Agustin Church of Paoay. Photo by Dannah Erika Eclarin

If his family were ever to watch his film, Nichole hopes he will not receive any negative reactions from them.

“Nagdakkel nga opportunity para kaniami a trans man detuy inubrana nga film. Tapos naging boses detuy film to represent the LGBTQIA+ community, especially sa mga trans man, trans woman,” Nichole shared.

(This film is a great opportunity for us trans people. This can be used as a voice to represent the LGBTQIA+ community, especially the trans men and trans women.)

‘World still not kind’

Most of Ryand’s short films center on the victories, trials, and unique narratives of the Ilokano queer community.

For him, telling local stories is important to shifting negative perceptions in conservative regions. It also fills the gap, he said, in a local film landscape that lacks diverse queer representation.

“When no one tells their story, no one would listen; nothing will change as to how society treats us, because even if the world is progressing, unfortunately, the world is still not kind enough for all of us,” Ryand added.

“In the end, this is not just Nichole’s story,” he said. “It is a found story, shaped by years of witnessing him and understanding too late what he was going through, while still singing beside him.” – Rappler.com

World.title: OpenAI works to understand full scope of agent activity as user data leak emerges
World.content:
OPENAI. A man walks past an OpenAI booth at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026

SAN FRANCISCO/WASHINGTON, US – Two months after OpenAI disclosed the accidental hacking of Hugging Face, the ChatGPT maker is still working to understand the full scope of its rogue agent activity, two people briefed on the matter told Reuters.

The latest example came on Friday when OpenAI said its agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users. OpenAI declined to say if the images were AI-generated or identified real people. It also declined to say when the images were posted.

The disclosure and researcher reports on Friday of other previously unknown activity involving several US agencies reveal a new area of privacy risk for the company, and illustrate how difficult it is even for an AI firm at the cutting edge of the technology to inventory all the unauthorized activity tied to its agents. OpenAI’s ongoing battle also reflects a yawning gap between the strength of the models the company is testing and its capacity to oversee or even track their actions.

As of mid-September, one person briefed on the matter estimated that OpenAI had found roughly two dozen incidents of its agents acting in undesirable ways. But the number has continued rising as OpenAI teams sift through internal logs of the agents’ activities and find previously unknown cases, the two people close to the company said.

OpenAI said its review would take months to complete given the scale of the work.

The company also said it had notified dozens of third parties about improper activity.

Most of the leaked images have been taken down and OpenAI said it was lobbying hosting providers to remove the rest.

OpenAI’s agents had access to these images because the company relies on anonymized user data for part of its model-training process, according to the company, former employees and outside researchers. Enterprise data is not eligible for training, while ChatGPT consumers need to opt out of allowing the company to use their data for training.

Before user posts are used for training, they go through an anonymization process that strips out metadata, names and other contact information and should make it difficult to trace back to any individual user, the company said.

But the practice carries risks because there is a chance that the data may not be fully stripped of personally identifiable information and that it might leak in the course of the model’s work, three people familiar with OpenAI’s practices said.

OpenAI agents accessed US websites

OpenAI said late on Friday its models accessed information from the websites of the US Securities and Exchange Commission and the US Census Bureau during research and training activity, but found no evidence of unauthorized access, compromised accounts or security breaches.

Separately, AI research nonprofit Transluce said agents appearing to originate from OpenAI made an unsuccessful attempt to hack a US Department of Education civil rights website.

Transluce said the incident was part of broader AI agent activity probing government websites using tactics including exposed credentials, anti-bot bypasses and fake accounts.

More than 15 cases

In the two months since OpenAI first announced that its agents broke containment, there have been more than 15 different OpenAI-related incidents of varying levels of severity disclosed by the company, by outside researchers, or — just on Wednesday — by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the United Nations, who said OpenAI agents broke into a government health data portal in June.

Past incidents have varied in nature, ranging from spam-like messages left on internet sites all the way to the break-in at Hugging Face, which involved a swarm of agents abusing previously unknown software vulnerabilities to escape their networks and penetrate the AI repository as they hunted for answers to a test. OpenAI also said its agents took aim at its own infrastructure.

Albanese told reporters in New York that OpenAI uncovered the activity in August, and disclosed it on September 10 via an email to a general government inbox. He said he directly told OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that this disclosure process was unacceptable.

OpenAI said some of the sites involved are operated by government, universities and public agencies because the models that are conducting research seek out reputable sources of public information.

A locked-down process

The July 21 announcement that ​OpenAI’s agents had slipped out of control and hacked Hugging Face sparked widespread worries within the AI industry over its ability to control the more powerful AI models under development now. Since then, Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google and Meta have said they’ve found similar behavior by their agents after the Hugging Face incident prompted them to search.

OpenAI has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain.”

Even so, two people familiar with OpenAI’s investigation into its agents’ activity described it as locked down and shaped by company lawyers. The process has been unusually compartmentalized for a company that some former employees say was more open about these issues in the past, the people said.

Roughly 100 people were in some way involved in the process to understand the Hugging Face hack, three people briefed on the matter said. During that process, evidence of other incidents surfaced.

Reuters has previously reported that OpenAI investigators looking into the Hugging Face breach were discouraged by the company’s lawyers from expanding the scope of the investigation to include other incidents. OpenAI said its lawyers did not discourage deeper investigation.

Many incidents have been uncovered by outside researchers rather than OpenAI directly. In several episodes, the agents took problematic actions that went unnoticed by the company for months.

Earlier this month, a small group of investigators discovered that the company’s agents had hijacked a mostly defunct German wiki site to share tactics to cheat on some tasks, bypass OpenAI’s restrictions and mask their behavior.

This week, the AI research firm Transluce said it discovered that OpenAI agents had bypassed the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare’s anti-bot controls. The firm also found two other cases that it linked to OpenAI agents. Those incidents were separate from the activity disclosed by Albanese.

In a statement, OpenAI said “much of the activity described in Transluce’s report overlaps with cases at varying stages of investigation in our ongoing review of misaligned model activity.” The company said it is prioritizing the most severe cases in its review.

Since the Hugging Face hack, researchers across the AI industry have grown worried that companies will not be able to predict or control their technology. Some have taken the path of former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who publicly resigned this month in a viral social-media thread that said the AI labs are “gambling with our lives.”

In response to those concerns, Altman and his counterpart at Anthropic, CEO Dario Amodei, called for the industry to “pace” the development of AI and move cautiously in its pursuit of “recursive self improvement.” Altman doubled down on that message this week while addressing the United Nations.

Even so, both companies rolled out new models on Tuesday. – Rappler.com

World.title: It’s an ADMM-Plus joint sail, but where were the Southeast Asians?
World.content:
ADMM-PLUS SAIL. The BRP Jose Rizal leads 10 other warships during a division tactics drill in the West Philippine Sea on September 23, 2026.

In an Philippine and Japan-hosted and ASEAN-led joint sail, most Southeast Asian navies were absent. So was China.

It was a breathtaking sight to see — 10 gray ships, sailing alongside each other — as the Philippines’ flagship, the BRP Jose Rizal, led the way.

Fine weather, for the most part, graced the two-day maritime activity under the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM)-Plus and its Experts’ Working Groups (EWGs) as navies of Southeast Asia and their partners practiced how they could help each other out in case of emergency in the South China Sea.

The partners showed up big time.

India and New Zealand sent two vessels each, including Wellington’s resupply vessel, the HMNZS Aotearoa. Japan’s JS Ise, a helicopter destroyer, was a domineering presence in the lineup. Australia and the US also sent a warship each.

Singapore sent the RSS Justice while Brunei sent the KDB Darussalam, although it would later bow out of the seaphase activity.

Play Video

Manila’s BRP Tarlac, the first landing platform dock to be delivered under the revised modernization program of 2012, joined the Rizal as well.

So where was the rest of the Philippines’ SEAblings — or fellow members of ASEAN? And where was China, a dialogue partner to both ASEAN and ADMM-Plus?

Where the exercise took place could offer a clue — waters between Zambales and Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal), a high-tide feature that’s within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, claimed by several countries, and under China’s virtual control since 2012.

Bajo de Masinloc has been a flashpoint for tensions between Manila and Beijing for years — most notably in 2012, when the two countries had a tense standoff in the shoal. While Manila retreated under a truce the US had supposedly brokered, Beijing did not.

At least one China Coast Guard vessel and several of its auxiliary Chinese Maritime Militia stand guard at the shoal’s sole entrance at all times.

That 2012 standoff is what spurred the 2012 Revised Armed Forces of the Philippines Modernization law. It’s also what pushed Manila to bring Beijing to court, and eventually win the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award — the same award China does not recognize.

But back to the ADMM-Plus drill.

ADMM-PLUS SAIL. The BRP Jose Rizal leads 10 other warships during a division tactics drill in the West Philippine Sea on September 23, 2026.

It wouldn’t be a stretch to think that Beijing, since it claims sovereignty over and has control of, Bajo de Masinloc, would want to boycott any joint drill near it. It wouldn’t be surprising if China convinced — or pressured — other ASEAN countries to opt out of the drill, too.

Talk is, both things happened.

ASEAN members, however, were in full attendance in the land-based events, including in subject matter expert exchanges and even a Future Leaders’ Program.

China’s ties with the 11 members of ASEAN vary dramatically. Most surveys indicate that the Philippines tends to be an outlier in the region when it comes to its perception of China, mostly because of West Philippine Sea issues.

In a lengthy statement, the Philippines’ Department of National Defense said it remains committed to the “principles, purpose, and objectives” of ADMM and its EWG as it “[provides] important platforms for practical cooperation, camaraderie, confidence-building, and mutual understanding among participating countries in addressing contemporary security challenges.”

The DND, whose head, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. is also chair of ADMM, said the joint sail’s location was done by the book — through the usual ADMM-Plus processes and “based on operational, logistical, and other practical considerations discussed during the Initial Planning Conference (IPC) in March 2025 and subsequent planning conferences, which was attended by all participating countries, including China.”

It went on: “The designated exercise location, which is near Bajo de Masinloc (BdM), has long served as a venue for the Philippines’ bilateral and multilateral maritime exercises, including the ASEAN Multilateral Naval Exercise (AMNEX) held in 2023. This is in consideration of the area’s proximity to the Philippines’ largest naval port facility, which ensures that the necessary infrastructure and logistical support to accommodate the widest possible participation are met, including adequate berthing facilities, sustainment services, and operational support for participating naval assets.”

By largest naval port facility, the DND was referring to Naval Operating Base in Subic, where most of the Philippine Navy’s newest warships are usually berthed. The day before the exercise, warhips of India, Singapore and Brunei were all docked at the same base.

The DND also clarified the Philippines’ position on Bajo de Masinloc as an “integral and longstanding part of the Philippine national territory.”

As a high-tide elevation, Bajo de Masinloc generates its own 12 nautical-mile territorial sea. Its classification as a high-tide elevation also means the arbitral tribunal could not rule on who had sovereignty over it, since that was beyond its jurisdiction.

Play Video

The tribunal did, however, say that since the shoal was the traditional fishing ground of Filipino, Vietnamese, Chinese, and Taiwanese fisherfolk, they should not be hindered from access to it. Beijing has routinely driven away Filipino fisherfolk who try to sail close to the shoal’s once plentiful waters.

Bilateral ties between the Philippines and China have vascilated between tense and strained in the recent years under Marcos, primarily over disputes in an area of the South China Sea that Manila calls the West Philippine Sea.

Tensions have eased considerably beginning 2026, as Marcos sought a “reset” and Manila assumed chairship of ASEAN.

But that reset is backdropped by a strong pushback against China, over its supposed untrustworthiness as a negotiator — chief of those critics being Teodoro, who chairs ADMM. The Philippine defense chief has also been sanctioned by Beijing for his remarks.

So what happens when he hosts defense ministers from ASEAN and its partners — including China — before 2026 ends? – Rappler.com

World.title: OpenAI’s models accessed public US Census, SEC data, Bloomberg News reports
World.content:
OPENAI. An OpenAI logo is displayed at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026

OpenAI's AI systems tapped into US government data, prompting a review of model activity and potential impacts, as reported by Bloomberg News.

OpenAI’s models accessed publicly available information from US government websites, including those of the Census Bureau and the Securities and Exchange Commission, Bloomberg News reported on Friday.

The company’s agentic AI systems interacted with SEC.gov, Investor.gov and publicly available Census.gov data, the report said, citing people familiar with the situation.

Asked for comment, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was “conducting an extensive review of misaligned model activity and notifying organizations when we identify potential impacts to their systems. We expect to make additional notifications as that work continues.”

The review has mostly found “routine research tasks,” and “some involved government websites because our models often turn to them as authoritative sources of public information,” the spokesperson said in a statement. – Rappler.com

World.title: The role of the news media in fighting the climate crisis
World.content:
By dismissing the narrative that people don’t care, and identifying what’s needed to urgently solve the problem, news outlets join with their audiences to solve the most urgent issue of our lives

As awful as the climate headlines have been in 2026 — from melting glaciers to historic wildfires to deadly heatwaves — here’s a sobering fact: there is a very good chance this will be the coolest year of the rest of your life.

This year will be hotter than the last, and last year was hotter than the one before that. Scientists now say that next year, especially with the El Niño weather pattern taking shape, will obliterate records, sending the planet well above the levels experts have held out as the dangerous tipping points of the climate crisis.

Amid all of this, it can be difficult to know where to turn for help and for solutions: governments around the world — and especially in petro states like the United States — seem to be making things worse instead of better. Individual choices can seem trivial given the scale of the problem.

There is, it turns out, an often overlooked solution to the climate problem — and that is journalism. Understanding what is happening, what’s causing it, and who is at fault (and don’t be fooled, there definitely are villains in this story), is a necessary predicate to solving the climate problem. Tuning out doesn’t make science, and reality, go away.

Our nonprofit has spent the last seven years studying how media around the world covers climate change, and helping news outlets do a better job of connecting with their audience about it.

Here’s the good news: the audience is interested.

Peer-reviewed studies show that, on average, 89 percent of people on earth not only care about the climate crisis, but they want their governments to work on fixing it. The problem is that many of those people don’t know they are part of an overwhelming climate majority; they think they’re siloed, on the sidelines. They also don’t know that their neighbors often think like they do and, most critically, they don’t vote like they’re part of the solution.

ALSO ON RAPPLER

This is where journalism comes in. For the past two years, dozens of reporters from around the world have been working to tell the story of the 89 percent in their communities, profiling them and giving them a voice. And the world is taking notice: people have begun showing up on social media identifying themselves as part of the 89 percent, and in August,the global drinks company Oatly began featuring the 89 percent message on its cartons worldwide.

Journalism has the potential to help the public break through on climate change. By dismissing the narrative that people don’t care, and identifying what’s needed to urgently solve the problem — in the voting booth, on the streets, in people’s homes — news outlets have an opportunity, and duty, to join with their audiences to solve the most urgent issue of our lives. That connection will not only help address the climate problem, but it also will help close the trust gap plaguing journalism. People support news outlets that cover what they care about.

It won’t be easy, though.

For decades, the fossil fuel industry — Remember those villains we referenced earlier? — has been investing hundreds of millions of dollars into campaigns intended to mislead the public about the dangers of burning fossil fuels. They have funded disinformation campaigns aimed at undercutting climate science and have sought to erode trust in journalism that is accurately covering the problem.

The rise of social media has resulted in a targeted, coordinated effort to flood consumers with climate lies. A tiny minority of online trolls continues to scare some newsrooms away from being as aggressive in their climate coverage as the story demands.

Journalism has an opportunity to right this wrong — reporting factually and urgently on the crisis we face. And consumers — all 89 percent of us — can use this opportunity to rediscover the value of an independent press, and celebrate the people who are telling the truth about the crisis that is endangering us all. – Rappler.com

Kyle Pope is the co-founder and executive director of strategic initiatives for Covering Climate Now, a global collaboration of newsrooms committed to more and better climate coverage. This opinion piece was commissioned as part of the World News Day campaign, a worldwide campaign highlighting the essential role of journalism in providing facts and clarity.

World.title: Tiny things for big feelings: Small objects are becoming our emotional companions
World.content:
Squishies and plushies aren’t just cute to look at, but sources of comfort, too

I have a habit of always checking my bag before I leave the house.

Phone? Check. Wallet? Check. Keys? Check. My green Inhaler? Essential. My octopus crochet stress ball? Definitely.

Some of these – specifically, my inhaler and octopus ball – are not exactly something you’d consider as necessities, but I always bring them with me.

Whenever I feel nervous, I reach for my inhaler. And when I’m bored waiting for the jeepney to fill up, I wrap my hands around my squishy ball. I like to think of them as my comfort objects.

But what exactly are comfort objects?

Simply put, comfort objects are things that bring us joy, evoke memories, or give us a sense of nostalgia and comfort during nerve-wracking moments.

Popular choices among my peers include dumpling-shaped squishy stress balls, keycap keyrings, cute plushies, fidget keychains, and worry stones. The thing is, comfort objects aren’t one-size-fits-all. They can mean different things to people.

For one friend, it’s a bear keychain from a memorable family trip to Switzerland. Another friend turns to her collectible Fuggler plush whenever she feels stressed after an intense pickleball game.

I know someone who keeps an inhaler with him and says that sniffing it before quizzes helps him focus. Another person loves having her Squidward plushie around to keep her company through a long checklist of tasks.

Sometimes, we carry these objects simply because they’re adorable. For others, they’re reminders of people and places, or something tactile to hold when they’re feeling overwhelmed.

In child psychology, a related concept is the transitional object, an item that helps a child cope with separation or anxiety. Think of a teddy bear that makes a child feel safe when their mother briefly leaves the room, or a favorite bedtime toy that makes the monsters in the closet seem less scary.

While this concept is commonly discussed in childhood development, the desire to find comfort in familiar objects can continue into adulthood.

A 2025 study of 2,729 Filipinos aged 18 to 29 examined depression, anxiety, and stress among emerging adults in the Philippines. Researchers found clusters of severe and extreme levels of these conditions in areas including Metro Manila and several provinces in Luzon. The study used convenience sampling, so its findings should not be treated as representative of every Filipino young adult. Still, it points to the reality that stress and mental health concerns are part of the landscape many young Filipinos are navigating.

Which brings us back to the tiny things. Maybe we’re not always looking for something that will fix everything. Sometimes, we just want something that makes the next few minutes a little lighter.

Pick your tiny thing

Thinking of getting your own comfort object? There’s no official starter kit. It depends on what your hands and your personality are like.

The Squeezer

For people who need something to keep their hands busy, slow-rise squishies are a good place to start. They come in the shapes of food, animals, balls, and practically anything you can imagine. The texture is soft, and it’s soothing to squeeze.

🛒 Buy one here

The Clicker

For anyone who loves a satisfying click, keyboard keychains are a fun take on the classic fidget toy. They’re functional and decorative, and you can clip one to your bag for something to fiddle with while waiting for class, commuting, or killing time.

🛒 Buy one here

The Nostalgic

Your comfort object doesn’t have to be a fidget toy. It could be a tiny plushie from someone you love, a souvenir keychain from another country, or a Filipino snack charm that brings back childhood memories. You’re carrying it because it means something to you, and personally, I think that is one of the sweetest things about it.

🛒 Buy one here

The softie

And then there are people who simply want something cute. Crochet charms and soft toys—you get the idea. There’s no complicated function. You just look at it and think, “Oh, that’s cute. I want that with me.” Honestly? Valid.

🛒 Buy one here

It doesn’t have to be that deep

Our purchases don’t always have to be practical. Your little squishy doesn’t need to justify its existence. Maybe you just like the way it feels, and it makes you smile —and that’s enough.

Comfort objects aren’t replacements for professional mental health support when someone needs it. But they don’t have to be a treatment to be meaningful, either.

My inhaler and a yellow crochet stress ball sitting beside my phone and keys help me get through the day. The traffic might still be bad, my deadlines will keep approaching, and I’ll probably find something new to worry about – but at least I’ll have something small to hold.

Sometimes, that’s how we get through big feelings, not by making them disappear, but by finding little ways to make them feel more manageable.– Rappler.com

This piece was written by Rappler volunteer Betina Andrea Santiago. Betina is a visual storyteller whose work centers on childhood nostalgia and pressing social realities. She enjoys exploring how visual media can drive empathy and is eager to use cinema to spark meaningful dialogue. A graduating Film major from the University of the Philippines Diliman, she aims to produce human-centered stories that give voice to everyday communities.

World.title: Last Weekend of September: What’s On in Astana and Almaty
World.content:
ASTANA – The final weekend of September features a variety of cultural events, including ballet, theater and concerts. The Astana Times editorial team has curated a lineup of events taking place this weekend.

Astana

“The Silk Road” ballet, Sept. 27

Travel back to the era of the Great Silk Road through an evening of dance, music and colourful stage imagery. The performance brings together different traditions and cultures, turning the historic route into a story told through movement.

Venue: Astana Ballet; 43 Uly Dala Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“The Nutcracker” ballet, Sept. 27

Step into a magical world with Tchaikovsky’s “The Nutcracker.” This enchanting ballet brings to life the beloved story of Clara, the Nutcracker Prince, and their journey through a fantastical land of sugar plums, snowflakes and unforgettable music.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konev Street. Tickets are available here.

Kairat Nurtas concert evening, Sept. 27

Kairat Nurtas, one of Kazakhstan’s popular pop singers, will celebrate 20 years on stage with a special concert. The evening will look back at key moments of his musical career and bring fans together for a lively night of music and entertainment.

Venue: Astana Arena; 48 Turan Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Evening of Viktor Tsoy’s music, Sept. 27

Spend an evening with the music of Viktor Tsoy and revisit songs that have remained popular across generations. Live performances will bring his familiar melodies back to the stage while capturing the distinctive atmosphere of his music.

Venue: Sintez Theater; 6 Akhmet Baitursynov Street. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Central Asia Drifting Cup, Sept. 27

Speed, roaring engines and spectacular tandem battles will take over the track as leading drivers compete for victory in an international drifting event. Motorsport fans can expect impressive manoeuvres, high-speed action and plenty of excitement throughout the competition.

Venue: STK Sokol; 76 km of the Almaty – Astana highway. Tickets are available here.

“Into the World of Theatre Through the Museum” exhibition, Sept. 26

Discover the history of theatre through archival photographs, stage costumes and other artefacts that tell stories from behind the scenes. The programme offers a closer look at the people, productions and traditions that have shaped the performing arts over the years.

Venue: Abay Opera Theater; 110 Kabanbay Batyr Street. Tickets are available here.

“Legacy” performance, Sept. 27

Based on “Memory” by Lavrenty Son and Stanislav Li, the production looks back at one of the most difficult chapters in the history of Koreans in Kazakhstan. Beginning with the 1937 deportation, the story follows people forced to leave their homes as they face hardship, loss and the challenge of building a new life.

Venue: Korean Theater of Musical Comedy; 158 Bogenbay Batyr Street. Tickets are available here.

The Golden Middle music fest, Sept. 26

Get into the festive spirit with an evening of live music, entertainment and the lively atmosphere associated with the famous Bavarian celebration. It is a chance to gather with friends, enjoy the programme and spend the evening in a relaxed festive setting.

Venue: Tirol restaurant; 98 Zhibek Zholy Avenue. Tickets are available here.

World.title: Kazakhstan Continues to Investigate Mangystau Military Tragedy, Five Officials Detained
World.content:
ASTANA – Five military officials have been detained as part of a pretrial investigation into the deaths of service members during a military exercise in the Mangystau Region, Deputy Interior Minister Sanzhar Adilov said at a Sept. 25 government commission meeting in Aktau.

The meeting reviewed the progress of the investigation and measures to support the families of the deceased service members and those affected by the tragedy. Adilov said the Military Investigative Department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs is conducting a pretrial investigation into the deaths.

“Five officials have been detained and placed in the temporary detention facility in Aktau: the chief of staff and first deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Naval Forces of the Armed Forces, two commanders of military units, the commander of a marine infantry company and the commander of the boat,” Adilov said.

He added that investigative and procedural measures are continuing, including the necessary examinations. Investigators will provide a legal assessment of the actions of all persons involved and establish the full circle of suspects.

Aid to families to be distributed transparently

Chair of the government commission Kanat Bozumbayev said the state would fully meet its obligations to support the families of the deceased service members. Legally guaranteed payments will be made without delays, while responsible specialists will be assigned to each family to provide ongoing individual support.

The commission also thanked members of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi, Kurultai deputies, political parties, entrepreneurs, and other citizens for their support. Funds raised through a special fund have reached the required level, and the fundraising campaign has been closed.

A special commission headed by Bekmurat Zhusipov, a member of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi and chair of the Mangystau Regional Public Council, has been established to ensure transparent and targeted distribution of the funds among the families and the affected service members. Law enforcement and state bodies have been instructed to ensure strict oversight of the use of the funds.

Defense Ministry pledges accountability

Defense Minister Lieutenant General of Aviation Dauren Kosanov expressed condolences to the families of the deceased service members and said those responsible would face punishment under the law.

“We remain in constant contact with the families of the deceased and provide them with all necessary assistance and support,” he said.

The government commission continues to oversee both the investigation and assistance to the affected families. All circumstances and causes of the incident are being established, with those responsible to be held accountable in accordance with the law.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans to Raise Oil Refining Capacity to Nearly 30 Million Tonnes by 2031
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to increase the combined capacity of its three existing oil refineries from 17.5 million to 28.8 million tonnes per year as the government moves to meet growing domestic demand for petroleum products and considers construction of a fourth refinery.

The plans were discussed at a Sept. 23 government meeting chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov on the implementation of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s instructions to modernize existing refineries and assess the construction of a fourth facility.

Existing refineries to undergo expansion

KazMunayGas Chairman Askhat Khasenov reported on the status and timelines of refinery expansion projects. According to him, the capacity of the Shymkent Refinery is planned to double from 6 million to 12 million tonnes of oil per year by 2030, while the Pavlodar Petrochemical Plant is expected to increase capacity from 6 million to 9 million tonnes by 2031.

At the Atyrau Refinery, an efficiency improvement project is scheduled for completion in 2027, increasing capacity from 5.5 million to 6.1 million tonnes annually.

The Shymkent refinery expansion will also require upgrades to oil transportation infrastructure, including increasing the capacity of the Kenkiyak–Atyrau and Kenkiyak–Kumkol main oil pipelines and the Tekesu station. A Shymkent–Almaty petroleum products pipeline with capacity of up to 3.5 million tonnes per year is also planned.

Fourth refinery under consideration

Deputy Energy Minister Kairkhan Tutkyshbayev reported on work to assess the construction of a fourth refinery. According to the Energy Ministry, Kazakhstan’s long-term demand for oil refining capacity could reach around 40 million tonnes per year.

Bektenov instructed the government to complete a comprehensive assessment and make final decisions on the fourth refinery by the end of this year. The assessment is expected to determine the facility’s optimal capacity, configuration, feedstock base, location and economic model.

Officials were also instructed to closely monitor the expansion projects, prevent delays and ensure the timely commissioning of new facilities, with further attention to increasing the depth of oil processing.

Government links refining investment to fuel prices

Bektenov said the expansion of refining capacity is closely linked to the economic conditions of the domestic fuel market.

“Increasing oil refining capacity is directly linked to the attractiveness of fuel prices on the domestic market. In the current situation, when gasoline and diesel prices in Kazakhstan are twice as low as in neighboring countries, investments in oil refining are economically unfeasible. Therefore, we need to actively continue market liberalization. This is a matter of economic security,” Bektenov said.

The government said the refinery expansion projects are intended to strengthen Kazakhstan’s ability to meet domestic demand for petroleum products over the medium and long term.

World.title: Kazakhstan, China Advance $440 Million Robotics Localization Project
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan and Chinese robotics manufacturer UBTech Robotics are advancing a $440 million project to localize robotics production in Kazakhstan, with plans covering manufacturing, research and development, programming and the creation of new jobs.

The project was announced on the sidelines of the Kazakhstan–China Investment Forum, which opened Sept. 25 at Koktobe Hall in Almaty and brought together more than 600 delegates, including representatives of Chinese corporations, Kazakh businesses, government bodies and development institutions.

According to Yerlan Nabiyev, Nero Group CEO, the cooperation with UBTech Robotics began after an initial meeting in November last year, held on the recommendation of Almaty’s city administration.

UBTech Robotics, a Chinese technology company founded in 2012 and headquartered in Shenzhen, specializes in humanoid and educational robotics. Nabiyev said a subsequent agreement on cooperation was signed during a Kazakhstan–China forum in July in the presence of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

“We have already started implementing the project to localize robotics production here in Kazakhstan on the territory of a special economic zone,” Nabiyev told The Astana Times.

Project to cover production, R&D and programming

The initial investment is estimated at nearly $440 million. According to Nabiyev, the project is designed to go beyond assembling finished products and will include research and development, research activities, programming and manufacturing facilities.

“This is an initial stage, which primarily involves localization not only of the production component. It is also R&D, research, programming, substantial job creation and, of course, production facilities,” he said.

Nabiyev said the project is intended to develop practical applications for robotics across different sectors rather than focus primarily on entertainment.

“Our goal is for robots not to replace people. Our goal is for robots to be assistants to people,” he said.

“We are now primarily focused not on entertainment content involving robots, but on their application first of all in education and services, of which there are many, practically in all sectors, in manufacturing — robots in logistics, robots for production purposes and so on,” Nabiyev added.

Robotics to expand educational opportunities

Nabiyev also highlighted the social dimension of the project, including the development of educational robotics in Kazakhstan. According to him, Nero Group currently employs more than 200 people and has expertise in electronics manufacturing, circuit boards and specialized technologies. The company expects its workforce to grow substantially as the robotics business expands.

He added that the company is preparing to include robotics in Kazakhstan’s national register of domestic manufacturers, with the relevant technological operations and share of local content to be reflected in the registration.

Nabiyev also said educational robotics production is expected to begin in October, with an initial target of supplying nearly 30 schools in Almaty by the end of the year.

Kazakhstan–China investment ties expand

The robotics project is part of broader efforts to deepen investment cooperation between Kazakhstan and China. The Kazakhstan–China Investment Forum, organized by Kazakh Invest with the support of the Investment Committee of the Foreign Ministry, is bringing together more than 300 companies, according to Kazakh Invest Chairman Sultangali Kinzhaкulov.

“Today we are reaching a level of high-quality investment cooperation: leading investors are coming to the country, building plants, establishing production and manufacturing products with high added value,” Kinzhaкulov told The Astana Times.

He noted that the forum is being held in this format for the first time and brings together investors that are operating in Kazakhstan or planning to enter the market. Nearly 50 commercial documents are expected to be exchanged during the forum, alongside an exhibition and B2B matchmaking meetings.

The Kazakhstan-China Investment Forum was attended by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who opened the event and outlined key priorities for expanding investment and economic cooperation between the two countries.

World.title: Tokayev Calls for New Investment Model as Kazakhstan, China Deepen Economic Partnership
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan and China should move from individual investment projects toward integrated production ecosystems, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Sept. 25 at the Kazakhstan-China Investment Forum in Almaty, outlining transport, industry, critical minerals, digitalization and agriculture as key areas for deeper cooperation.

More than 600 delegates, including Chinese corporations, Kazakh businesses, government bodies and development institutions, took part in the forum. Participants also observed a minute of silence in memory of the service members who died in the Mangystau Region.

Opening the forum, Tokayev said that Chinese investment in Kazakhstan has exceeded $29 billion, while more than 9,000 enterprises with Chinese participation operate in the country. The two governments are working to increase bilateral trade to $100 billion.

“China is the main trading partner of Kazakhstan. Following the results of last year, trade turnover approached a record level of $50 billion,” Tokayev said.

He noted that the ratification of the agreement on the promotion and mutual protection of investments had strengthened the legal foundation for cooperation, while the visa-free regime was helping expand business ties.

“Under conditions of profound transformation of the global economy, Kazakhstan and China are capable of offering a modern and effective model of constructive cooperation based on mutual trust, openness and common long-term interests,” Tokayev said.

Middle Corridor remains a strategic priority

Transport and logistics featured prominently in Tokayev’s address as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its role between Chinese and European markets.

“Together with international partners, we are increasing railway capacity, expanding highways and seaports, developing cargo aviation and border infrastructure. From Lianyungang to Aktau, a network of logistics hubs has been formed, connecting the Chinese coast with the Caspian Sea,” he said.

“A new important link in the logistics network will be the Kazakh-Chinese terminal in Chengdu, where the General Consulate of Kazakhstan is planned to open. We consider the development of the Middle Corridor, which is forming a modern configuration of transport links between Asia and Europe, a priority task,” Tokayev added.

Wang Haiyan, deputy director of the Institute of Russian and Eurasian Studies and director of the Center for Kazakhstan Studies at East China Normal University, said transport and logistics remain among the areas of greatest interest to Chinese investors.

“More than half of overland transportation between China and Europe passes through Kazakhstan,” Wang said in an interview with The Astana Times, highlighting that the third cross-border railway and infrastructure supporting the Middle Corridor could further strengthen Kazakhstan’s position as a logistics hub.

From individual projects to production ecosystems

Tokayev said industrial cooperation already includes a portfolio of 260 major joint projects worth more than $62 billion.

“Together with Chinese enterprises, an automotive cluster is developing in Almaty, silicon production is being created in the Karagandy Region, and projects are being implemented in metallurgy, petrochemicals and energy-storage systems,” he said.

He also highlighted projects by Lihua, Fufeng and Dalian Hesheng Holdings involving cotton-textile production and the deep processing of corn and grain.

“This is a good foundation for moving our partnership to a new level – from implementing individual investment projects to forming full-fledged production ecosystems with joint access to the markets of Central Asian countries, the Eurasian Economic Union, the South Caucasus and Europe,” Tokayev said.

He proposed launching the Kazakh-Chinese program “Common History Destiny. Designed and Made in Both China and Kazakhstan,” with the government tasked with forming a pool of promising projects together with Chinese partners.

Wang said the shift reflects growing Chinese interest in moving beyond raw-material acquisition toward processing and deeper industrial value chains.

Critical minerals and digitalization open new opportunities

Tokayev identified the mining and metallurgical complex as another priority, noting Kazakhstan’s reserves of uranium, copper, gold, coal, critical minerals and rare-earth metals. Tokayev also highlighted digitalization, smart cities and satellite technologies.

“Kazakhstan is open to cooperation with all leading technological centers of the world,” he said.

Wang identified digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence as emerging areas for investment, including smart cities, intelligent transport, 5G and 6G infrastructure and digital logistics. She also pointed to renewable energy and water-saving agricultural technologies as areas with further potential.

Forum proposed as annual investment dialogue

Tokayev said the forum should become a permanent platform for direct interaction between the two countries’ business communities.

“I propose holding it annually in September under the name Almaty Investment Dialogue Kazakhstan–China,” he said.

Around 300 companies are participating in the forum, including investors already operating in Kazakhstan and those planning to enter the market.

The forum underscores Kazakhstan’s effort to turn its growing economic ties with China into deeper industrial, technological and logistics cooperation, with joint production and access to wider Eurasian markets becoming an increasingly important focus.

Ten agreements signed during the forum

In the presence of Tokayev, representatives exchanged 10 signed agreements covering industrial production, renewable energy, investment financing, automotive manufacturing and urban development.

Among them are agreements on an electrolytic aluminum plant and an accompanying wind power facility in the Abai Region, a 450-megawatt portfolio of wind power projects in the Akmola Region, and the joint development of an energy project involving Samruk-Energy, China Energy Overseas Investment and SANY Renewable Energy.

Other agreements provide for the creation of a specialized investment fund at the Astana International Financial Center, financing arrangements between Development Bank of Kazakhstan and China Construction Bank’s Astana branch, as well as projects in automotive manufacturing, chemical production and real estate.

World.title: Kazakhstan Launches Direct Flights From Almaty to Chongqing
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s low-cost airline FlyArystan has launched regular flights on a new route connecting Almaty with Chongqing, expanding Kazakhstan’s air connectivity with China.

The new service began on Sept. 23 and will operate twice a week, on Wednesdays and Saturdays, using Airbus A320neo aircraft, according to the Civil Aviation Committee of the Ministry of Transport.

The new service will become FlyArystan’s fifth destination in China, complementing its existing routes to Urumqi, Yining (Kulja) and Xi’an. The launch of the new route is expected to strengthen air connectivity between Kazakhstan and China and contribute to the development of trade, business, investment, tourism and cultural ties between the two countries.

The Civil Aviation Committee continues to work on expanding Kazakhstan’s international flight network and increasing the number of international routes.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Political Reform, AI Push and Investment Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest covers constitutional reform, the country’s drive to become a regional AI hub, nuclear energy cooperation, investment opportunities and Astana’s new airport project.

Kazakhstan’s new political era: Constitutional reform

EU Reporter published an article examining Kazakhstan’s post-referendum political reforms, focusing on the new Constitution, the newly elected 145-member Kurultai, the creation of the vice-presidency and People’s Council, and how these institutional changes are being linked to broader economic, technological and EU cooperation.

“Constitutional reform is not only about institutions. Its significance lies in how effectively they serve citizens, strengthen governance and contribute to the country’s development,” reads the article.

Inside Kazakhstan’s push to become a regional AI centre

Al Jazeera published an article on Sept. 21 about Kazakhstan’s rapid push to become a regional AI hub, covering its government-backed digitalisation drive, development of local AI technologies and talent, and the environmental and human-rights concerns accompanying that expansion.

One of the article’s notable examples is how Kazakhstan’s AI sector is opening new career opportunities for women. Valeria Tio, managing director of Astana Hub, said a woman who had worked as a barista at the hub found a job as a developer after one year of studying through its Tomorrow School programme, calling it “a real social elevator.” The program has trained 500 people in 18 months, while new cohorts are now being opened across 12 regions of Kazakhstan.

Kazakhstan, UK discuss cooperation in peaceful use of nuclear energy

Kazakhstan and the UK discussed prospects for cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear energy during a meeting between the Agency of Kazakhstan for Atomic Energy, Deputy Chairman Timur Zhantikin and Lord John Alderdice, the UK Prime Minister’s Trade Envoy for Central Asia, reported Trend on Sept. 22.

“The meeting discussed current issues and prospects for developing Kazakhstan-UK cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear energy,” the agency said.

Kazakhstan: A nation set to capitalise from its vast natural resources and investor appeal

Credendo released an article on Sept. 24 about Kazakhstan’s economic and investment outlook, highlighting its abundant natural resources, strong macroeconomic fundamentals and strategic position, as well as efforts to diversify through the Middle Corridor, critical minerals, infrastructure, digitalisation and AI.

“Kazakhstan is endowed with substantial commodity wealth, including oil, gas, uranium and critical minerals, leading to strong trade and investment commitments in transport and digital infrastructure, logistics, energy and critical minerals. Moreover, Astana is trading its resources against access to technologies,” reads the article.

Changi Airports to participate in construction of new airport in Kazakhstan’s Astana

Singapore’s Changi Airports International (CAI), a subsidiary of Changi Airport Group, will be involved in the construction of a new airport in Astana, according to the Astana akimat, reported Trend on Sept. 23.

The Astana akimat, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport and CAI have signed a Framework Cooperation Agreement aimed at developing a long-term strategic partnership in the field of airport infrastructure in the capital.

Under the agreement, the parties reached formal arrangements in two main areas: cooperation on the construction of a new airport in Astana and the development of the existing Astana International Airport.

World.title: India, Kazakhstan Seek to Turn Strategic Partnership Into Deeper Trade and Investment Ties
World.content:
ASTANA – India and Kazakhstan should translate their strong political partnership into deeper trade, investment, digital and energy cooperation, participants said at the India-Kazakhstan Strategic Dialogue on Sept. 24.

During the India-Kazakhstan: Anchoring Regional Stability and Economic Integration in a Multilateral World session, speakers highlighted the gap between close political ties and relatively modest bilateral trade.

Indian Ambassador to Kazakhstan Sailas Thangal said the countries need to address structural barriers limiting economic cooperation, including connectivity, logistics, customs procedures, payment mechanisms, market access and regulatory issues.

“Business delegations and exhibitions alone are not enough to enhance our bilateral trade and commerce,” he said, calling for concrete measures to turn existing potential into commercial partnerships.

“India and Kazakhstan have the trust, we have the complementarity, we have the political will. What we need now is to convert this essence into connectivity, governance and concrete partnership,” he said.

Trade remains below potential

Rakhim Oshakbayev, director of the TALAP Center for Applied Research, described the $923 million in bilateral trade in 2025 as a “long-standing anomaly.”

“Our political relationship is excellent. Many speakers talked about this. We are strategic partners,” he said.

However, he noted that logistical constraints continue to limit economic ties, describing the situation as “high politics, low logistics, big friendship, small trade.”

India accounted for around 0.64% of Kazakhstan’s total foreign trade in 2025. Oshakbayev attributed the limited trade partly to difficult transport routes.

“We are close in the sky and far on the ground,” he said, proposing greater focus on high-value goods and services that depend less on traditional transport links.

Uranium, pharmaceuticals and digital cooperation

Uranium was identified as one of the most promising areas for expanding economic ties. Oshakbayev referred to a long-term contract between Kazatomprom and India’s Department of Atomic Energy, saying press reports have valued it at more than $4 billion.

“Uranium is a perfect product for difficult geography, very high value, very small volume,” he said, proposing broader cooperation around the agreement, including training and the nuclear fuel cycle.

He also highlighted pharmaceutical production in Kazakhstan, which could serve both the domestic market and the wider Eurasian Economic Union market.

Participants identified artificial intelligence, fintech, cybersecurity, e-government and digital payments as other areas of potential cooperation, saying Indian technology companies could use Kazakhstan as a platform for accessing regional markets.

Strategic autonomy and regional cooperation

Former Indian Ambassador to Russia and former Deputy National Security Advisor Pankaj Saran said India and Kazakhstan could contribute to regional stability through diplomacy, economic development and diversified international partnerships.

“Both India and Kazakhstan maintain that independence of decision making. How can we both show to our people and to the region that we can be friends with everyone. We don’t have to choose one against the other,” he said.

Saran highlighted Kazakhstan’s balanced foreign policy and India’s strategic autonomy as areas of commonality, pointing to cooperation in regional stability, Afghanistan, peacekeeping and economic development.

He also cited growing energy requirements linked to the expansion of artificial intelligence and data centers as an area for potential cooperation.

Participants also called for stronger business, academic and people-to-people ties through joint research, healthcare, tourism and education, as well as practical cooperation in transport, energy, critical minerals, agriculture and technology.

The discussions highlighted opportunities to build on the strong political foundation of India-Kazakhstan relations by expanding trade, investment and practical economic cooperation.

World.title: ‘Unresolved issues and conflicting narratives remain’ — Pashinyan on relations with Azerbaijan
World.content:
Pashinyan’s UN address

In his address to the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan spoke about the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established. At the same time, he addressed outstanding issues that the two countries still need to resolve. These include determining the fate of several thousand missing people, carrying out demining operations and securing the return of Armenians, whom Azerbaijan holds in its prisons.

Pashinyan stressed that, beyond these issues of concern to Armenian society, conflicting narratives and discourses among certain circles in Armenia and Azerbaijan also fuel pessimism. Sometimes, officials themselves voice these views.

“I think that we, meaning Armenia and Azerbaijan, have achieved more than satisfactory results. These should mean more to us than the use of conflicting narratives, whether about history, cultural monuments or anything else,” he said.

In effect, the prime minister was responding to a recent visit by diplomats to Karabakh, which Azerbaijani authorities had organised. During the visit, officials attempted to present the Armenian monasteries of Gandzasar and Dadivank as part of “ancient Albanian Christian heritage”.

The move sparked such public outrage that many politicians called on Armenia’s leadership to issue a strong official response. Tensions between Armenia and Azerbaijan rose against this backdrop. Politicians described the situation as a serious crisis that could hinder further progress in the peace process.

Against this backdrop, Pashinyan stressed that Armenia and Azerbaijan must now focus on “safeguarding peace, strengthening it and developing its institutions”.

In his address, Pashinyan also touched on other issues of current importance to Armenia, including the implementation of the Armenian-American “Trump Route” project (TRIPP), relations with the European Union and Russia, as well as the normalisation of relations between Armenia and Turkey.

“The main item on the Yerevan-Baku agenda is signing a peace agreement”

The Armenian prime minister placed particular emphasis on the fact that no one has been killed or injured in border shootings between Armenia and Azerbaijan for the past two and a half years. He described this as “the greatest achievement of cooperation in recent years”.

“Never before have independent Armenia and independent Azerbaijan experienced such a period, despite centuries of peaceful coexistence between Armenians and Azerbaijanis,” Pashinyan said.

In his view, Yerevan and Baku must build relations between the two states on the basis of this shared experience, respecting each other’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and political independence. This is particularly important given that the two countries have already agreed on these principles and even initialled a peace treaty.

“Signing and ratifying this agreement is the next important item on Armenia and Azerbaijan’s joint agenda. We will continue to work consistently towards this goal,”

“The implementation of TRIPP promises major benefits for all countries in the region”

Pashinyan believes that the peace established between Armenia and Azerbaijan has opened up new opportunities for the entire region. He said the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project would play an important role in this process. He assured his audience that its implementation was “becoming a reality” and would mark a historic milestone for Armenia:

“For the first time since the early 1990s, Armenia will have a railway link with Azerbaijan. This will also connect it to Russia, Central Asia and China.”

The “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP) is a transport route that will connect Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory.

The prime minister stressed that Azerbaijan had opened transit routes for Armenia and that rail services between Armenia and Azerbaijan had resumed via Georgia. However, he said, the implementation of TRIPP would establish a direct railway link between Armenia and Azerbaijan:

“In the near future, we will restore the railway sections in Meghri and Yeraskh in Armenia, which existed during the Soviet era but were later destroyed. The railway routes I mentioned will then reopen.”

He said Armenia also expected to restore railway links with Turkey. Alongside TRIPP, he described this as a potential milestone in international logistics, one of the most significant developments in decades:

“This will open up a new railway connection between China, Central Asia, Turkey and the European Union.”

Pashinyan says restoring the railway link between Armenia and Azerbaijan (Nakhchivan) will establish a rail connection between the Persian Gulf and the Black Sea:

“This is an important detail because it shows why and how the implementation of TRIPP promises enormous benefits for all countries in the region. These potential benefits could become a cornerstone of long-term stability and peace, particularly between Armenia and Azerbaijan.”

According to Pashinyan, building pipelines, power lines and roads as part of TRIPP would allow not only Armenia but the entire South Caucasus to become a “crossroads of peace”.

“A plan to seize the state was drawn up”: on elections in Armenia

The prime minister also spoke about the circumstances surrounding Armenia’s recent parliamentary elections. For the second time or more, he openly accused foreign actors of interference:

“Several external and internal forces devised and carried out a plan to seize the state. They used mass disinformation, hybrid and other tools, as well as widespread distribution of election bribes.”

He stressed that Armenia’s state institutions had prevented the seizure of power thanks to their resilience. Pashinyan believes this, in turn, reflects the democratic and institutional reforms that the country has carried out in recent years:

“The people of Armenia voted for peace. And we must consistently work to further strengthen and institutionalise peace.”

Ties with the EU deepen as relations with Russia undergo transformation

Pashinyan also spoke about Armenia’s balanced foreign policy.
